scenes.title: Lantern Night

beats: On Lantern Night Tamsin and Pim cross the Chain Bridge with the crowds to watch the great clock of the Guildhall strike midnight, the clock their father built with Edwin Leckie.
Just before midnight the great clock stops dead, and the crowd turns to look at the Orrs.
Pim wants to climb the tower and look at the works at once; Tamsin takes him home to Gilt Street.
card.goal: Get Pim home before he makes things worse.

paragraphs: By ten o’clock the whole of Callowmere seemed to be on the move, and most of it was trying to cross the Chain Bridge at once. Lantern Night came once a year, on the longest night, and the city kept it the way it kept everything: loudly, in its best coat, with something hot in its hand. Tamsin Orr held her brother’s sleeve in one gloved fist and her purse in the other, and let the crowd carry them up the stone steps at the west end, where the frost had been salted and stamped to grey slush and still tried to take her feet from under her.

Gilt Street ran along the west bank of the Varrow and the Guildhall stood on the east bank, and the only way between them was the Chain Bridge. The bridge creaked on its great iron links under so many boots, and below it, on the frozen river, the lanterns had been set out in their hundreds: paper ones and tin ones and horn ones in red and amber and blue, strung along the ice road from the sledge stand under the bridge down towards the sea, so that the Varrow looked like a street of its own, lit for a wedding.
‘Smell that,’ Pim said, and stopped dead, so that a woman behind them trod on Tamsin’s heel and said something unkind about it.
‘Keep walking.’
‘Chestnuts, Tam.’
‘I can smell them. Walk.’

He walked, but his head swung round like a weathercock towards the chestnut seller at the middle of the bridge. Pim was seventeen and had grown four inches since the summer, nearly all of it in the legs, and he had their father’s fair hair and their father’s way of wanting everything he could see. Tamsin was small and neat, with her mother’s black hair in a single plait down her back and her mother’s dark brown eyes, and she had learned young to want only what she could pay for. She bought a twist of chestnuts all the same, because it was Lantern Night, and because it was cheaper than arguing.
‘Burnt,’ Pim said happily, with his mouth full. ‘Every one of them burnt. Perfect.’

Ahead of them the Guildhall rose out of the east bank like a cliff, every window lit, and above it, in its square tower, the great clock looked down on the river with its white face and gilded hands. Twelve years ago their father and Edwin Leckie had built it between them in the long workshop behind the clock-house of Orr & Leckie on Gilt Street, wheel by wheel and pinion by pinion, and carried it over this same bridge on a dray in pieces. Tamsin had been twelve. She remembered her father asleep at the bench that year with a file still in his hand.

Every Lantern Night since, the city had crossed the river to hear it strike midnight. The guild liked to say that the Orr clock had not lost a minute in twelve years, and the guild did not praise lightly.

‘Mr Leckie always stood there,’ Pim said, pointing with a chestnut at the lamp-post by the Guildhall steps. ‘Every year. He said you got the best of the bells by the lamp, because the sound came down off the tower and bounced back off the bank.’
‘I know where he stood.’
‘He ought to be here.’
‘He went away, Pim.’ She heard how short it came out and tried again, more gently. ‘He’ll come back when he comes back.’

Edwin Leckie had gone away at the end of the autumn, with one bag and no explanation worth the name, and he had not come back. He had been their father’s partner for as long as Tamsin could remember and the nearest thing to an uncle they had; he had taught Pim to hold a graver before Pim could hold a spoon. She had kept the house’s books since the winter their father died, first with Edwin looking over her shoulder and correcting her sums, and later, when there was nothing left to correct, alone, and she knew to the penny what the house could stand. It could stand a little. It could not stand very much.

The square in front of the Guildhall was packed so tight that people stood on the horse trough. Someone had pasted a printed bill to the railings beside them, with the guild’s arms at the top and a great deal of small black type underneath, and Pim bent to squint at it the way he always did at print, as if it might hold still if he caught it by surprise.
‘What’s it say?’
‘That the guild wishes the city joy of Lantern Night, and that anyone caught throwing chestnut shells on the ice will be fined a shilling.’
‘It doesn’t say that.’
‘It says something very like it.’

He grinned and let it go. Pim could take a clock apart in the dark and put it together again by touch, but letters slid about on a page for him like minnows in a stream, and he had never learned to read a word. Numbers held still for him; clock faces held still for him. He could read a dial across a crowded square faster than anyone she knew, and he did it now, tipping his head back.
‘Nine minutes,’ he said. ‘Near enough.’

The crowd knew it too. A hush came over the square in patches, the way frost comes over a window, and then broke again in laughter, and then came back. Down on the river the skaters slowed and stopped and turned their faces up. The minute hand stood a little past the ten, and Tamsin, who did not care for crowds and did not, if she was honest, care very much for bells, found that she had gone as still as everyone else, waiting for the moment when the whole city would hear the thing her father had made.
The minute hand moved. Pim counted under his breath. It moved again.
The great clock stopped at seven minutes to midnight.

Nobody noticed at first but Pim. She felt him go rigid beside her, the way a dog goes still at a sound no one else has heard, and then he said, ‘Tam,’ in a voice she had not heard from him since he was small. A man near them began to count down from seven, too soon, and a few people joined in. Then the count ran out, and the bells did not ring, and the murmur changed its note.

It took perhaps half a minute to go through the whole crowd. She watched it happen. Faces tipped up to the tower; faces tipped down again; and then, one after another, faces turned round to look for someone, and found her. That was Orr’s girl. That was Orr’s boy. She heard the name pass along the railings like a coin passed from hand to hand, Orr, Orr, the Orr clock, and nobody said anything unkind, not yet, but nobody needed to.

‘It’s the escapement,’ Pim said. ‘Or the frost’s got into the oil. Or it could be the pallets, Tam, if the cold’s shrunk the—I need to see it. I could be up there in five minutes. Less. The tower door’s round the side, and the beadle knows me—’
‘No.’
‘I’d only look.’
‘You’d have your hands in it to the elbow before anyone could stop you, and then whatever’s wrong with it would be your fault.’
‘It’s already ours,’ he said, loudly enough for everyone round them to hear, and a man in a guild collar two rows ahead turned to look at them.
That decided it. Tamsin took her brother by the arm, hard, and turned him towards the bridge.
‘We’re going home.’
‘Tam—’
‘Now, Pim. Smile at people. Walk.’

It was harder going back than coming. The whole city was facing the wrong way, and they had to push against it, through coats and elbows and wet wool, with their name following them a little way and then falling behind. On the bridge the wind came down the river from the north and cut through her shawl. Below, the lanterns on the ice went on burning, red and amber and blue, as if nothing had happened, and at the west end the steps had frozen again in the hour they had been gone, so that she had to hold the chain rail and go down sideways, with Pim talking the whole way about pallets and oil and how far a brass rod shrinks in a hard frost.

Gilt Street was dark and empty, every shop shuttered. Tamsin found the key of the clock-house by feel and got the door open, and only when she had pushed Pim inside did she let herself look back once over the rooftops at the tower on the far bank. The great clock’s face still shone white in its lamps. Its hands still said seven minutes to midnight.
Behind her in the dark hall Pim said, ‘I could have it going by morning, Tam, if they’d only let me.’
‘Go to bed, Pim.’

scenes.title: The hidden page

beats: Unable to sleep, Tamsin goes down to the counting room to look out the old ledgers for the great clock’s accounts.
In her father’s last ledger she finds a page sewn shut and cuts it open: a loan from the guild, borrowed against the house and never repaid in the guild’s books.
Under the guild’s law any house with an unpaid debt at the Reckoning is forfeit to the guild.
card.goal: Find out why the clock’s failure matters so much.

paragraphs: The house had been asleep for an hour, and Tamsin had lain awake for all of it. Pim had gone up grumbling, still talking through his door about pallets and frost, and then had fallen asleep all at once in the middle of a sentence, the way he had done since he was a baby. She had listened to the clocks. There were eleven of them in the rooms above the shop, and every one of them was right, and every one of them ticked on as if the great clock across the river had never been built, let alone stopped.
At a little after one she gave up, put her shawl over her nightgown and her boots on her bare feet, lit a candle, and went down to the counting room.

It was a narrow room behind the shop, with one window onto the yard, a high desk, a stool, and shelves from floor to ceiling of ledgers bound in brown calf. Each ledger was a year of the house. The newest were in her own small, careful hand; behind those were the years in which Edwin had kept the books with her, and behind those, high up, the years of her father, their spines lettered in faded gilt. She had not needed those in years. The accounts of a dead man do not change.

But the guild would want to know, tomorrow or the day after, who had been paid to keep the great clock, and on what terms, and whether the house of Orr & Leckie had promised more than it could keep. She wanted to know before they asked. So she climbed onto the stool with the candle in one hand and ran a finger along the high shelf until she found the year of the clock.

It was all there, as she had known it would be. Her father’s hand was square and upright and plain, like a row of fence posts, and he had written down everything: every bar of brass from the foundry, every pound of steel, every day’s wages, the dray that had carried the pieces over the bridge. She read the contract with the guild, copied out in full. The house would keep the clock in good order for as long as the house stood; the guild would pay a fee each spring for the keeping of it. Nothing about frost. Nothing about what should happen if it stopped.
She put that ledger back and, because she was there, and because she was not going to sleep anyway, took down the one beside it.

Her father’s last ledger was thinner than the others. Its entries ran through the summer and the autumn and deep into the winter, and then they stopped, a third of the way down a page, in the middle of an ordinary week. Her father had drowned eleven winters ago, when the ice gave way under him below Corran Weir, the winter Tamsin turned thirteen. After that the pages were blank, a whole fat block of them, the creamy paper gone faintly yellow at the edges. She had never been able to look at that blank for long.
She was turning back through the autumn, looking for the bells, when two of the pages would not part.

At first she thought they had stuck with damp. Then she held the book to the candle and saw the thread. Two leaves had been sewn together along all three open edges, with tiny even stitches in black silk, so close to the margins and so neatly drawn that you would turn past them as a single thick page without a second look. She looked at the stitches for a long while. They were not careless. Whoever had sewn this had meant it to stay shut, and had meant nobody to notice that it was shut.

Tamsin got down from the stool, set the ledger on the desk, and took the penknife from the drawer where she kept it for cutting quills. Her hands were perfectly steady. She slit the stitches one by one along the top and down the side and along the bottom, and pulled the loose black silk away in short curls, and opened the page.

It was her father’s hand. She would have known it anywhere. It was dated in the middle of the autumn, eleven years ago, the last autumn of his life, and it said that Aldous Orr, for the house of Orr & Leckie, had that day borrowed of the guild of Callowmere, for the casting and hanging of the bells of the great clock, the sum written below; and that the house on Gilt Street, its workshop, its stock and tools and fittings, stood pledged against the debt until it was paid. He had written the sum out in words, the way he always did, and underlined it twice.
Four hundred and twelve crowns, borrowed against the house and everything in it.
Tamsin read it three times. Somewhere above her a clock struck the quarter and the others took it up, a little ragged, as they always were.

Four hundred and twelve crowns was more money than the house had seen together in any year she had kept its books. She had known the bells had cost a great deal; she remembered the founder’s men coming up Gilt Street with their bill, and her father taking them into this room and shutting the door. She had never known how he paid them. Nobody explains such things to a girl of twelve.

Pinned behind the leaf, folded small, there was a second paper. It was thicker and greyer, guild paper with the guild’s arms printed at the head, and it was a copy of the same loan as it stood in the guild’s own books, written out in a clerk’s narrow, slanting hand. The sum was the same. The date was the same. And across the foot of it, in a different ink but the same narrow hand, someone had written: Not repaid. Carried forward.

There was no date on that line. There was nothing in her father’s ledger, before the page or after it, to say he had ever paid a penny back. She went through the autumn again, and the winter after it, entry by entry. Brass. Wages. Coal. The hire of a sledge to Hollin. Nothing to the guild. Nothing at all.
She sat down on the stool, because her knees had decided it for her.

Her mother had been a Hollin woman, and she had raised Tamsin to speak Hollish before she ever spoke the lowland tongue. When Tamsin was frightened as a child it was Hollish that came first into her head, the hill words for dark and cold and wait, and it was Hollish that came now: a line of one of her mother’s songs, about a shepherd counting sheep that would not stay counted. Her mother had died of the marsh fever when Tamsin was nine. Her father had lasted four years more, and kept them fed, and kept the house, and kept this.

On the shelf by the window, where it had always been, stood the little calf-bound book of the guild’s law. Every house kept one. She did not need to open it, but she opened it anyway and turned to the chapter on the Reckoning, because she wanted to see the words and not only remember them. They were short. When the guild sat a Reckoning, every house laid its books open before the Wardens on Thaw Day, and any house found with a debt unpaid to the guild was forfeit to the guild: house and workshop, stock and tools, the very name over the door. There was no appeal, and no time given to pay.

She thought of the faces in the square turning one by one to look at her. A clock that stops in front of the whole city on Lantern Night is not a small thing. It makes a guild want to look very closely at the house that built it. And if the guild looked closely, sooner or later it would look here.

She took out her father’s watch. It hung on its chain at her waist, where it had hung every day since the spring they buried him: a plain silver case, worn smooth at the edges by his thumb and then by hers. She pressed the catch and the lid sprang up. A.O., engraved small inside it. Twenty minutes to two. It had never lost a minute either.

No one else in the world knew about that page now but Tamsin. Whoever had sewn it shut had kept their silence for eleven years, and the guild’s clerk had written his two words and filed his copy and, for all she knew, forgotten them. Her father was eleven years in the ground. Edwin was gone away. Pim was asleep upstairs with his mouth open, dreaming of pallets and oil.

She folded the guild’s paper along its old creases and laid it back behind the leaf. She closed the ledger. Then, after a moment, she opened it again and began to read the page from the top, slowly, with her finger under each word, as if the sum might come out different if only she were careful enough.

scenes.title: The millrace

beats: Tamsin walks down to the river stairs behind the house and watches the ice in the dark.
The black water at the edge of the ice brings back the day at Ambry when she was seven.
Pim comes looking for her, full of ideas about the clock, and she decides to keep the ledger to herself.

paragraphs: The river stairs went down from the back of the yard behind the clock-house, between the dyer’s wall on one side and the old net-loft on the other, eleven worn steps to a landing stage that nobody had tied a boat to since the summer. Tamsin went down them before dawn with her shawl over her head and a lantern she did not light. She knew every step. She had gone down them in the dark a thousand times, to be alone.

The Varrow lay below her, white and wide and quiet. The night’s lanterns had burned out on the ice, all but a few far off along the bank towards the bridge that still guttered red in their paper, and the sky over the east bank was only beginning to lose its blackness. Across the river the Guildhall tower stood up against it, a darker shape on the dark.

It was colder than it had been at midnight. The frost on the rail of the landing stage stood up in little white feathers she could have blown away. She stood on the last step with the unlit lantern hanging from her hand and looked at the place where the ice met the stone.

It never quite met. There was always a gap along the foot of the river stairs, a hand’s width or two of open water where the drain from the yards came out warm and kept the river from closing. In the dark it was simply black, blacker than the sky, blacker than anything, a long slit of moving water with the ice lipped over it like a frozen mouth. She could hear it more than see it, a small busy sound, sucking at the stones.
She had never learned to swim, and since the millrace at Ambry she could not bear water above her knees.

She had been seven. It was summer, and her father had gone up to Ambry, a day north along the river, to mend the clock in the mill, and he had taken her with him because her mother was heavy with Pim that year and the house was too small for a child who would not sit still. She remembered the millrace best: a channel of stone running fast and green and narrow under the wheel, so fast that the water stood up in ridges and did not look like water at all, but like something glassy and solid that you could step on. She had wanted to see the wheel turn from close by. She had leaned out.

There had been no splash that she remembered, only the cold, which was not like any cold she had known, and the noise, which filled her head, and the green going brown and then black. She had not known which way was up. The water had not cared which way was up. It had rolled her like a pebble along the bottom of the race, and taken her shoe, and pressed her against something hard, and she had opened her mouth to scream for her father and the river had come in instead.

Then a hand in her hair. She remembered that exactly: not a hand on her arm or her collar but a fist in her hair, wound tight and hauling, so that the pain of it was the first thing that told her she was alive. A miller’s boy, flat on his belly on the stones, had seen her go in and reached down into the race and caught the only part of her he could reach, and pulled. She had never learned his name. Her father had given him a whole crown and had not been able to speak for the rest of the day.

She stood on the river stairs now, seventeen years later, and watched the black slit of water at the edge of the ice, and felt the old stupid tightness come up through her ribs. It was not fear, exactly. Fear is a thing you can argue with. This was older than argument, and it lived in her legs, and it had decided long ago that it would go no deeper into any water than her knees, and that was the end of the matter.

Her father had gone under the ice. She had always known it, the way you know a thing you were told when you were too young to hold it: that the ice had given way below Corran Weir and he had gone down into the black water under it, coming home. She had never let herself think of that with the millrace in her head at the same time. She did now, for a moment, standing there, and then she put it away again, because it did no good, and because there was a page upstairs that needed her to think.
Four hundred and twelve crowns. The guild’s clerk and his two words. She had turned it every way she could think of in the dark, and it had come out the same every time.
‘Tam?’

The yard door banged and a lantern came bobbing down the stairs behind her, too fast, swinging wildly. Pim had pulled his coat on over his nightshirt and his boots on without stockings, and his hair stood straight up on one side where he had slept on it.
‘I looked everywhere. You weren’t in bed. You weren’t in the shop.’ He stopped two steps above her, breathing white. ‘What are you doing down here? It’s perishing.’
‘Looking at the river.’

‘It’s only lying there. It does that all winter.’ He came down beside her and held up his lantern, and the light fell on the black water at the foot of the ice and showed it moving, quick and oily, and she looked away. Pim did not notice. Pim had never in his life been afraid of water; he had swum in the Varrow every summer since he was six, like an otter, and come home green with weed and whistling.

‘Listen,’ he said. ‘I’ve been thinking about it all night. I think it’s the pendulum rod. It’s steel, the rod, and steel shrinks in a hard frost, not much, but enough, and if it shrinks enough the beat goes wrong and the escapement can’t catch it, and then it just—’ He made a small, final gesture with his free hand, like a man snuffing a candle. ‘Stops. And the oil’s probably thick as honey up there. Nobody’s been up to clean it since Mr Leckie went. I could fix it, Tam. I could have it going by noon, honestly, if they’d let me up the tower.’
‘They won’t let you up the tower.’
‘They might. It’s our clock.’
‘It’s the guild’s clock. We only built it.’
‘That’s the same thing.’ He looked at her sideways in the lantern light, and something in her face must have reached him at last, because his voice changed. ‘You didn’t sleep at all, did you?’
‘A little.’

‘You look like the morning after a wake.’ He nudged her shoulder with his elbow, gently, the way he had done ever since he grew tall enough to reach it. ‘It’s only a clock, Tam. It stopped. Clocks stop. That’s what they’re for, half the time: giving clockmakers something to do.’
She laughed, which surprised her, and he looked very pleased with himself.

For a moment, standing on the stair with his warm bulk beside her, she nearly told him. It would have been so easy. She could feel the words lining up behind her teeth: Pim, I found something in Father’s ledger. He would listen; he always listened. And then he would go straight up Gilt Street and tell the baker, and the baker’s wife, and the boy who swept the bridge, and anyone else who stood still long enough, not out of malice but because Pim believed that a trouble shared with the whole street was a trouble halved. When she turned twenty he had told every shop between here and the bridge what he was giving her for her birthday, a fortnight before he gave it.
She would not tell Pim; Pim could no more keep a secret than a sieve could keep water.

It was not his fault. It was only how he was made, the same as his long hands and his quick eyes. But it meant that whatever came next, she would have to do it by herself, and do it before anyone guessed there was anything to be done.
‘Come on,’ she said. ‘I’ll make porridge.’
‘With treacle?’
‘With what’s left of the treacle.’

He went up the stairs ahead of her two at a time, the lantern swinging, already talking again about steel and frost and how he would want the long-nosed oil can, and the soft brushes. Tamsin followed more slowly, with one hand closed round her father’s watch, and did not look back at the water.
‘And the little mirror on the stick,’ Pim called down from the top. ‘For seeing round the back of the wheels. Tam, are you listening? We’ll want the mirror—’

scenes.title: The Warden of the Wharf

beats: The guild summons the house of Orr & Leckie, and Tamsin and Pim cross the Chain Bridge to answer.
Corvin Slade calls the stopped clock the house’s shame and announces that the Reckoning will sit at noon on Thaw Day, with every house’s books laid open.
Slade asks after Edwin Leckie and observes that without Leckie’s key the house cannot even open its own deeds.
Pim is given leave to look at the clock’s works but not to touch them.
card.goal: Find out what the guild means to do.

paragraphs: The summons came at ten, in the hand of a guild runner in a blue coat who would not come in out of the cold and would not wait for an answer. It was sealed with the guild’s arms in green wax and addressed to the house of Orr & Leckie, not to any person in it. Pim turned it over in his long fingers and then held it out to her without a word, the way he held out everything with writing on it.
‘The Warden of the Wharf requires the attendance of the house at the Guildhall at noon,’ she read. ‘In the matter of the great clock.’
‘The Warden himself?’
‘So it says.’
‘Then he’ll let me up.’ Pim’s face lit like a lamp. ‘He must, Tam. Who else is going to mend it?’

She did not answer that. She went upstairs and put on her good grey dress and her good dark coat and did her plait again, tighter. At her belt, on its own short chain beside her father’s watch, hung the Orrs’ key to the guild vault: a long iron key with a bow shaped like a clock-wheel, which she had worn every day for eleven years and never once had cause to use.

They crossed the Chain Bridge at half past eleven. In daylight it was only a bridge again, grey and creaking, swept by a wind that came straight down the river from the hills. The steps at the west end had iced in the night into a long glassy slope. Tamsin went up them holding the chain rail with both hands, a step at a time. Pim went up beside her as if they were dry; he had legs like a heron and the balance of a cat.
Below them, at the ice-road stand, the sledge drivers were harnessing their dogs, and the yapping came up to them. Nobody on the bridge looked twice at the Orrs. That, Tamsin thought, was something.

The Guildhall was warmer than the street and smelt of beeswax and old paper. A clerk met them in the hall and took them up a broad stair and along a passage hung with the portraits of dead Wardens, and showed them through a tall door at the end.
Corvin Slade, Warden of the Wharf, received them in the long room under the clock.

It ran the whole width of the tower, with windows on three sides and a fire at one end that did not seem to reach the other. Overhead, through the boards of the ceiling, Tamsin could feel more than hear the presence of the great clock: its bulk and its stillness, like a held note. Slade stood at a table by the middle window with the light behind him. He was a tall man, and thin, in a black coat, perhaps fifty-five, with grey hair brushed close to a narrow head.
‘Miss Orr,’ he said. ‘Master Orr. Thank you for coming so promptly. Please, sit, if you would.’

His voice was low and very courteous. His eyes were a pale, washed blue, like ice over shallow water. They rested on Tamsin’s face for a moment, then on Pim’s, then came back to Tamsin and stayed there, as if he had already decided which of them was worth his attention.

He came round the table to draw out a chair for her himself, and she saw why he had not come forward to meet them. He leaned on a silver-headed cane and favoured his right knee, which had been stiff since a fall on the wharf steps years before. He managed it so smoothly that it was almost a kind of grace, the cane going down a half-beat before the bad leg every time. Tamsin sat. Pim stood behind her chair, staring up at the ceiling.

‘I shall not keep you long,’ Slade said, settling himself again behind the table. ‘You know why you are here. Last night, before the whole city, on the one night of the year when the whole city is watching, the great clock of this guild stopped.’
‘The clock is twelve years old,’ Tamsin said. ‘It has never stopped before.’

‘No. That is why it was remarked.’ He laid his long white hands flat on the table. ‘I will not pretend with you, Miss Orr. It was the house’s shame. Your father’s name is on that clock; every child in Callowmere knows it. When it fails, it is not the guild they look at.’

‘The guild has been patient with a great many houses these last years,’ he went on. ‘Too patient, some of the Wardens feel. I have therefore been instructed, and I will tell you frankly that I agree with the instruction, that the Reckoning will sit this year. At noon on Thaw Day, in this hall, every house of the guild will lay its books open before the Wardens. Every house. Every book.’
‘Thaw Day,’ Tamsin said. Her voice came out level, which pleased her.
‘Six weeks and more. Time enough, I should think, for any well-kept house to put its affairs in order.’ He smiled slightly. ‘You keep the books of Orr & Leckie yourself, I understand.’
‘I do.’

‘Since your father’s death. And he kept them very carefully before you, of course. A careful man, Aldous Orr.’ The pale eyes did not move from her face. ‘I am sure there is nothing in your father’s books to trouble anyone. Old accounts can be awkward things at a Reckoning. A sum written down and never crossed out. But I am sure that is not so with yours.’
Tamsin thought of black silk curling away under her penknife, and of two words in a clerk’s narrow hand, and kept her face perfectly still. Behind her she heard Pim shift his feet.
‘Our books are in order,’ she said.
‘I am delighted to hear it. And Master Leckie? I had hoped he might come with you today. It is his house too, after all. His name is over your door.’
‘Mr Leckie is away.’
‘Still?’ Slade raised his brows, very slightly. ‘Upriver, I heard. In the hills.’
Leckie had gone upriver in the autumn to his sister in Hollin, and no word had come back from him since. Tamsin had written twice and heard nothing.
‘He is with his sister,’ she said. ‘He’ll be home when the weather allows.’

‘I hope so, for your sake.’ Slade leaned back, and the cane, propped against the edge of the table, gave off a small silver gleam. ‘You will know, of course, that your house’s deeds lie in the guild vault, with those of every other house on Gilt Street. That does mean, I am afraid, that without Master Leckie’s key your house cannot even open its own deeds. Should anyone have need to see them. At a Reckoning, for instance.’

The guild vault would open only to two keys turned together: the Orrs’ key, which hung at Tamsin’s belt, and Edwin Leckie’s, which had gone north with him. She felt hers heavy against her hip, iron and useless, and was aware that Slade’s eyes had gone down to it and come back.
‘I hadn’t thought anyone would need to,’ she said.
‘No. One doesn’t, until one does.’
The fire ticked in the grate. Above them the great clock hung in its frame, saying nothing at all.
‘Sir,’ Pim said. ‘Please. May I see the works?’
Slade looked up at him as if he had forgotten he was there.

‘I know that clock,’ Pim went on. ‘I was only five when they put it up, but I’ve seen every drawing, sir, I know every wheel in it. I think it’s the pendulum rod, or the oil, or both. If I could only look, I could tell you what’s wrong with it inside an hour. Less.’
‘Pim,’ Tamsin said.

But Slade had raised one hand, and was considering her brother with something that was very nearly amusement. ‘You may look, Master Orr,’ he said at last. ‘You may not touch. Not a wheel, not a pin, not a drop of oil. The guild has engaged no one to repair its clock, and until it does, the clock will stay exactly as it is.’ He rang a small brass bell on the table, and the clerk appeared at the door as though he had been waiting with his hand on it. ‘Take Master Orr up to the clock room. He is to look and not to touch. If he so much as lays a finger on the works, bring him down.’
‘Thank you, sir,’ Pim said, and was through the door before Tamsin could catch his sleeve, his boots loud on the tower stair.
Slade watched him go. Then he turned his pale eyes back to her and smiled, and for the first time the smile went very nearly as far as them.
‘A gifted boy,’ he said. ‘His father’s hands, everyone says so. It would be a great pity, Miss Orr, if he were to find himself with nowhere left to use them.’
Tamsin stood up. Her knees held, which she had not been sure of. ‘Good day, Warden.’
‘Good day, Miss Orr.’ He was already reaching for his pen. ‘Six weeks and more. Do give my regards to Master Leckie, when he comes home.’

scenes.title: The bridge steps

beats: Tamsin crosses to the Guildhall to see the vault for herself, and the clerk says the deeds cannot be shown without both keys.
Coming back over the Chain Bridge she slips on the iced steps at the west end.
A bargeman helps her up and walks her to the bonesetter on Gilt Street.

paragraphs: Two days after Lantern Night the great clock of Callowmere still said seven minutes to midnight, and the east bank had already learned not to look at it. Tamsin looked. She crossed under the Guildhall tower soon after eight with the Orrs’ key on her belt and a copy of the sewn page folded small inside her glove, written out in her neatest hand. Somewhere in a sleepless night she had decided that she would see the deeds of her own house with her own eyes before she believed anything more about them.

The vault clerk kept a high desk at the foot of the cellar stairs, behind a brass rail that generations of waiting elbows had rubbed to the colour of butter. He was a young man with a scrubbed pink face and beautiful cuffs, and he heard her out with his quill held politely aloft, as if he might at any moment write down something she said.
‘Orr and Leckie, Gilt Street,’ Tamsin finished. ‘I don’t ask to take anything away. I ask to read one paper, in your sight, by your lamp. You may stand at my elbow the whole while.’

‘I should be glad to, Mistress Orr, but the deeds of every house in the guild lie behind the same door, and that door opens to two keys turned together, or it does not open at all. Yours is one.’ He nodded at her belt, where the key hung heavy against her hip. ‘Master Leckie’s is the other.’
‘Master Leckie is not in the city.’

‘So the Warden told us.’ He looked truly sorry about it, which was worse. ‘Without both keys, the deeds cannot be shown. Not to you, not to me, not to the Warden himself. It is the whole virtue of the arrangement that nobody has.’

She tried the register, and he showed her the register: a vast calf-bound book in which some clerk long dead had written, against the name of her house, the two words Deeds held, and nothing more. She tried, heaven help her, being charming, which had never once worked for her and did not start working now. The clerk received it with the same grave courtesy he had given everything else.
‘Bring me Master Leckie and his key,’ he said at last, ‘and I shall carry the lamp down myself.’

She went up the cellar stairs and out into a wind that came straight down the river from the north, smelling of nothing at all, which meant more snow by night. On the Guildhall steps she composed, too late, all the things she ought to have said to the young man with the cuffs, and every one of them was cleverer than anything she had managed underground.

What she had wanted, she admitted to herself, crossing the square, was not the deed at all. She had wanted a second piece of paper to argue with the first. Her father’s hand on the sewn page said four hundred and twelve crowns, borrowed against the house that autumn to pay for the bells of the great clock. The guild’s books said the same, and said it had never been paid. She had wanted the deed to say something else, anything else, a condition or a clause or a date, some small dull thing a bookkeeper could take hold of. Instead she had a key that opened half a door.

The Chain Bridge carried her back over the river on its great black links, each one furred with frost as thick as a cat’s coat. Below, the Varrow lay white and still from bank to bank, scored with runner tracks, and on the ice just downstream the drivers at the ice-road stand had their braziers lit and their dogs out, a long scribble of noise and smoke. She was doing sums. Leckie and his key were gone north, and Leckie, by every sign, did not mean to come home. The Reckoning would sit on Thaw Day regardless. The books of Orr & Leckie would be laid open on the long table with every other house’s, and the sewn page would be read out in her father’s own hand.

The west end of the bridge came down to the Gilt Street side by a flight of broad stone steps, worn hollow in the middle by two hundred years of feet. In winter they held ice, black and glassy, and the sand the bridge-wardens threw down each morning had blown off again by nine. Tamsin knew this. She went down them anyway, the way she went down everything when she was angry: quickly, looking at nothing, chin tucked into her collar, with the sentence she should have said to the clerk going round in her head like a wheel.
The third step from the top took her feet clean away.

There was no slither and no warning, no moment of grabbing at the air. One instant she was upright and furious and the next the sky was where the steps had been and she was coming down on her back with her skirts round her knees and her hood over her eyes. She put out a hand to save herself. Everybody does. She heard the bone in her right wrist go with a small, dry snap.
Then she slid the rest of the way, five more steps on her backside, bumping like a sack of coal off a cart, and fetched up at the bottom against the iron boot-scraper with her boots in the air.

For a little while there was no pain at all, only a vast astonishment. A woman selling hot chestnuts at the bridge foot laughed, then stopped laughing. A dog came and sniffed Tamsin’s ear. She lay looking up at the frosted chains and thought quite clearly that she must get up before anybody from Gilt Street saw her. Then she tried to push herself up, and the pain arrived all at once, as if it had been waiting politely round a corner.

It went up her arm to the elbow in a white sheet. She made a noise she had not known she owned and sat up holding the wrist against her chest with her other hand. Through the glove she could feel that it was the wrong shape. Only a little, a step in the line of it where there should have been none, the way a cracked plate still looks like a plate until you turn it to the light.
It was her right hand, the one she wrote with.

That was the first sensible thought she had, and it frightened her more than the pain. All the books of the house were in that hand. Eleven years of her father’s figures copied fair, and her own since, the wages book, the day book, the letters to the guild. Forty-four days until Thaw Day, and every one of them wanting a pen.
‘Here,’ said a voice above her. ‘Don’t you try and stand on your own, you’ll only go again.’

He was a bargeman, or had been until the river shut; she could tell by the tarred canvas coat and the way he stood on the slick stones as if they were a deck. He had big red hands, a muffler wound up to his nose, and eyebrows white with frost. He got an arm under her good side and lifted her to her feet as easily as a coil of rope, and held her there while the bridge foot tilted and came level again.
‘That’s broke,’ he said, looking at the way she held her arm. ‘I heard it go from up top.’
‘It’s nothing. I can walk.’

‘You can, and you will, but not home.’ He turned her gently, the way a man turns a boat, towards the mouth of Gilt Street. ‘There’s a bonesetter along here. Old Fane. He did my boy’s collarbone, and never charged what it was worth.’

She did not argue, which told her a good deal about the state of her. They went along Gilt Street at the bargeman’s pace, his hand under her good elbow. The clockmakers’ signs creaked overhead, gilt hands and gilt suns and one great gilt key, and every shop window had its row of faces showing the right time, as if to make a point to the tower across the river. At the clock-house of Orr & Leckie the shutters were half down and a lamp was lit at the back bench. She could see the top of Pim’s fair head bent over something small and bright.
‘Walk on this side,’ she said, and moved so that the bargeman’s bulk was between her and the window.

He looked down at her and then across at the clock-house, and whatever he thought of it he kept to himself. He only shifted over, so that his broad back filled the view, and said something about the weather that needed no answer.

Hesketh Fane’s shop stood further along, a narrow front with small greenish panes in the window and a brass mortar hanging over the door. The bargeman pushed the door open with his shoulder. A bell jangled somewhere inside, and the warm smell of camphor rolled out to meet them.
‘Mind the step,’ called an old voice from the back of the shop, and Tamsin, to her own horror, began to laugh.

scenes.title: Hesketh Fane

beats: Hesketh Fane, the old bonesetter, sets Tamsin’s wrist and binds it in a splint.
He asks what has frightened her worse than the fall, and she tells him about the hidden page.
Fane talks of his late wife Elsbet, who came from the hills and loved the snowbells of Hollin; Tamsin makes him a promise.
card.goal: Get the wrist set; decide to go north.

paragraphs: Hesketh Fane would not set the bone until the middle of the afternoon. He made her sit through the dinner hour in the chair by his back-room fire with her arm propped on a cushion and a cup of something bitter inside her, willow bark and poppy and a taste like old pennies, because a bone, he said, was like a tradesman with a grievance: it went back best when it had stopped shouting.

By three the room had soft edges. Fane drew his stool up to her knee. He was a thin old man, stooped as a heron, with white whiskers that stood out from his cheeks like frost on a hedge and sleeves rolled up over forearms like knotted string. He had been her father’s friend for thirty years. She had never once seen him hurry.
‘Look at the kettle,’ he said.

She looked at the kettle. He took her hand in both of his and pulled, a long steady draw and a turn, and something in her wrist ground and slid and settled, and the room went white and then came back with the kettle still in it.
‘There,’ said Fane mildly. ‘That’s the worst of it done. You may call me whatever you like now. Aldous used to.’

He bound it while she sat with her eyes shut. She felt the lint go on, soft as wool, and then two thin slats of limewood laid along the inside and outside of her forearm, from the knuckles nearly to the elbow, and then the linen winding round and round, firm and even, the way he would have bandaged a clock spring if clock springs bled. Last of all he knotted an old grey shawl into a sling and settled the whole thing against her chest.
‘A month in the splint,’ Fane said, ‘and no lifting with that hand till Thaw Day.’
‘A month,’ said Tamsin, opening her eyes.

‘At the least. It was a clean break, and you’re young. Another inch and we’d be talking of spring.’ He sat back on his stool and wiped his hands on a cloth. ‘You’ll do everything with the left. Eating, buttoning, washing your face. It will make you cross.’
‘I keep the books of the house. I can’t keep them with my left hand. My left hand writes like a hen walking through ink.’
‘Then the hen must learn,’ said Fane, ‘or the books must wait.’

She said nothing to that. She looked at the fire. The poppy made her slow, and she found that she was turning the same few figures over and over without meaning to, the way a tongue goes back to a loose tooth. Four hundred and twelve. Forty-four days. One key. The shop was very quiet. Somewhere at the front a shelf clock ticked, a good plain movement her father had made, she thought, and a pot of something simmered on the hob and smelt of cloves.

‘I’ve set a great many bones on Gilt Street,’ Fane said after a while, ‘and most people, when it’s done, look at the arm. You’ve looked at the floor since you came in, like a girl adding a column that won’t come right. Something frightened you before you ever got onto that bridge. Something worse than the fall.’
‘The bridge-wardens,’ Tamsin said, ‘for not sanding the steps.’

He waited. He had a gift for waiting; it came, perhaps, of so many years spent beside people who did not want to say where it hurt. The fire settled. The shelf clock ticked. And Tamsin, who had held it shut inside her for two days and two nights like the sewn page itself, found that she could not hold it any longer, not with her arm on a cushion and the camphor in her nose and this old man looking at her the way he had looked at her when she was nine and her mother had just died.
So she told him: the ledger, the sewn page, the four hundred and twelve crowns.

She told it badly, out of order. How she had sat up with the ledger on Lantern Night after the clock stopped, because she could not sleep and the figures were the only thing that would stand still. How she had found the page sewn shut along all three edges in black silk, by whose hand she could not say. How the entry said the money had been borrowed from the guild that autumn, eleven years ago, against the house itself, to pay for the great clock’s bells. How nowhere in the ledger, nowhere at all, was there a line to say it had been paid back. The Warden in his long room under the clock, courteous as a knife, announcing the Reckoning on Thaw Day. The clerk this morning with his beautiful cuffs. Master Leckie gone north with the other key, without a word to anyone.
‘And Pim?’ Fane asked, when she had stopped.

‘Pim doesn’t know. He mustn’t.’ She heard her own voice sharpen and could not help it. ‘He would be sorry, and kind, and he would tell the lamplighter before supper and the whole wharf by morning. Not out of malice. He has never had a secret in his life that stayed one past the end of the street.’
‘No,’ Fane agreed, and his whiskers moved in something that was not quite a smile. ‘He has not.’
He got up and poured two cups of the clove stuff from the pot on the hob, and put one into her left hand and folded her fingers round it.

‘I remember the autumn of the bells,’ he said. ‘Your father came in here with a gash across his thumb from the bell-frame and talked of nothing but bronze for an hour while I stitched it. He was worried about money. Every clockmaker is worried about money, but he was worried that year.’ He turned his cup. ‘I can’t tell you what he did or didn’t pay, Tamsin. I can tell you that Aldous paid the coal man the day the coal came, and never in his life owed a man a penny past its time if he could help it. If he sewed that page shut, I don’t know why. But I don’t believe it was shame.’
It was not proof. It was not anything a Reckoning would hear. But it was the first thing anyone had said in two days that was on her side, and she had to look at the kettle again for a moment.
‘Edwin will know,’ Fane said. ‘Where has he gone?’
‘North. To his sister, I think. Bettany. She lives in Hollin.’

‘Hollin.’ He said the word as if it were a coin he had not handled for a long time. His eyes went past her to the shelf above the fire, where a little blue pot stood empty except for a crust of old earth. ‘Elsbet came from the hills, you know. Not from Hollin itself, but near enough to walk to chapel there on feast days when she was a girl.’
‘I remember her,’ Tamsin said. ‘She gave me barley sugar.’

‘She gave everyone barley sugar. It was how she made friends in a city she never much liked.’ He nodded at the blue pot. ‘Every autumn she would plant a snowbell bulb in that, and every spring it came up blind, or not at all. City air, she said. City water. In Hollin they flower under the snow in the last of the winter, little pale bells hanging their heads, and you find them by the green they make beneath the crust before ever you see a flower. She used to say the whole valley above the town smelt of them on a still morning.’ He was quiet a moment. ‘I always meant to take her up to see them. There was always next year. She died three winters ago, and now I’m too old to sit on a sledge for four days and too stiff to climb a hill when I got there.’

Tamsin set down her cup. The fire was warm on her face and the splint was heavy on her chest, and inside her the figures had stopped turning and lay down in a row, the way they did at the end of a long column when the total finally came right. Leckie had the other key. Leckie had gone to Hollin. She had her mother’s tongue, and a left hand, and forty-four days. Nobody was going to bring Edwin Leckie home for her.
‘How long does the ice road stay open?’ she asked.

Fane looked at her for a long moment, and then at the sling, and then at her face again. Whatever he had been going to say about splints and lifting and sitting quietly by the fire till Thaw Day, he did not say it.
‘You’re very like him,’ was all he said. ‘He never could leave a thing half mended either.’
‘I’ll bring you a snowbell from Hollin,’ Tamsin said. ‘I promise.’

‘Bring yourself back first,’ said Fane, ‘with both arms on. Then we’ll talk about flowers.’ And he took the empty cup out of her hand and went to see to the kettle, and, she thought, to wipe his eyes.

scenes.title: The pigeon loft

beats: Tamsin climbs to the guild pigeon loft to ask Orla Finch how she could send word home from the north.
Orla explains how guild pigeons fly, and the rules no pigeon breaks.
Orla gives her birds from the Callowmere loft in a wicker basket, and asks no questions.
card.goal: A way to send word home.

paragraphs: The guild pigeon loft sat on the roofs above the west wharf like a hat on a tall man, and the way up to it had plainly been designed by someone who expected visitors to have two hands. There was an outside stair, steep and iced, and then a walkway along the roof leads with a rope for a rail, and then a ladder. Tamsin went up the stair with her shoulder to the wall, crossed the leads one step at a time with her good hand on the rope, and stood at the foot of the ladder looking at it for some while on the fourth morning after Lantern Night, her breath going up in clouds.
‘If you mean to climb that with one arm,’ said a voice from above, ‘you’ll break the other one, and then where will you be?’

A head looked down at her out of the loft door: a square, weathered face, grey-streaked hair cropped short as a boy’s, a leather apron. Orla Finch had kept the guild birds since before Tamsin was born, and had a name on the wharf for saying exactly what she thought and then giving you her last bit of bread.

‘Stay there,’ said Orla, and came down the ladder herself, backwards and quick, and went up again behind Tamsin with one hand flat between her shoulder blades the whole way, so that there was nowhere to fall but forwards. At the top she hauled her in over the sill by her good arm like a sack of meal and set her on her feet.

The loft was warm after the wind, and dim, and full of the soft throaty talk of birds. Nest boxes ran in rows along both walls, a hundred of them or more, and in nearly every one a pigeon sat puffed up against the cold and watched her with one orange eye. It smelt of grain and dust and feathers and something sharper underneath that Tamsin decided not to think about. At the far end a little window looked east across the river, and through it she could see the Guildhall tower, and the great clock’s face, and its hands still standing at seven minutes to midnight.
‘Your father mended my trap bell,’ Orla said, following her look. ‘And my clock, the winter before the bells. Never sent a bill. What do you want?’

‘If a person were going north,’ Tamsin said, in the words she had rehearsed on the stair, ‘up the river, a good long way, for some weeks, and wanted to send word home. Could it be done with birds? And how?’
Orla did not ask which person, or why. She took a pigeon out of the nearest box, as easily as taking an apple off a shelf, and held it against her apron with its wings folded under her fingers.
‘They fly by daylight and never after dark,’ Orla said, ‘and only ever home to this loft. Nowhere else, not for any money.’
‘Only here?’

‘That’s the whole of it. People think a pigeon’s like a postboy, that you can tell it where to go. You can’t. It goes where it lives. This one was hatched in that box there, and wherever you let it go, Ambry or Corran or the far end of Lake Dun, it’ll turn round in the air twice and come straight back to that box, because that’s home.’ She stroked the bird’s grey head with one thick finger. ‘So you can send to us. Nobody can send to you. Get that into your head now, so you don’t stand on some riverbank a week from here waiting for an answer that can’t come.’
‘And the dark?’

‘Never in the dark. Let one go at dusk and it’ll sit on the first roof it finds and the owls will have it by midnight, or it’ll set off and lose itself and you’ll never see it again. Mornings, if you can. The earlier the better, so it has the whole of the light to get home in. They’ll fly in frost, and in a fair wind, and against a fair wind if they have to. They won’t fly in a blizzard, and they won’t fly at night, and there’s no bird in this loft or any other that will, whatever anybody tells you in an inn.’

She put the pigeon back in its box, and it shuffled and settled as if nothing had happened, and Orla went to a shelf under the window and came back with a little tin tube no longer than Tamsin’s smallest finger, a scrap of paper thin as an onion skin, and a stub of pencil.

‘The message goes in this,’ she said, ‘rolled tight, and the tube ties to the leg here, above the foot, with waxed thread. Not to the wing, whatever the storybooks say. A bird with a thing tied to its wing is a bird in the river.’ She held out the pencil. ‘Write me something. Let’s see what we’re dealing with.’

Tamsin took the pencil in her left hand. It felt like holding a spoon with her foot. She bent over the shelf and wrote, slowly, the first thing that came into her head, which was all well, and the letters came out tall and short by turns, leaning on one another like drunk men going home. The double l in well staggered right off the line. She looked at it with loathing.

‘I’ve had worse from the Warden’s own clerks,’ said Orla, who was looking at it with interest, ‘and they’ve two good hands apiece. Write small, write plain, and don’t try to be clever. Nobody up here wants your fine phrases. Who’s to read it at this end?’
Tamsin hesitated. It was a small hesitation, but Orla saw it.

‘Your brother,’ she said. ‘And your brother can’t read. I know that.’ She said it the way she might have said that Pim was tall, or fair, or fond of currant buns. ‘He came up here last spring to look at the trap bell after your father’s work wore out, and he told me so himself before he’d got his coat off, cheerful as you like. Letters slide about on him, he said. Then he read that clock over there to the minute from the other end of the loft, and told me it was losing two a day and why.’
‘He reads numbers perfectly,’ Tamsin said. ‘Faces, figures. It’s only words.’
‘Well, then.’
‘Anything that comes, I’ll read to your brother myself,’ Orla said.
Tamsin found that her throat had closed up for no good reason, and she was glad of the dim light. She nodded.

Orla went along the boxes, choosing, and talking to the birds under her breath as she went, a low steady mutter that was half scolding and half something gentler. She lifted one out and looked at its eye and its feet and put it back. She lifted another and kept it. In the end Orla gave her three of them in a wicker basket with a leather strap, enough for three messages home.

‘Corn once a day, a handful between them, no more,’ Orla said, buckling the lid. ‘Water every morning, and break the ice on it first. Keep the basket out of the wind but don’t smother it; they’ll suffocate under a blanket quicker than they’ll freeze in the open. Don’t let them get wet. Don’t let a dog near them. Don’t let anybody tell you they’re good eating.’ She held the basket up so Tamsin could see in through the weave: three round shapes in the straw, shifting, murmuring. ‘Tubes and thread and paper are in the pocket on the side. If you lose the pencil, use a burnt stick. It’ll read.’

Tamsin waited for the question. She had braced herself for it all the way up the stair: where are you going, and why now, in the dead of winter, with your arm in a sling and the Reckoning coming. Everybody on Gilt Street had been asking her something for five days, with their eyes if not their mouths.
Orla asked nothing at all. She only settled the strap over Tamsin’s good shoulder, so that the basket hung at her left hip, and tugged it once to see that it sat right.
‘What do I owe the loft?’ Tamsin asked.

‘Your house pays its loft dues on quarter day like everybody else’s, and your father mended my clock for nothing. We’re square.’ Orla went to the door and looked down at the ladder, and then back at Tamsin with the basket and the sling, and sighed through her nose. ‘I’ll go first this time. If you fall, fall on me. And mind you bring my birds back to me, one way or another.’

scenes.title: The Long Patience

beats: At the ice-road stand on the frozen river below the Chain Bridge, Tamsin looks for a driver willing to go all the way to Hollin.
Kit Ansel, a sledge driver from Dunmere, agrees to take her for half the fare now and half in Hollin.
Pim comes down to see the dogs, and Tamsin tells him she is going to fetch Master Leckie home for the Reckoning, and nothing more.

paragraphs: The ice-road stand on the afternoon of the seventh day was the busiest place in Callowmere, and the loudest. It lay on the frozen river just below the Chain Bridge, a broad trampled square of grey ice marked out with poles and lanterns, and from one end of it to the other there were sledges: coal sledges and ore sledges and sledges stacked with barrels and salt fish. There were braziers every few yards, and men stamping round them, and a woman selling hot cider out of a copper can on her back. There were dogs everywhere, yelping, singing, fighting, sleeping curled nose to tail on the ice with frost on their backs, and over all of it hung the great black chains of the bridge and the smell of woodsmoke and dog.

The Varrow ran south out of the hills to the sea, and in deep winter it froze hard enough to be a road. Every child in Callowmere knew that, and knew too that the road ran only one way that mattered: north, upriver, past Ambry and Corran Weir and over Lake Dun, towards the hills where the river began. Tamsin stood at the edge of the stand with the cold coming up through her boot soles and looked at the long white road going away between the banks. It seemed a great deal longer from down here than on a map.
She had been at it an hour, and she had a list of refusals.

‘Ambry, yes,’ the first driver said. ‘Corran, if you pay for the dogs’ meat.’ The second would go as far as Dunmere and no further, and said so twice. The third, an old man with a face like a walnut, took his pipe out of his mouth to laugh at her. Past Dunmere the river widened into the lake and then stopped being any use, he said, and the road up the valley to Hollin was no road at all in winter, only rock and drift and a town that shut its doors in your face in a language you couldn’t understand.
‘I understand the language,’ Tamsin said.
‘Then you won’t need me,’ said the old man, and put his pipe back in.

She found Kit Ansel at the downstream end of the stand, sitting on the backboard of a long, low sledge with a dog’s harness across his knees and an awl in his hand, laughing at something. The something turned out to be a small rough-coated dog who had got the end of a strap in her teeth and was walking backwards with it, growling, while he held on to the other end and made no great effort to win. He was a big man, broad as a door, with a short brown beard and a sheepskin cap pushed back on his head, and when he looked up at her his eyes were grey and amused.
‘You’re the lady asking for Hollin,’ he said. ‘The whole stand’s heard about you. The old fellow with the pipe thinks you’re mad.’
‘Tobias is welcome to his opinion. Will you go?’

‘I’m from Dunmere,’ he said. ‘I’m going home tomorrow anyway, with nothing to carry but my own dinner. Hollin’s past my door, but not so far past.’ He let the little dog have the strap, and she trotted off with it in triumph. ‘What’s in Hollin?’
‘A man I need to fetch home.’

He waited, in case there was more, and when there was not he only nodded, as if that were as good a reason as any for crossing a frozen country in the dead of winter. Tamsin liked him a little for it, and distrusted herself for liking him.
‘Four days north to Hollin on the ice,’ Kit said, ‘if the ice holds and the dogs don’t sulk.’

He named a price. Tamsin, who had not kept the books of a clock-house for eleven years for nothing, named a smaller one, and pointed out that he was going as far as Dunmere regardless. He laughed, a big easy laugh that made two of the dogs look round, and named a middling one. They settled on half the fare now and half in Hollin, and she counted the first half out of her purse with her left hand, slowly, the coins sticking to her glove, while he watched without offering to help, which she liked him for too.

Kit ran six dogs: Hob in the lead, then Fen and Bracken, Sloe and Rusk, and little Tansy at the back by the runners. He named them for her one by one, and each in turn looked up at the sound of its name, Hob last and most gravely, as a leader should. Rusk, Kit said, had the best nose and the worst manners on the river, and Fen and Bracken would fight each other all night and pull together all day. Tansy was the little thief with the strap. She was half the size of the others and came and leaned her whole weight against Tamsin’s shins, as if they had known each other for years.
The sledge was called the Long Patience; the name was burned into its backboard in square black letters.

Tamsin looked at the words for a moment. It was an odd name for a sledge. Most of those on the stand were called Swift or Lucky or after somebody’s wife. But she was carrying a reason of her own north that she had no intention of explaining to this man, and it seemed to her only fair that he should keep his.
‘You’ll not be driving with that arm,’ he said instead, nodding at the sling. ‘You’ll ride in the basket under the skins and keep your mouth shut on the hills. Can you do that?’
‘The first part,’ Tamsin said.
‘And they speak the hill tongue up there, in Hollin,’ he said, grinning. ‘The old fellow says you claim to have it.’
‘My mother was a Hollin woman.’
‘That’s as well.’ Kit had no Hollish beyond ‘thank you’ and ‘how much’, and he said so cheerfully. ‘Which gets a man fed,’ he added, ‘and no further. You’ll have to do the rest of the talking.’

There was a shout from the river stairs, and Tamsin knew it before she turned round. Pim came down onto the ice at a run, all elbows and knees, his scarf flying out behind him and his fair hair sticking out from under his cap. He was seventeen and had grown four inches since the summer, and had not yet worked out where all of them were. On the way across the stand he said good afternoon to the cider woman, asked the old man with the pipe how his chest was, slipped, saved himself on a stranger’s sledge and stopped to admire the stranger’s bindings, and arrived beside Tamsin out of breath and beaming.

‘Old Fane said you’d be here. Are these yours?’ He had already dropped to his knees among the dogs, and Hob, who did not care for strangers, was allowing his ears to be rubbed. ‘Is this a claw brake? Somebody’s put a pin through where the rivet went.’
‘I did,’ said Kit, interested.

‘It wants a washer, or it’ll wear the hole oval. I could do it for you tonight, if you bring it up to the house.’ Pim looked up at Tamsin, and then at the sledge, and then at the basket under its skins, and his face changed. ‘You’re going somewhere.’
She had chosen the words in the night, and still they were hard to get out.
‘I’m going north to fetch Master Leckie home,’ she said. ‘For the Reckoning. Someone has to go and bring him.’
‘Is that all?’
‘That’s all.’

Pim considered it, sitting back on his heels with Tansy trying to get into his lap. He was not stupid; he was never stupid. But he was seventeen, and trusting, and he had never in his life looked for a second meaning in anything his sister said to him.
‘Why did he go, though? Without saying?’
‘That’s one of the things I mean to ask him.’
‘I could come. I could mend things on the way.’

‘You could keep the house,’ she said, ‘and wind every clock in the shop each morning, and see that nobody steals the brass. And Orla Finch has given me three birds, and anything I send, she’ll come down and read to you herself.’

He made a face, but it was a small one; he had never been able to stay put out for long. He held out his hand, and she knew what he wanted, and took their father’s silver watch out of her coat with her left hand and gave it to him. He snapped it open the way their father used to, with his thumb, and glanced at the face, and at the two letters engraved inside the lid, A.O., as he always did.
‘Twenty-two minutes past three,’ he said. ‘And it’s gaining. When do you go?’
‘Dawn tomorrow,’ said Kit, getting up off the backboard. ‘From right here, with the dogs fed and the lady in the basket. Hob doesn’t wait for anybody, so don’t be late to wave.’
‘I’m never late,’ said Pim, with great dignity, handing back the watch. ‘I’m a clockmaker. Bring that brake up tonight, and stay for supper. Do the dogs eat herring?’

scenes.title: North on the ice

beats: They leave Callowmere at dawn, the dogs running north up the frozen Varrow.
Kit teaches Tamsin the calls for the dogs while she holds on with her good hand.
At the city’s edge Tamsin sees a lean man hiring a sledge of his own, and later that sledge behind them on the ice.

paragraphs: They left Callowmere in the blue hour before sunrise, while the lamps were still burning along the Chain Bridge and the frost lay thick as fur on every mooring rope of the west wharf. Kit had the dogs in harness before Tamsin reached the stand. Six of them stood stamping in their traces, breathing out a low cloud that hung over their backs, and behind them the Long Patience waited with its load lashed down: her bag and his, a sack of frozen fish for the dogs, a coil of line, an axe, and the wicker basket of pigeons wrapped in a horse blanket and wedged where her feet would go.
‘You came,’ Kit said, as if he had laid money against it.
‘I paid you half,’ said Tamsin. ‘I was hardly going to let you keep it for nothing.’
He laughed, a big easy sound that made two of the dogs look round. ‘In you get, then. Sit low, brace your feet, and hold on with whatever hand you’ve got going spare.’

She had the left. The right lay across her chest in its splint, bound from knuckle to elbow in Hesketh Fane’s linen and slung from her neck in a knotted shawl, and five days of it had taught her that most things in the world were made for people with two hands. A sledge, it turned out, was one of them. She climbed in sideways, sat down on the sheepskin harder than she meant to, found the rail with her left hand and gripped it until her fingers ached inside her mitten.
Kit stepped onto the runners behind her. ‘Hob,’ he said, quite quietly. ‘Hup.’

The lead dog leaned into his collar, the line came taut down the whole length of the team, and the Long Patience jerked, hissed, and slid. Tamsin’s head went back. Then they were moving, properly moving, the runners singing on the ice and the dark arch of the Chain Bridge sweeping over them and away, so fast that she had no time to think of the steps at its west end, or of anything else at all.

The city went by on either hand. On the west bank the warehouses stood shuttered and blind, and above them, on the roofs, she caught the grey shape of the pigeon loft against a sky the colour of pewter. On the east bank the Guildhall rose out of its own shadow, and high in its tower the great clock still said seven minutes to midnight, as it had said for a week. Her father had built that clock with his own hands and Edwin Leckie’s, and it had stopped, and everyone in Callowmere had looked at the Orrs as though they had stopped it themselves.
‘Now then,’ Kit said over her head. ‘You’d best learn to talk to them. If I go over the side, you’ll want to stop them before they reach the sea.’
‘We are going north,’ said Tamsin. ‘The sea is behind us.’

‘Then they’ll run to Hollin without me and eat the fish. Listen. Hup is go. Gee is right. Haw is left. Steady is slow, and whoa is stop, and they’ll argue with whoa, but Hob won’t. On by means leave it alone, whatever it is, a fox or a fish-hut or a dead gull.’

She tried a call of her own. Her voice came out thin and polite, a voice for asking a clerk to look again at a column of figures, and the wind took it before it had gone the length of the team. Hob did not so much as turn an ear.
‘He thinks you’re making conversation,’ Kit said. ‘Say it like you mean to be obeyed. Say it like you’re owed money.’
‘I generally am,’ said Tamsin, and filled her chest with air so cold it hurt, and called out, ‘Hob! Gee!’

Hob swung right, as neatly as a gate on its hinge, and the whole team followed him round a fish-hut she had not even seen, and back onto the line of the road beyond it. Behind her Kit gave a shout of laughter. Tamsin found she was grinning into her scarf like a child, and could not stop, and did not much want to.

The road ran up the middle of the Varrow between two rows of stakes, each as tall as a man and capped with a tin lantern, the glass furred white with frost. At night they were lit, Kit said, a string of little lights going north for miles. By day they were only stakes, but they told you where the ice had been tested and where it had not, and nobody with any sense went outside them. Along the margins the reeds stood frozen into the river, pale as old straw, their heads bowed with rime. Here and there a fish-hut squatted on the ice near the shore, a wooden box no bigger than a privy, with a thread of smoke going straight up from a tin chimney and a hole cut in the ice beside the door. The dogs ran on, ears up, as if the whole river had been laid down for them that morning.

The last of the city came down to meet them at the north stairs, below the north gate where the bank road came in, and where a few drivers waited on the ice for whatever trade the morning brought. Kit called the dogs down to a trot to thread between a coal sledge and a woman pushing a handcart full of cabbages, and so Tamsin was looking at the stairs, and saw him.

He stood among the drivers with his back half turned to the river, counting coins from a purse into the palm of a man in a sheepskin hood. He was a lean man in a bottle-green coat, with a clerk’s ink-stained cuffs. Among all that fleece and fur he looked as though he had stepped out of a counting-house door and kept on walking until the street ran out. As the Long Patience drew level he turned his head. It was the briefest look, and then he went back to his coins. But she had seen his eyes go to the sledge, to Kit, to her, and to the splint across her chest, and rest there a beat longer than a stranger’s eyes had any business resting.
‘Who is that man?’ she said. ‘The one in the green coat.’

Kit looked. ‘Never seen him. Somebody’s clerk, by the cut of him, hiring his way somewhere he’d sooner not go.’ He clicked his tongue at the dogs, and the north stairs fell behind them, and the city with them.

They ran on through the morning, and the morning went by in white and grey. The sun came up at last over the east bank, low and red and without warmth, and laid the shadows of the stakes across the ice in long blue bars that the sledge crossed one after another until Tamsin’s eyes ached with them. Her left hand cramped on the rail and she changed her grip, and changed it back. Her right arm throbbed in its sling with every jolt, a dull, steady complaint, like a creditor who knew he would be paid in the end and could afford to wait.

When the sun stood as high as it meant to go, which was not very high, Kit called a halt in the lee of a reed bed and threw the dogs their fish. Tamsin climbed out, stiff as a folding rule, and stamped the feeling back into her feet. She took her father’s silver watch from inside her coat with her left hand and thumbed the lid open: a quarter past twelve. She looked at the letters engraved inside the lid, A.O., as she always did, and shut it again.
Then she turned and looked back the way they had come.

The road ran south between its two lines of stakes, straight and empty for a mile, then bent with the river out of sight. Empty, except for one dark mark on the ice a long way back, between the stakes, just where the river turned.
She watched it. It did not get any bigger.
‘Kit,’ she said.

He came and stood beside her, chewing, and looked where she was looking. He had a driver’s eyes; he looked for a long time before he said, ‘Six dogs, a piebald in the lead. That’s Joss Merrow’s team, from the north stairs.’
‘And it has stopped.’
‘Resting his dogs, same as me.’
‘When we stop.’
Kit shrugged his big shoulders. ‘It’s the Varrow. The road’s free to anyone with a sledge and the fare. Half the north comes down it and goes back up again.’
‘Half the north was not standing on the stairs this morning, counting money into Joss Merrow’s hand.’
‘No,’ Kit agreed, and he looked south a good while longer than a man needs to look at nothing, before he went back to the dogs and began, without any hurry, to check their feet.

Nobody went north in midwinter, the drivers at the stand had told her; not past Dunmere, not for any fare. Not bookkeepers. Not clerks. She told herself the ice road was free to anyone, and found she believed it no more than Kit had.
Then they were off again, the stakes ticking past once more; and behind them, small and dark and keeping its distance, the other sledge came on.

scenes.title: The inn at Ambry

beats: They reach Ambry at dusk and take beds at the inn beside the mill.
Over supper Kit asks why a bookkeeper would go to Hollin in midwinter, and Tamsin tells him only that Leckie is needed for the Reckoning.
In the night she hears water running somewhere under the ice and does not sleep.

paragraphs: They came into Ambry as the light went, with the stake-lanterns pricking out one by one along the road behind them and the first stars showing over the east bank. The village sat on the west bank where the river bent: a scatter of roofs under snow, a squat church with a squatter tower, a green with a frozen pond in the middle of it, and the mill, black and tall at the water’s edge, its great wheel locked in a beard of ice. Kit swung the dogs up a ramp of trodden snow onto the bank and along to the inn beside the mill, a long low house with a lamp over its door and smoke pouring from both chimneys.

Tamsin kept her eyes on the lamp. She knew the mill was there, the way you know a step is there in the dark. She knew there was a channel cut from the river to turn the wheel, and a sluice, and a footbridge with a rail set too high for a small child to reach, and she looked at none of it. She looked at the lamp, and the door, and the snow on the step, and when Kit asked whether she was frozen through she said yes, which was true, and let it stand for everything else.

The innkeeper was a broad, floury woman who might have been the miller’s wife as well, for all Tamsin could tell, and she had two beds under the eaves, a stew on the fire and straw in the cart-shed for the dogs. Tamsin did the sum in her head before the woman named a price, and the price was fair, and she paid it out of her purse left-handed, coin by fumbled coin, while the woman watched the splint and said nothing about it, which Tamsin liked her for.

Kit was a long while with the dogs. When he came in at last he brought the cold with him on his coat and stamped it off on the mat, and sat down across the table from her by the fire, and pushed his hat to the back of his head.
‘Your clerk’s at the Wheatsheaf,’ he said.
‘He is not my clerk.’

‘Somebody’s clerk, then. I took a turn round the green to stretch my legs. Joss Merrow’s dogs are in the yard over there, on the far side, and there’s a lamp in the front window and a green coat hung up by the fire.’ He took the bowl the innkeeper set in front of him and breathed in the steam of it as though it were a hymn. ‘He’ll have paid twice what you paid. The Wheatsheaf waters its beer and then charges you for the water.’
‘Then I hope he enjoys it,’ said Tamsin, and found that she did not want to think about the green coat at all, so she ate.

The stew was mutton and barley and something that might once have been a turnip, and it was the best thing she had tasted in a week. The bread was grey and heavy and still warm. A pair of carters sat at the next table arguing about a horse, and an old dog slept under the settle with its nose in its tail, and the fire roared up the chimney with a sound like applause. Feeling came back into her feet slowly and then all at once, in a burning rush that made her eyes water. Kit ate as though he meant to make up for the whole day in one sitting, and between mouthfuls told the innkeeper that Hob had a corn on his off hind foot and Rusk had eaten a mitten, and the woman laughed and brought him more bread without being asked.

He wiped his bowl with the last of it, and leaned back, and looked at Tamsin across the table with his grey eyes, frankly curious, the way a man might look at a clock that had been sent to him in pieces.

‘I’ve driven all sorts north,’ he said. ‘Tinkers. Priests. A man with a bear once, and that was a long week. Never yet a bookkeeper. What takes a bookkeeper up to Hollin in the dead of winter, with her arm in a sling and her brother left minding the shop?’

She had known he would ask. She had known it since the stand, and she had had the whole length of the river to make her answer ready, and still she took a mouthful of beer first, to give her hand something to do.
‘Master Leckie is wanted at the Reckoning,’ she said, ‘and I am going to fetch him home.’
‘The Reckoning,’ Kit said. ‘That’s the guild’s great day, is it? Every house’s books laid out on a long table and the Wardens going through them with a comb.’
