‘On Thaw Day. Yes.’
‘And your Master Leckie can’t get himself home for it.’

‘Master Leckie is sixty-one and does not care for the cold, and he does not answer letters.’ All of which was true. ‘He was my father’s partner. He has his share in the house. When the house’s books are opened, he ought to be standing beside them.’

Kit seemed to turn that over. She watched him do it and kept her face as still as she knew how, the face she wore across the counter when a customer queried a bill she knew to be right. The fire cracked. One of the carters slapped the table and laughed.
‘Fair enough,’ Kit said at last. ‘Every fare’s got business they don’t tell the driver. I only ask so I know how fast to go.’
‘As fast as the ice will let you.’
‘That fast.’ He grinned, and the grin took any edge off it. ‘Then we’d both best sleep. Hob doesn’t care for lie-abeds.’

He did not press her, and she was more grateful for that than she let him see. She said good night, and took her candle up the narrow stair, and lay down under three blankets and her coat in the little room under the eaves, and blew the candle out.

It was very quiet. That was the first thing. In Callowmere there was always something: a cart on Gilt Street, the watchman calling the hour, the tick of a dozen clocks through the wall from the workshop, Pim snoring across the landing like a saw in green wood. Here there was nothing. The cold sat in the room like a lodger who had paid in advance. She could hear her own heart, and the small brisk tick of her father’s watch where she had laid it on the chair by the bed, and after a while, under both of them, another sound.
Water.

It was very faint. It came up through the boards and the walls and the frozen ground, from somewhere below her and to the left, where the mill stood: a low, steady, private sound, running and running, the sound of water that had found its way under the ice and meant to go on in the dark whether anyone wanted it or not. The river was frozen into a road. The wheel was locked fast. But the race still ran beneath it all, deep and quick and black, just as it had run when she was seven.

She did not let herself go any further than that. She knew the rest of it; she had known it for seventeen years, and it did not need telling again. She lay on her back with her eyes open and her good hand flat on the blanket, and listened.

After a time she got up, because lying still had become worse than the cold, and went to the window with a blanket round her shoulders. The glass was thick with frost-ferns. She scraped a hole in them with her thumbnail and put her eye to it. The green lay white and empty under the stars, the pond a grey coin in the middle of it, and on the far side the Wheatsheaf stood dark except for one window, low down at the front, where a lamp still burned. Somebody over there was awake as well. She watched the light for a long while, and it did not go out, and she did not turn her head towards the mill.

She went back to bed and began to do sums, because sums were what she had. Half the fare paid at the stand, half owing in Hollin. Two beds and two suppers at Ambry. Four days north, if the ice held and the dogs did not sulk, and four days home again. Thirty-nine days to Thaw Day. She worked it from the other end and got the same answer, and worked it a third time to be sure. Under the floor the water ran on, and did not care how many days there were.
When the window greyed at last and Kit’s boots went down the stair, whistling, she was still awake, and her eyes felt full of sand, and somewhere below her the water was still running.

scenes.title: Dace Wilmot

beats: On the ice beyond Ambry the man in the green coat drives up beside them and introduces himself.
Kit takes against him at once and drives on hard.
Kit talks about Dunmere and his brother, and Tamsin finds herself liking him.

paragraphs: They went down off the bank at Ambry in the grey before sunrise, and Tamsin kept her eyes on Hob’s tail until the mill was well behind them. The dogs were fresh and half mad with it, yelping as they ran, and Kit let them have their heads for a mile before he steadied them. The day came up hard and clear. The stakes marched north ahead in their two long lines, the last lanterns still faintly burning in the dawn, and the frost hung in the air and glittered, so that every breath seemed to have sparks in it.

She did not see the other sledge until it was nearly on them. She heard it first, a second hiss of runners under their own, and the panting of dogs that were not Kit’s dogs, and then a piebald head came level with the Long Patience’s backboard, and a driver in a sheepskin hood was shouting his team on, and the other sledge drew alongside so close that its runners all but kissed theirs.

The man in the bottle-green coat sat in its basket with a rug pulled to his chest. In the clear morning light he was older than she had thought on the stairs, forty or thereabouts, with a narrow, clean-shaven face and a smile that turned up at its corners and went nowhere else. There was ink on his cuffs even here, a day out of any counting-house, as if it had soaked into the cloth and become part of the pattern.
‘Good morning,’ he called across the gap. ‘A fine morning for it. I wonder if I might introduce myself, since we seem to be keeping company.’
Tamsin said nothing. Behind her Kit said nothing either, very loudly.
‘Dace Wilmot,’ the man said, lifting his hat, ‘clerk to the guild, travelling north on the Warden’s business.’
‘Then I wish you a good journey,’ said Tamsin.

‘Thank you. And you are Mistress Orr, I think, of Orr and Leckie on Gilt Street.’ He set his hat back on his head and settled it. ‘I have seen you at the Guildhall. I was so very sorry about the great clock. A sad business, and on Lantern Night of all nights.’
‘It was a clock that stopped, Master Wilmot. Nobody died of it.’
‘No, indeed. Quite right.’ The smile did not move. ‘You will be going up to fetch Master Leckie, I suppose.’
She had not said so. She felt it go into her like a splinter, small and cold, and held her face still. ‘Will I?’

‘Forgive me. The Warden happened to mention that Master Leckie had gone north in the autumn. Rather suddenly, I understand. We were all a little concerned for him. Is he well, do you know? Has he written to you?’
‘He is not a great writer of letters.’

‘No? Then you won’t know where he lodges. In Hollin itself, or out at one of the mine villages? I ask only because I carry some papers that want his signature, and it would save me knocking on every cold door in the valley.’
‘Then you had better ask in Hollin,’ said Tamsin. ‘They will know better than I do.’

‘I shall. I shall.’ The two sledges ran on side by side, the stakes flicking past between them like the teeth of a comb. ‘And did he take a great deal with him, would you say? Books, papers, that sort of thing? A man who packs in a hurry so often leaves behind the very thing he needs, and takes the very thing that other people need.’

She thought of Corvin Slade’s cool, courteous voice telling her that Master Leckie’s key had gone north with him. ‘I was not there to help him pack,’ she said. ‘I am a bookkeeper, Master Wilmot, not a valet.’
The sledge shifted under her as Kit moved his weight on the runners. She did not have to turn round to know what his face was doing.
‘You’ll forgive us,’ Kit said, in a voice that did not much care whether they were forgiven or not. ‘I’ve dogs to run, and they don’t like company. Hob! Hup! Hup!’

Hob went as if he had been fired from a gun. The whole team flattened out behind him, and the Long Patience leapt away so hard that Tamsin was thrown back against Kit’s knees and had to clutch at the rail with her left hand to stay in at all. Kit jumped down and ran beside the sledge, pushing, and then swung himself back onto the runners and shouted the dogs on again. She heard Joss Merrow yelling at his own team behind them, and for a quarter of a mile the piebald head hung at their shoulder, bobbing, and then it was at their backboard, and then it was gone. Merrow’s dogs had been driven hard since Ambry to catch them up, and had nothing left to give. Kit’s had all day.

He did not ease the pace until the other sledge was a speck between the stakes, and not even then, not until the river turned and the speck was hidden behind a shoulder of the east bank. Only then did he call Hob down to a steady trot, and only then did Tamsin let go of the rail and flex her cramped fingers.
‘You might have warned me,’ she said.
‘I might.’ He was breathing hard, and grinning, but there was no laughter in it. ‘I didn’t like him.’
‘I gathered.’

‘Every time I stand my sledge on the ice at Callowmere, I pay the Warden a crown in wharf dues for the privilege, and another to get off it again. I know what the Warden’s business smells like.’ He spat over the side, neatly, downwind. ‘That one asks questions like a horse-coper looking at your teeth. He knew your name.’
‘Plenty of people know my name. We are the clock family. Everyone in Callowmere has looked at us this week.’
‘Maybe.’ He let it lie. That was twice now that he had let something lie, and she noted it, the way she noted a sum that came out right.

For a long while after that they ran in silence, and it was not an uncomfortable silence. The sun climbed. The river narrowed between higher banks, and the farms grew fewer, and the fish-huts thinned out until there were none at all. A heron stood in the frozen reeds like a grey nail and did not move as they passed. Somewhere in the second hour Kit began to talk.

He talked about Dunmere, which stood on the north shore of Lake Dun, a day beyond Corran, and had the best pies on the whole river at the Heron and the worst ale. He talked about the lake in summer, which went on and on until you could not see the far side, and about the lake in winter, when it froze so hard you could drive a cart across it and folk built whole streets of fish-huts out on the ice and lived there for weeks. He talked about Hanne Roe, who mended dogs, and could set a dog’s leg better than any bonesetter could set a man’s, and he said so with a sideways look at her splint that made her laugh out loud before she could stop herself.
Then he said, in the same easy voice, ‘My brother Davey would have liked you. He liked anybody who answered back.’
She turned her head to look up at him. ‘Would have?’

‘Would have.’ He was watching Hob, not her. ‘He was fishing. He went out too early in the year, when it looked hard and wasn’t, the way it does in the first cold. He was nineteen and knew everything.’

Kit’s brother Davey had gone through the ice of Lake Dun five winters ago, and the lake had kept him. Kit did not say it like a story he had told before, though she thought he must have told it often; he said it plainly, the way you might say a road was closed. Underneath the plainness she could hear the place where it had been mended, and how it had been mended, and that it still did not quite take the weight.
‘I am sorry,’ she said.
‘So am I. Every winter.’ He clicked his tongue at Fen, who was looking at a crow. ‘On by, you fool. There. That’s enough of that.’

Her father had gone through the ice too, the winter she was thirteen. She did not say so. It sat in her mouth like a stone and she kept it there, and looked out at the white banks going by, and found to her surprise that she wanted to tell him, and that she liked him: liked his big hands on the handlebar and his talk to the dogs, and the way he had let her answer stand at Ambry without poking at it, and the way he had dealt with Dace Wilmot, which had not been polite at all.
‘Hollin is a long way to drive a stranger,’ she said instead, ‘for half a fare.’
‘Half now and half at the other end,’ said Kit. ‘That’s the bargain. And you’re not such a stranger as you were at sunrise.’

scenes.title: Corran Weir

beats: They come to Corran Weir, the great stone weir across the river two days north of Callowmere, with its bell tower on the bank.
Old Brannock the weir-keeper shows them the thaw bell and what it means.
Before the light goes Tamsin writes a few lines for Pim and sends a pigeon home.
She looks at the black water below the weir, where the ice is always thin.
card.goal: Rest at the weir; send word.

paragraphs: They heard the weir long before they saw it. It began as a sound like wind in the late afternoon, though no wind was blowing: a low, steady roar that came down the river to meet them and grew, mile by mile, until the dogs were running with their ears laid back and Tamsin could feel it through the rail under her mitten. The banks rose higher on either side, bare grey rock showing through the snow, and the river narrowed between them, and then the road curved and there it was.

Corran Weir ran clean across the Varrow from bank to bank, a great wall of grey stone higher than a house, so old that nobody on the river could say who had built it. Even in the depth of winter the water still came over it. It poured through the ice at the crest in a broken white curtain and fell into a pool at its foot where no ice would stay, a churning black throat that steamed in the cold air. Below the pool, for a long way downriver, the ice was grey and soft-looking and wrong, and the stakes would have nothing to do with it. Well short of the weir they swung away to the west bank, to a ramp of packed snow, and Kit followed them up it.

On the bank above stood the weir-keeper’s house, low and stone-built, with smoke going up from its chimney, and beside it a tower, square and narrow and taller than anything else in sight, open at the top under a little pointed roof. Something dark hung in the opening. The thaw bell, Tamsin thought, before anyone had told her.
‘Corran Weir,’ Kit said, halting the dogs in the yard. ‘Two days out of Callowmere. That’s fair going for a fresh team, with a clerk at our heels.’
She looked back down the river, south, the way they had come. The road ran away between its stakes, grey in the failing light, and there was nothing on it at all.

The door of the house opened and an old man came out, big and slow and bent at the shoulders, in a sheepskin coat that had seen better winters, with white stubble on his jaw and a lantern in his hand though it was not yet dark. He held the lantern up and looked at Kit, and at the dogs, and at Tamsin with her arm in its sling.
‘Kit Ansel,’ he said. ‘I thought you’d have more sense than to be out on the river this week.’
‘Never had any, Brannock. You know that.’
‘I do.’ The old man’s eyes came back to Tamsin. ‘And who’s this you’ve brought me?’
‘A fare for Hollin,’ said Kit. ‘She pays on time and she doesn’t complain, which is more than I can say for you.’

Old Brannock grunted, and nodded to her, and said, ‘Mistress,’ and asked nothing more. After the morning, Tamsin was content to leave it so. She had heard her own name in a stranger’s mouth once already today, and she was in no hurry to hear it again. On the river, it seemed, a fare was a fare.

While Kit saw to the dogs, Brannock took her across the yard to the foot of the tower. It was colder inside than out, a stone shaft smelling of rope and pigeon-dung and old frost, and when she tipped her head back she could see straight up through the dark to the square of grey sky at the top, and the bell hanging against it. It was bronze, green with weather, broad as a cart-wheel at the mouth. A rope as thick as her wrist came down from it to a cleat on the wall at her side.

Brannock laid his big hand on the rope, not pulling, only resting it there, the way a man might rest his hand on a horse. ‘When the ice goes, I ring her. Not before. When it starts to lift and rot, and the water comes up black through the cracks, and I can put my stick through it at the edge, then I ring her. On a still day they hear her at Ambry. If the wind’s right, they hear her up the river nearly to Lake Dun.’
‘And then?’
‘And then that’s an end of it.’

When the thaw bell at Corran rang, the Wardens closed the ice road by law, and no runner might go out on the river again until the next winter. Brannock told it to her in fewer words than that, and gruffly, as though she should have known it already. But she had never had any cause to think about the thaw bell before. Now she stood under it and thought about it very hard.
‘When will that be?’ she said.
‘When the ice says so.’ He shrugged. ‘Not for weeks yet. Some years it’s the back end of winter, some years later. I’ve rung her as early as a month before Thaw Day, and once not till after.’

Thaw Day was fixed; the Reckoning would sit on it whatever the weather did. The bell was not fixed at all. It rang when the river chose. Tamsin looked up at the green mouth of it, high in the dark, and did a sum she did not like the answer to, and came out into the yard again without saying anything.

The sun was low by then, a red smear over the western hills, and she remembered Orla Finch in the loft, brisk as a hen: daylight, and never after dark. She fetched the wicker basket from the sledge and sat on the bench by the house wall with it on her knees, and took out the paper and the stub of pencil she had brought, and wrote.

It took a long time. Her left hand did not know how to make letters; it made them as a child does, large and leaning, the loops of them wandering off the line as if they had somewhere better to be. She thought of all she might put down and could not, and in the end she put down only what was needed: that she was safe, and on her way, and that he was to mind himself. She signed it with a T that looked like a gallows. Orla would read it out to Pim in the loft, and he would grin and ask her to read it again, and then go and tell everyone on Gilt Street that his sister was safe, which was exactly what she wanted Gilt Street to hear.

She rolled the paper small and fed it into the little tube, and then found she could not hold a pigeon and tie a knot with one hand. Kit came over without being asked, wiping fish off his fingers, and took the bird out of the basket and held it against his chest in his two big palms, its heart going like a watch against his thumbs. She tied the tube to its leg with her left hand and her teeth, badly, and then again, better.

She let the first pigeon go from the weir-keeper’s yard while the sun was still up, and watched it beat away south towards home. It climbed and circled once over the tower, as Orla had said they would, and then set off down the river as straight as a stretched line, a grey fleck against the red, smaller and smaller, until it was gone.
Two birds left in the basket. She counted them, the way she would count coin, and put the blanket back over them.
Then, because she could not help it, she walked to the low wall at the river end of the yard and looked down.

From up here she could see the whole of it: the white curtain of the weir, the black pool smoking at its foot, and below the pool the long grey reach where the ice lay thin and treacherous, darker in patches where the water showed through, and edged with a grey slush that stirred as she watched it. She thought of her father, as she always did on any stretch of river ice, and of how the Varrow had taken him the winter she was thirteen. She thought of the water closing over a head, and her knees went weak under her as if the cold had already reached them, and she put her good hand flat on the frozen coping of the wall and held on.

‘Below the weir the ice is never to be trusted,’ Brannock said, behind her. She had not heard him come. ‘Winter or no winter. Water’s always moving under it, working at it. The stakes take you up the bank well short of it, and you keep to the stakes.’
‘Yes,’ said Tamsin.

He stood beside her a moment, looking where she looked, and she could not read his face at all in the dusk. Then he said, ‘There’s soup on. Come in, mistress, before you freeze to that wall,’ and went back across the yard to his door, and stood there holding it open, waiting for her, with the lamplight falling out over the snow.

scenes.title: The weir-keeper

beats: Brannock hears the name Orr and tells Tamsin he pulled her father’s sledge out of the river eleven years ago.
Her father was coming home from Hollin with brass for the house, in a hurry to beat the thaw.
Kit says the ice above the weir is rotten this year and they must cross by the old track on the east side.
card.goal: Learn what happened to her father.

paragraphs: The frost had come down hard in the night, and by morning every rail of the weir-keeper’s yard wore a fur of white. Tamsin stood by the woodstack with her coat buttoned to the chin, which had taken her the better part of five minutes, left-handed, while the splint on her right wrist knocked against every button as though it wished to be consulted. Beyond the yard wall the great stone weir ran across the river from bank to bank, a long grey lip of masonry with the ice heaped and shouldered along its top. Below it, where the water still spilled under the crust and would not lie quiet, the river showed black in patches the size of tablecloths. She did not look at those for long.

Kit was in among the dogs, sorting harness. He had them out of the shed and pegged along the line in their order, Hob at the front with his ears up and his grave yellow eyes on the gate, then Fen and Bracken, Sloe and Rusk, and little Tansy at the back, who had got her hind leg through her trace and was trying to sit down in it. The two birds that were left to Tamsin muttered in their wicker basket on the sledge. She had put a sack over it against the cold, and every so often the sack shifted, as if the pigeons were holding a meeting underneath and could not agree on the minutes.
‘Mistress Orr,’ Kit called, ‘will you hold this one for me before she hangs herself?’

Tamsin went and crouched by Tansy and held her collar with her left hand. The little dog licked her chin and then her ear, and then made a determined attempt at her plait. It was a moment before Tamsin understood that someone was standing behind her, and another before she understood that he had stopped there on purpose.

Old Brannock had come out of the house with the porridge pot in one fist and a ladle in the other. He was a broad, slow, weathered man of about seventy, with a face like a walnut and white hair that stood straight up from his head as though the wind had been at it for half a century and had at last given up trying to lay it flat. The night before he had fed them, shown them the bell, and said perhaps twenty words in all. Now he was looking at her as if she were a sum that would not come out.
‘Orr,’ he said. ‘He called you Orr.’
‘That is my name.’
‘You’ll be no kin to Aldous Orr. The clockmaker, out of Callowmere.’
Tamsin stood up. Her knees had gone stiff with crouching, and the cold went into them. ‘He was my father,’ she said.

Brannock put the pot down on the wall. He wiped the ladle on his sleeve, which did not improve either of them, and set that down as well. Then he jerked his head towards the corner of the yard where the bell tower stood, and walked off without waiting to see whether she followed. She followed. Behind her she heard Kit stop working, and then the small sounds of the harness start again more slowly.

From the foot of the tower they could see the whole of the weir and the river below it, running south between its white banks towards home. Brannock pointed with a thick finger, and she saw where he meant: a place some forty yards down from the stone, a little out from the west bank, where the ice had a sullen, sweating look and a single black seam ran across it like a crack in a plate.
‘Aldous Orr went through the ice just there, below the weir,’ Brannock said. ‘Eleven years back. We never found him till the spring.’

Tamsin knew it already. She had known it since she was thirteen, when a guild runner had come to the door on Gilt Street with his hat in his hands and asked for her mother, and she had had to tell him that her mother had been dead four years. She had known it through the long spring after, and at the burying, and every winter since, when the river froze and the ice road opened and men went out on it laughing. But she had never seen the place. It was smaller than she had imagined. She had always pictured something vast, a white plain with a hole in the middle of it like an eye. It was only a corner of a river, forty yards below a wall.
‘You were here,’ she said.

‘I was here.’ Brannock’s breath went up in a plume and was taken by the wind. ‘He came down off the upper ice at dusk, out of the north, and stopped at my gate for a word. Sledge piled high as a hayrick, all lashed under canvas. Brass, he said, from the foundry at Hollin, for the house. For your house, I suppose. He was pleased as a boy with it.’
‘He had been to Hollin for brass,’ Tamsin said. ‘I remember. He said he would be home before the thaw.’

‘That was the trouble of it.’ Brannock looked at the black seam and not at her. ‘The thaw had come early that year. There was water on the ice at noon, and the bell was due any day. I told him, go round by the bank road, there’s no road below the weir for a laden sledge. He said the bank road would cost him a day, and if the bell went while he was on it he’d be a twelvemonth getting his brass home. He laughed. He said he’d built a clock that kept better time than any bell, and he’d beat this one.’ The old man shook his head. ‘He went down on to the ice below the weir, and I watched him from this spot, and he got as far as there.’

Tamsin found that she had put her left hand flat against the cold stone of the tower. She did not take it away. The splinted arm she held against her coat, as Hesketh Fane had told her to, and it ached in time with her heart.

‘I went out with the hooks and the long ladder,’ Brannock said. ‘The sledge had caught crossways on the edge and hung there. I got it out, near enough the whole load. Him I never saw. The water had him under before I was off the bank.’ He was quiet a while. ‘I’m sorry for it, mistress. I’ve been sorry for it eleven years. I thought somebody might come.’

He went into the house then, without a word more, and she heard him moving things about. When he came out he had something wrapped in a bit of oiled rag, which he held out to her on his palm. She took it left-handed and turned back the rag.

It was a brass wheel, a little larger than a crown piece, with fine teeth cut all round its edge and four spokes curving out from the hub. There was green in the bottoms of the teeth where the river had got into them, but the faces had been rubbed bright. Her father had cut wheels like it at the long bench in the back of the shop, whistling through his teeth, and had let her sweep up the brass filings for the scrap tin.
‘It came off the load,’ Brannock said. ‘The canvas tore when I got her up. That rolled out on to the ice and lay by my boot. I kept it. Don’t ask me why.’
‘Thank you,’ Tamsin said, and could say nothing else, and closed her hand on it.

Kit had come up behind them so quietly that she had not heard him on the snow. He had the long ash pole over his shoulder, and his beard was white with his own breath. He looked at the black seam below the weir, and then at her, and she saw him decide not to say any of the things that came first into his face.

‘I was out on the upper ice at first light,’ he said instead. ‘Above the weir. It’s rotten this year, all along the west side. There’s a spring comes in under the bank up there, and the ice over it has gone grey and soft as cheese. I’d not put a dog on it, let alone the sledge.’
‘The spring’s been bad since the autumn rains,’ Brannock said.

‘So we can’t go up the west side.’ Kit shifted the pole. ‘There’s the old track that crosses over above the weir and runs up the east side. The stakes are still in it, most of them. That’s our road. It’s a slow one, but it’s sound, or it was.’

Tamsin looked north, past the tower and the long grey stone, to where the river went on under its snow towards the hills. She put the brass wheel in the pocket of her coat, next to her father’s watch, and buttoned the flap over both of them with her clumsy left hand.
‘Then we had better go by the old track,’ she said.

scenes.title: Rotten ice

beats: They cross the river above the weir on the old track, the dogs uneasy.
Tamsin walks behind the sledge to lighten it, testing the ice with Kit’s pole.
A long crack runs out from the bank, and Kit shouts for her to go wide.

paragraphs: They took the sledge up the bank road past the weir, and the noise of the water followed them a long way. It was not loud, exactly. It was the sound of a great deal of river going somewhere under a lid, a low continual grumble that she felt in the soles of her boots more than she heard. By the time they came down off the bank on to the upper ice, the sun had risen as high as it meant to, which was not very high, and had gone behind a lid of its own. The light was the colour of pewter. Nothing threw a shadow.

The old track left the west bank a quarter of a mile above the weir and slanted out across the river towards the east side, marked by a line of birch stakes. Most of them stood upright. Some leaned like drunk men after a feast, and one or two had gone altogether, so that the line had gaps in it, as a sentence will when the clerk has blotted it. On the far side, faint against the grey, she could see where the track met the east bank and turned north along it.

Kit stopped the dogs at the first stake. He looked a long while at the ice, which here was white and dull and crusted with old snow, and then at the place upriver where the spring came in under the west bank. Even from where they stood she could see the difference: a long greyish stain on the river, darker than the rest, as though somebody had spilled tea on a tablecloth and tried to wipe it with a sleeve.
‘You’ll walk,’ Kit said. ‘Behind. It takes your weight off the runners, and the less we put on any one place the better I like it.’
‘I can walk.’

‘I know you can.’ He held out the ash pole. It was taller than she was, with an iron shoe on the end of it, worn bright. ‘Take this. Every few steps, give the ice in front of you a knock. If it rings, it’s good. If it goes dull, or you feel it give, stop where you are and call me. Don’t step back. Just stop.’

She took the pole in her left hand. It was heavier than it looked, and she could not hold it as he did, with one hand over the other; the splint saw to that. She tucked her right arm inside the front of her coat, as if it were a letter she was keeping dry, and settled the pole against her shoulder and her one good hand, and found that if she leaned it a little forward she could swing the iron shoe down without overbalancing. It was not elegant. It would do.
‘Hob,’ Kit said, not loudly. ‘Away, Hob. Steady now.’

The dogs went out on to the track. They did not go as they had gone on the open river below Ambry, with their tails up and their breath smoking and Hob leaning into his collar as if he could pull the whole of the north towards him. They went carefully, with their heads low. Hob put each forefoot down and then seemed to think about it before he gave it his weight. Bracken kept looking back over his shoulder at Kit. Little Tansy, at the back next to the sledge, had her ears flat to her skull and made a small continuous whine in her throat, like a kettle a long way off.
‘They know,’ Tamsin said.
‘They know the ice is talking,’ Kit said. ‘They don’t much like what it’s saying.’

She heard it then, now that he had named it. Under the scrape of the runners and the creak of the harness the ice was making sounds of its own. There was a ticking, quick and dry, like a clock with its case off. There was a long low groan that started somewhere far off to her left and travelled under their feet and away to the right before it faded. Once there was a sound exactly like a door being shut in a big house, three rooms away. Each time it came, all six dogs stopped together and lifted their ears, and Kit spoke to them, and they went on.

Tamsin knocked the ice with the pole. It rang. She walked four paces in the tracks of the runners and knocked again. It rang. She found that she was counting under her breath, the way she counted columns in the ledger at the end of the quarter, four paces and a knock, four paces and a knock, carrying the figures in her head. It helped. She had always found that if a thing could be counted, it could be borne.

They passed the first leaning stake, and then a gap where two were missing, and Kit took them across the gap by eye, very slowly, talking to Hob the whole way in a low rumble that was not quite words. The grey stain of the spring lay off to their left now, upriver, and the far bank had come nearer. She could see alders on it, and a dark shape among them that might have been a hut, and a white slope going up to a line of black trees.

The river was deep here. She knew it as surely as if Brannock had told her: deep and slow and pulling south, under the ice, towards the weir. She could feel the whole cold weight of it under her boots. Water over her knees, and she could not bear it. Water over her head, and there would be no bearing anything. She made herself look at the back of the sledge instead, at the sacking over the pigeon basket and the loose end of a strap that bounced as the runners went over the ruts. Four paces and a knock. It rang.
‘Halfway,’ Kit said over his shoulder. ‘You’re doing well.’
‘I am walking,’ Tamsin said. ‘I have been doing it since I was a year old. You need not make a festival of it.’
He laughed, very quietly, and she heard the dogs’ ears go up at the sound of it, and felt a little better.

Four paces. A knock. It rang, but not so clearly. She stopped. She knocked again a little to one side, and that rang true, and she let out her breath and went on. The light had grown no brighter. A few dry flakes had begun to come down out of the grey, not falling so much as wandering, and they settled on the dogs’ backs and did not melt. Somewhere behind them, a long way off now, the weir went on with its low grumble, and she thought of her father coming down off this same ice at dusk, eleven years ago, pleased as a boy with his brass.
Then the river spoke.

It was not like the other sounds. It was a crack as sharp as a pistol shot, so loud and so near that she felt it in her teeth, and after it came a high singing whine, like a wire drawn tight and plucked. Every dog on the line flattened to the ice. Tamsin turned her head.

A line had opened in the river. It started at the west bank behind them, at the edge of the grey stain where the spring came in, and it was running out across the ice towards them faster than a man could walk, a thin black thread drawn on the white. It did not run straight. It jinked and forked and joined itself again, and wherever it went the ice on either side of it seemed to sink a fraction, as if it were sighing. It crossed the old track twenty yards behind her. It turned, as though it had seen her, and came on along the line of the runners.
‘Tamsin!’ Kit was half round on the sledge, one arm flung out. ‘Go wide! Wide, away from it, off the track. Now!’

She went wide. She went to the right, away from the black thread, the pole held out in front of her like a blind woman’s stick, her boots sliding on the crust. Behind her the crack sang again, higher, and she heard the ice on the far side of it settle with a sound like a sack of meal let fall. She did not look back. She looked at the far bank, at the alders and the black trees, and she walked towards them as fast as she dared, and under her feet the ice began to tick like a clock wound too tight.
Ahead of her, out of nothing, a second thread of black came running from the left to meet the first, and the white between them shivered and began to spread apart.

scenes.title: Through the ice

beats: The ice gives way under Tamsin and she goes into the black water.
Kit throws the dog-line and hauls her out on his belly, with the dogs pulling.
In the scramble little Tansy is dragged against the edge and hurts her foreleg.

paragraphs: For a moment the ice held, and she thought it would go on holding. She had the pole out in front of her and her weight thrown forward, and the far bank seemed no farther away than the width of Gilt Street. Then the floor of the world tipped quietly to one side, like a table with a leg gone, and the white slab she stood on slid down into the river and took her with it.
Tamsin went under, and the cold shut her mouth and her eyes, and her arms beat at the water to no purpose at all.

There was no sound. That was the first thing, and afterwards it was the thing she remembered best. Up above, a moment before, there had been the singing of the ice and Kit shouting and the dogs, and now there was nothing at all, only a dark green pressure against her ears and the cold, which was not like cold but like being struck on every inch of her at once. Her coat filled and dragged at her. Her boots were lead. She did not know which way was up. She opened her eyes because she could not help it and saw a dim grey ceiling, very close, and understood that it was the underside of the ice, and that the river was carrying her along beneath it, gently, as a woman might carry a child to bed.
She was seven years old and the millrace had her, and the wheel was turning somewhere in the dark, and nobody was coming.

Something hard struck her shoulder. Her head came up into air and light, and she was in the hole, in a churn of grey slush and black water, with the edge of the ice in front of her face. She had been carried no more than a yard. It felt like a mile. She threw her arms over the edge and it broke away under them, and she went down again, and came up again choking, and threw her arms over the next piece, which held for long enough to let her breathe.

‘Don’t climb!’ Kit’s voice came from somewhere a long way off, though he could not have been far. ‘Tamsin! Don’t climb out, you’ll only break it. Lie still on it. Kick your legs out behind you. Kick, and lie still!’

She did not know how she could do both of those things at once. Her legs had gone somewhere below her and would not answer. The current had hold of them and was pulling them under the ice, south, downriver, towards the weir, with a patient, steady drag that did not hurry because it did not need to. She kicked. She thought she kicked. Her chin was on the ice and the water was at her mouth and every breath came in half river.

She saw him then. He had come back across the ice towards her, not walking but lying flat on his belly, spread out like a man swimming, pushing himself along with his toes and his elbows. He had the dogs’ spare line, the long one he kept coiled on the back of the sledge, and the far end of it ran away behind him to the sledge itself, where he must have made it fast. The sledge stood thirty yards off on the white, and beyond it the six dogs stood in their traces with their heads all turned the same way, towards her, very still.

‘I’m going to throw you a loop,’ Kit said. He was near enough now that she could see his face, which had gone the colour of tallow under the beard, and his grey eyes, which were perfectly steady. ‘Get your head through it. Your head and your shoulders. Don’t try to hold it. Just get it round you. Do you hear me?’
She could not answer. She nodded, and her chin knocked the ice.

The rope came out of his hand in a long slow curl and fell across the water in front of her. The loop lay on the slush like a ring on a plate. She got her head down into it, and the river came into her nose and eyes, and she brought her head up again with the rope across her face and then down over her ears, and shrugged at it like a horse at a collar until it was round her shoulders and under her arms. It bit there. It was the best thing she had ever felt.
‘Good,’ Kit said. ‘That’s good. That’s it. Now lie on the ice and let us do the work.’
He rolled half on to his side, without lifting himself, and filled his chest, and roared over his shoulder in a voice she had not heard him use before.
‘Hob! Hob, pull! Away, all of you, pull!’

The line jerked tight. For a terrible moment nothing happened except that the rope tried to take her head off and the current tried to take the rest of her. Then she was moving. She came up out of the water on to the ice on her belly, like a seal on a rock, and the edge broke in front of her and she went down a little and came up again, and the edge broke again, and the dogs pulled, and Kit was shouting to them, and she came up the third time and the ice held. She slid out across it, streaming water, her cheek scraping on the frozen crust, and Kit caught hold of the back of her collar as she went past him and came with her, both of them dragged along on their stomachs like two sacks behind a cart.

Ahead of them there was a great scrabbling and yelping. The sledge had lurched when the line came tight, and slewed half about, and run back across the lip of the first crack where the ice had dropped a little and left a ragged edge. The dogs were scrambling for a grip. Hob had his head down and was hauling with his whole body, and Fen and Bracken beside him, but at the back, where she was nearest the sledge, little Tansy had lost her feet. The runner came round against her as it slewed, and she screamed, high and thin, like a child.
Tansy’s off foreleg had gone down between the ice and the sledge, and afterwards she would not put it to the ground.
‘Whoa!’ Kit bellowed. ‘Whoa, hold, hold there!’ The dogs stopped. The line went slack. Tamsin lay on the ice with her face in the snow and did not move, because she could not think of any reason to.

Kit got to his feet. She heard him go to the sledge, and heard the little dog crying, and his voice going low and gentle, the voice he used on the dogs when they were tired. When he came back to her he was carrying Tansy in his arms. The dog’s foreleg hung at a wrong angle, and she was licking his beard over and over, as if it were his fault and she forgave him.

He laid Tansy on the sledge among the sacks, beside the pigeon basket, and threw a blanket over her. Then he came back and knelt on the ice and got the rope off over Tamsin’s head, and pulled her up to sitting, and then to standing. Her legs would not do as they were told. Her coat had already begun to stiffen on her; she could hear it crackle when she moved. Her plait hung down her back like a length of frozen cable. She was not shivering. She thought that she ought to be, and that it was strange she was not.
‘Can you walk?’ Kit said.
‘I have been doing it since I was a year old,’ Tamsin said, or meant to. Her teeth had begun to knock together so hard that it came out as nothing at all.

‘That’s the shivering,’ Kit said. ‘Good. Shiver all you like. You’ve earned it.’ He put an arm round her and turned her towards the east bank, where the alders stood dark against the snow, and the low shape she had seen among them. ‘There’s a hut. We’ll have a fire in it inside the quarter-hour or I’ll know why. Come on now, Tamsin Orr. One foot. Then the other.’
Behind them the river closed its black mouth slowly over the place where she had been, and the slush in it turned and turned, and was still.

scenes.title: The fishing hut

beats: Kit gets her to a fisherman’s hut on the bank and makes a fire.
Drying out and shaking, Tamsin decides he has earned the truth.
Kit says he will see her to Hollin and back whatever happens.

paragraphs: The hut belonged to some fisherman who would not want it again until the spring. It stood among the alders a little way up the east bank, a low box of tarred planks with a turf roof and a door held shut by a wooden peg, and inside it smelled of old fish, old smoke and old pipe. There was a hearth of flat stones at one end, with a hole in the roof above it, and a stack of split driftwood against the wall, a bench, and a coil of net hanging from a nail like a grey beard. To Tamsin, when Kit pushed open the door and half carried her through it, it looked like the finest room in the north.

Kit had a fire going before she had sat down. Shavings from the bag on the sledge, a twist of tarred cord, the flint and steel, and then the driftwood laid on in a careful square, small pieces first. The flame went up yellow and then white, and the smoke found the hole in the roof after only a little argument, and the warmth began to come out into the hut in slow waves.
‘Coat,’ Kit said. ‘Boots. Everything. You can’t get warm in wet wool, it’ll only draw the heat out of you.’
‘I am aware of the properties of wool,’ Tamsin said, through her teeth.

‘Then you’ll not mind taking it off.’ He fetched her bag in from the sledge, and it was dry, by some mercy, having been lashed high under the canvas. He hung a blanket over the coil of net for a curtain, and went out to see to the dogs, and stayed out longer than the dogs could possibly have needed.

It took her a long time. The buttons of the coat had frozen in their holes, and the laces of her boots had frozen into knots, and her fingers had become things that belonged to somebody else. But she managed it in the end, and stood in the corner in her dry shift and her spare skirt and both her shawls, and wrung the river out of her plait on to the floor. When Kit came back in, stamping snow, she was sitting on the bench as close to the fire as she could get without being in it, shaking so hard that the bench shook with her.

He had Tansy in his arms again. He had taken off his own great coat outside and wrapped the little dog in it, and now he laid the bundle down on the warm stones by the hearth, so that only her pointed face showed, and the dark wet shine of her nose. She whined once when he settled her, and then put her chin on her good paw and watched the fire.
‘Is it bad?’ Tamsin said.

‘Bad enough. It’s not the end of her. There’s a woman in Dunmere who can do more for a dog than I can.’ He crouched and put his hand on the bundle. ‘She’ll ride the rest of the way. She’ll like that. She’s always thought she was too good to pull.’

He hung her coat on two pegs by the fire, where it steamed and dripped and gave off a smell of wet sheep and river. He stuffed her boots with dry grass and set them by the hearth. Then he unwrapped a pan from his pack, and in a little while there was a broth of sorts bubbling over the flames, brown and salty and smelling of onions. He gave it to her in a tin cup. She held the cup against her chest and let the heat go into her through the metal, and drank, and felt it go all the way down, like a lamp carried through a dark house.

Things came back to her one by one as she warmed. The pigeons: she asked, and Kit went out and brought the basket in, and the two birds sat in it with their feathers puffed out like a pair of offended aldermen, quite dry and quite unharmed. Her father’s watch: she had it out of the coat pocket and opened it, and the river had got under the lid and misted the glass, but behind the mist the hands were moving and the small sound of it went on, tick and tick, as though nothing had happened. It seemed to her a great piece of impudence. She closed the lid on the letters cut inside it and held it in her lap.

And the brass wheel. That was in the same pocket, at the very bottom, cold as a stone. She took it out and turned it to the firelight, and the light ran round its teeth. It had been in the river once already, eleven years ago, and had come out. Now it had been in again, and come out again. She sat and looked at it while the fire cracked and the shaking went slowly out of her.

Kit sat down on the floor across the hearth from her, with his back to the wall. He had not said anything about the river. He had not said anything about her father, though he had stood behind her in Brannock’s yard and heard the end of it. He was looking at the fire, with his big hands hanging loose between his knees, and she saw that they were not quite steady either, and that the knuckles were raw where the rope had gone through them.

She thought of him coming across the ice towards her on his belly. She thought of the loop lying on the black water like a ring on a plate, and the steady grey eyes over the beard, and the voice that had roared at Hob. He had not had to do any of it. A hired driver could have stood on the bank and been sorry, and no one would have blamed him. Davey had gone through the ice of Lake Dun five winters ago, and there had been nobody to throw Davey a rope.
Then, because he had pulled her out of the river, she told Kit Ansel about the four hundred and twelve crowns.

She told it all in order, as she would have laid out an account. The great clock stopping on Lantern Night, and the crowd turning to look at her and Pim. The ledger in her father’s desk, and the page in it that someone had sewn shut, and what was written on it when she cut the stitches: four hundred and twelve crowns, borrowed from the guild against the house, the autumn before he died, and no line anywhere in the guild’s books to say that it had ever been paid. The Reckoning on Thaw Day, when every house laid its books open, and any house that owed the guild was forfeit to it. Corvin Slade, with his cane and his washed-out eyes and his cold courtesy, announcing the Reckoning as if he were reading out the price of herring. Master Leckie gone north with the second key to the vault, and with whatever he knew, which might be nothing, and might be everything.

‘So that is why a bookkeeper goes to Hollin in midwinter,’ she said. ‘I told you a part of the truth at Ambry. That is the rest of it. If Master Leckie cannot help me, Pim and I will be out on Gilt Street by the end of Thaw Day, and the house will be the guild’s.’

Kit did not say anything for a while. The fire had burned down a little, and he leaned forward and put on two more pieces of driftwood, and she watched the colour come up into his face, and understood that it was not the heat.

‘Four hundred and twelve crowns,’ he said at last. ‘And a dead man who can’t speak for himself, and a girl who was only a child when he died, and a clock he built them with his own hands still standing in their tower. And they’ll have the roof off your head for it.’ He picked up a stick and broke it in two and threw both halves in the fire. ‘I’ve no love for the guild. I’ve paid their wharf dues and their ice tolls since I was nineteen, and never saw a farthing of it come back in anything I could put my hand on. But this is a filthy business. This is the kind of thing that makes me want to walk into their hall and knock somebody down.’
‘That would not help,’ Tamsin said. ‘Though I should like to see it.’

‘I daresay it wouldn’t.’ He let out a long breath through his nose. ‘Well, then. Here’s what I’ll do instead.’ He looked up at her across the fire, and his grey eyes were very steady, as they had been out on the ice. ‘I’ll see you to Hollin, Tamsin Orr, and I’ll see you back again, whatever happens, and whatever the guild has to say about it. You have my word on that.’
She found she had to look down at the brass wheel in her lap for a moment before she could answer him.
‘I cannot pay you any more than we agreed,’ she said.
‘I never asked you to,’ said Kit, and reached across and took the empty cup from her, and filled it again.

scenes.title: Lake Dun

beats: They go on north at first light with Tansy riding on the sledge in a nest of sacks.
The river opens out into Lake Dun, and the ice road runs across it to the town on the far shore.
Kit points out his mother’s old house on the waterfront.

paragraphs: They went on north at first light, with Tansy riding on the sledge in a nest of sacks.

Kit had built the nest before Tamsin was awake, out of grain sacks and oilcloth and the old grey blanket he kept for the dogs, and when she came out of the fisherman’s hut with her coat still stiff from its night by the fire, the little bitch was already installed in it like a dowager in a box at the theatre. Only her head showed, and the bad foreleg, wrapped in a strip torn from Kit’s spare shirt. She watched the others being put into harness with an expression of deep and personal injury.
‘She thinks she’s been demoted,’ Kit said.
‘She’s been promoted. She rides, and they pull.’

‘You tell her, then.’ He bent and rubbed the dog’s ears, and Tansy turned her face away from him with great dignity, and he laughed, though not with his whole chest the way he usually did. ‘She’ll forgive me by Dunmere. She always forgives me by Dunmere.’

Tamsin climbed in beside the nest and settled the wicker basket between her boots. The two birds left in it shifted and muttered under the cloth. Kit stepped onto the runners behind her, called to Hob, and the sledge jerked, slid, and found its pace on the river.

She had thought she would be afraid of the ice that morning, and she was. Every time the runners hissed over a darker patch she felt the cold close over her face again, felt the black water shut her eyes, and her whole body went tight and waiting. Kit must have seen it in the set of her shoulders, because after the first mile he leaned down over her and said that the ice here was a yard thick if it was an inch, and that a coach and four could dance on it.
‘Have you seen a coach and four dance on it?’
‘Not personally. But I’ve heard reports.’

It was not much, but it loosened something in her neck, and after that she watched the dogs instead of the ice. Hob ran in the lead with his ears pricked and his plumed tail carried high. Fen and Bracken ran behind him, then Sloe and Rusk at the wheel, and at the very back, where Tansy should have been, there was an empty space in the traces that the eye kept going to and coming away from. Now and then Tansy lifted her head out of the sacks and looked at that space, and whined once, very low, and put her chin down again.

The banks on either side were alder and frozen reed, and the reeds stood up out of the snow like the bristles of an old brush. There was no wind. The sky was the colour of milk left too long in the jug, and the morning sun was only a paler place in it.
Then, between one bend and the next, the banks began to fall away.

The alders thinned and stepped back, and the reeds thinned, and the snow on either side grew flatter and wider, until all at once there were no banks at all, only a great white plain running away in front of them to a line that might have been the far shore or might have been nothing but the place where the sky gave up. The river had opened out into Lake Dun.
Kit called the dogs to a halt. They stopped willingly, tongues out, steaming, and sat down in the snow as if this were a custom they knew.
‘Why are we stopping?’

‘We always stop here.’ He did not explain at once. He stood on the runners with his cap in his fist, looking out across the lake, and after a moment she understood that he was not resting the dogs. ‘Dunmere folk say the lake remembers,’ he said at last. ‘Everyone who crosses it, and everyone it’s kept. So you take your cap off, coming onto it. You let it know you’re only passing.’

Tamsin had no cap, only her hood. She pushed it back, and the cold went at her ears like a pair of pincers. She did not ask whether he believed it. She knew that his brother had gone through the ice of this lake five years ago, and that he had told her so on the road north, in the flat voice people keep for the things they have said too often to themselves. She sat bareheaded beside the dog in the sacks and looked at the white silence, and it seemed to her that the lake looked back, not unkindly, but with a great deal of time on its hands.
Kit put his cap on again. ‘Hob,’ he said, and they went out onto Lake Dun.

The ice road ran straight across it, marked every hundred yards or so by a pole frozen upright with a rag of red cloth tied at the top. The poles went away in front of them, smaller and smaller, until they were no more than stitches in the white, and at the end of the stitching, so faint she took it at first for a smear on her own eyes, lay a low grey line with smoke standing up from it.
‘Dunmere,’ Kit said. ‘North shore. Two hours, if the dogs keep their minds on it.’

It was the quietest country she had ever been in. In Callowmere there was always something: the wharf bells, the carts on the cobbles, the great clock striking the quarters in its tower, before it stopped, or the gulls, or Pim. Out here there was only the hiss of the runners and the dogs’ breath and the small creak of the sledge timbers, and under all of it a vast hush that swallowed every sound as soon as it was made. Twice the ice gave a long, deep groan somewhere far off, like a door opening in a cellar, and both times Tamsin’s heart stopped and started again, and both times Kit told her it was only the lake settling before she could ask.

She took her father’s silver watch out of her coat to see how the morning went. It was not yet nine. She opened the lid out of habit, not to read anything, only to see the two letters engraved inside it, A.O., worn soft at the edges by the thumb that had opened it ten thousand times before hers. She closed it and put it away, and the warmth of it stayed against her ribs.

The smear of grey grew into a line, and the line grew into a town. She saw roofs first, steep and dark and heavy with snow, then the smoke rising straight from a hundred chimneys, then the stone quay running along the waterfront with fishing boats drawn up and frozen into the ice beside it, their masts bare and leaning at all angles like a box of spilled matches. A long low building near the middle of the quay had a sign hanging from an iron bracket, too far off yet to read.

‘That’s the Heron,’ Kit said, nodding at the sign. ‘Best eel stew on the lake, and the worst beer. And there,’ he lifted his chin to the left, towards the western end of the quay, ‘the one with the crooked chimney and the green shutters. That was my mother’s house.’

She looked. It was a narrow house, two windows up and one down beside a door, squeezed between a chandler’s and a net loft. The chimney leaned as if it had been listening for something for a long time. Someone had hung washing out on a line under the eaves, and the shirts had frozen into the shapes of men with their arms up.
‘Who lives there now?’

‘A cooper and his wife. They let me look in at the kitchen when I come through, if I bring them a fish.’ He was quiet for the length of three poles. ‘Davey and I used to sit on that step and watch the sledges come in off the lake. Mother would knock on the window with her thimble when it was time for supper. You could hear it right across the quay.’

Tamsin thought of her own mother, who had sung while she cooked, and of the kitchen on Gilt Street, and of Pim alone in it now, burning the porridge. She said nothing, because there was nothing that would not have been smaller than what he had said, and Kit seemed to want nothing from her but that.
Tansy put her head out of the sacks and sniffed. The smell of the town had reached them: woodsmoke and fish and tar, and under it, faint and unmistakable, the smell of a great many dogs.
‘Hanne Roe,’ Kit said, and some of the stiffness went out of his voice. ‘Her yard’s behind the quay, at the top of the slip. If anyone can mend that leg, she can.’

Tansy whined and struggled to sit up in her nest. Up ahead, Hob had caught the scent too. His ears went forward, his tail went up, and without a word from the runners the whole team leaned into the traces and began to run for the shore.

scenes.title: The dog-healer

beats: Hanne Roe, the Dunmere dog-healer, looks at Tansy’s leg and says she will never run in harness again.
Tansy will stay with Hanne and her daughter; Kit says goodbye to her.
The healer’s fee and the supplies cost more than Tamsin has, and she goes to the pawnbroker on the quay.
Before she leaves the healer’s yard she sends a pigeon home.
card.goal: Pay for Tansy and go on.

paragraphs: Hanne Roe’s yard lay at the top of the slip behind the quay, a square of trodden straw and snow fenced with driftwood and old oars. Kennels made from upturned boats ran along two sides of it, and from every one of them, as the sledge came through the gate, a dog put its head out and gave its opinion. A sharp voice from the doorway silenced them.

The voice belonged to a broad, weathered woman of about forty in a man’s sealskin coat, with her fair hair cropped short as a boy’s. Behind her skirts a girl of seven or eight peered out, all eyes and plaits.
‘Kit Ansel,’ the woman said. ‘I heard you were on the river. What have you done to my favourite?’

‘Not me. The ice at Corran.’ Kit lifted Tansy out of the sacks as if she were made of eggshell and carried her across the yard. ‘She went down between the edge and the sledge. She won’t put the foot to the ground.’
‘Bring her in where it’s warm. Mina, the lamp.’

The girl ran ahead of them into a low room that was half kitchen and half surgery, with a stove at one end and a long scrubbed table at the other. Kit laid Tansy on the table on a folded blanket, and the little dog lay very still and looked at the ceiling, as dogs do when they have decided that the worst is about to happen and would rather not watch.

Hanne unwrapped Kit’s strip of shirt and set it aside with a sniff at the quality of the knot. Then she took the foreleg in both her big red hands and began to feel along it from the shoulder down, as if she were listening to it. Tansy trembled. When Hanne’s thumbs reached the joint above the paw the dog yelped, once, and turned her head and licked the healer’s thumb by way of apology for the noise.
‘I know, my lamb,’ Hanne said. ‘I know.’ She went over the leg a second time, and then she straightened and looked at Kit, not at Tamsin.

‘The bone’s cracked through just above the joint,’ she said, ‘and the cords at the back are torn. It’ll knit. She’ll walk on it by spring, and run about the yard, and chase the gulls off the slip. But she’ll never run in harness again, Kit. If you put her in the traces she’ll go lame in a mile and stay lame.’
Kit did not say anything for a moment. He stood with his fists in his coat pockets and looked at Tansy, and Tansy looked at the ceiling.
‘You’re sure.’
‘I’m sure. You knew it before you came in, or you’d not have carried her like that.’
‘I knew it.’ He breathed out through his nose. ‘I wanted it said by somebody who’d know better.’

Mina had crept up to the table and was standing on tiptoe with her chin on the edge of it, so that her face was level with Tansy’s. Tansy turned her head a little and looked at her. Then, very carefully, she stretched out her neck and put her nose against the girl’s cheek.
Hanne knelt in the straw and began to bind the leg.

She had moved Tansy down onto the floor by the stove, where there was a bed of clean straw. Tamsin knelt at Tansy’s head and held her, as well as she could, with her left arm round the dog’s neck and her own right wrist kept well out of the way in its splint against her chest. She could only help one-handed. Hanne laid two thin slats of ash along the leg, front and back, padded them with tow, and wound the linen round and round, firm and even. Watching it, Tamsin felt the ache start up in her own bones as if in sympathy: the same slats, the same linen, the same patient winding she had sat through in Hesketh Fane’s shop that seemed a year ago now and was barely eight days. She caught Kit looking from the dog’s leg to her arm and back again, and saw the corner of his mouth move in spite of everything.
‘A matched pair,’ he said.
‘Don’t,’ Tamsin said, but she was not cross.
‘She’ll stay here, then,’ Hanne said, tying off the linen. ‘With us. Mina’s been at me for a dog of her own since she could talk. If you’ll allow it.’
Mina looked up at Kit with her whole heart in her face.
‘I’ll allow it,’ Kit said.
Tansy would stay in Dunmere; from here on Kit ran five dogs.

He said goodbye to her before anything else was settled. He crouched down in the straw beside her, a big man folded small, and put his hand on her head, and said something to her too low for Tamsin to hear. Tansy thumped her tail twice on the straw and licked his beard. Then he stood up and went out to the other dogs in the yard without looking back, and Tamsin, who had seen his face as he passed, looked carefully at the stove until he had gone.

The reckoning came after, as reckonings do. Hanne asked three crowns for the binding and for Tansy’s keep until the leg was sound, which was fair, and less than fair, and Tamsin knew it. Then Kit came back in, red about the eyes and brisk, with a list of what the team needed for the last day north and the long run home: dried fish and tallow for the dogs, a new trace, lamp oil, a sack of meal. Tamsin added it up in her head as he spoke, and then she opened her purse on Hanne’s table and counted what was in it. She counted it twice. It came to a good deal less than the sum.
‘I can wait for the money,’ Hanne said, seeing her face.
‘No.’ Tamsin closed the purse. ‘Thank you. But no. I don’t leave debts behind me.’ She heard how it sounded, and did not take it back.
Through the low window she could see the sun standing as high as it would go over the lake. She took her father’s watch out of her coat and opened it. Both hands stood at twelve.

The pigeon basket was in the sledge. She brought it into the yard and set it on an upturned boat, and Kit held the lid while she lifted out the nearer of the two birds. Writing the message was the hard part. She had to do it left-handed, with the slip of thin paper held flat on the boat’s hull under Kit’s broad thumb, and the letters came out shaky and uneven. She kept it short, because Orla would have to read it aloud to Pim and Pim would want to know only one thing.
Dunmere. Still safe. Kit is good. Mind the house. T.

Kit rolled the slip into the little tube on the bird’s leg, and she held the hen against her coat for a moment, feeling the quick small heart. Then she opened her arm and let her go. The pigeon went up in a clatter, circled the yard once above the barking dogs, and turned south over the white lake towards home. Tamsin watched until she could not tell the bird from the sky.
She sent the second pigeon home from the dog-healer’s yard at noon; one was left in the basket.

The pawnbroker’s shop stood at the far end of the quay, a narrow brown front with three tarnished brass balls hanging over the door and a window full of other people’s lives: a fiddle without strings, a wedding ring on a card. Tamsin walked there alone in the early afternoon. Kit had offered to come, and she had told him to see to the dogs, and he had understood her and not argued.
Inside it was close and dim and smelled of dust and old wool. The pawnbroker was a soft, pale man with spectacles pushed up on his forehead.
She laid her father’s silver watch on the pawnbroker’s counter and did not let herself look at it again.

She heard him pick it up. She heard the click of the lid and knew he was reading the two letters inside, and she looked instead at a stuffed pike on the wall above his head, which had a fly-blown, surprised expression, as if it had not expected any of this either. He named a sum. She named a higher one, because she was her father’s daughter and a bookkeeper, and he named one between, and she took it, because it was enough. He wrote out a ticket and pushed it across the counter with the coins.
‘A fortnight,’ he said. ‘After that I sell.’
‘I’ll be back long before that.’
‘They all say so,’ said the pawnbroker, not unkindly, and put the watch away in a drawer.

Outside on the quay the wind had got up off the lake, and the light was thickening. Without thinking she put her hand to her coat to see how late it was, and found nothing there but the ticket, and stood for a moment quite still among the frozen boats before she turned and walked back towards the dog-healer’s yard with the money.

scenes.title: The Heron

beats: In the Heron inn Tamsin and Kit eat by the fire and talk low about the debt and what Leckie might know.
Kit is sure the Warden will not come north himself.
When they get up Tamsin sees Dace Wilmot on the next settle, his back to them, and knows he heard every word.

paragraphs: The Heron was full that night of fishermen and sledge drivers and the smell of eels, and Kit found them a settle by the fire as if the place had been holding it for him. It was one of a row of high-backed oak settles set back to back along the length of the room, so that every pair of drinkers sat in a sort of wooden stall with the fire on one side and somebody else’s shoulders on the other. Theirs was the last before the hearth. The heat came off the logs in a wall, and after four days on the ice it made Tamsin’s face burn and her eyes water.

The stew came in a black pot with two wooden spoons stuck upright in it. Kit had not lied: it was the best eel stew she had ever eaten, thick with onions and barley and pepper, and the beer was very bad. She ate left-handed, which still made her feel like a child at her first table, and twice she slopped broth down the front of the splint and had to wipe it off with the corner of her shawl. Kit pretended not to see. He had been quiet since the afternoon, and she knew why, and did not make him talk about it. Instead she let him eat, and drank her terrible beer, and waited until the noise of the room had risen high enough to cover them.
‘Four hundred and twelve crowns,’ she said then, keeping her voice down. ‘I keep saying it to myself, to see if it sounds any smaller. It doesn’t.’
Kit wiped his beard. ‘Say the rest of it, then. Lay it out for me like one of your ledgers.’

So she did, low and plain, the way she would have done it for a client who owed the house money. Four hundred and twelve crowns, borrowed from the guild against the house the autumn before her father drowned, to pay for the bells of the great clock. A page sewn shut in his ledger, so that she had found it only because two leaves would not part. No entry anywhere in his hand to say that it had been paid back, and none in the guild’s books either, or Slade would never have dared to send for her and talk about the Reckoning. On Thaw Day every house’s books would be laid open, and a house with an unpaid debt to the guild would be forfeit, clock-house and workshop and the roof over Pim’s head.
‘And the vault,’ Kit said.

‘The vault opens to two keys turned together.’ She touched the iron key on her belt, under the edge of her coat, to be sure it was still there. She did it twenty times a day. ‘Ours, and Edwin Leckie’s. Whatever is down there, I can’t get at it without him.’
‘And what do you think is down there?’

She turned her spoon over and looked at it. ‘I don’t know. That’s the honest answer. But my father never in his life borrowed a farthing without writing down the day he paid it back. He wrote down the day he paid the coal man. He wrote down the day he bought Pim a whistle at the Lantern fair, and what it cost, and that it was a bad bargain because it only played one note. And then there is a page of four hundred and twelve crowns, and he sewed it shut, and he never wrote another word about it.’ She put the spoon down. ‘Either he was ashamed, or he was hiding something. And Mr Leckie was his partner. If anyone knows which, it’s him.’
‘And he ran off north this autumn, and never said why.’
‘Yes.’
‘People don’t run four days north in the back end of the year for nothing,’ Kit said. ‘He’s frightened of somebody.’
‘I know.’
‘You know who.’

She did not answer that. She looked at the fire, and the fire looked back with its little red eyes, and she thought of Corvin Slade’s pale, washed-blue gaze coming down on her, courteous and cold as a January window, and of the silver head of his cane catching the light as he turned away.

‘He wants the house,’ she said. ‘He has wanted it for years. It’s the best frontage on Gilt Street, and it backs onto the wharf, and he is Warden of the Wharf. If it comes to the guild at the Reckoning, it comes to him. And he has people, Kit. He has clerks and wardens and men who owe him money, and they can go where he likes.’
Kit snorted softly and leaned back against the settle, and the old oak creaked under his weight.
‘Slade won’t come himself,’ Kit said. ‘He never leaves Callowmere in winter, not with that knee.’
‘You sound very sure.’

‘I’ve run the ice road nine winters. Everyone on it knows the Warden. He takes the dues at the wharf with his own hands, and he counts them twice, and he never sets foot past the north gate from first frost to thaw. Says the cold gets into the bone.’ He tapped his own right knee. ‘The steps of that wharf did for him long before you or I came along. A man who walks with a cane doesn’t ride four days on a sledge for anybody’s house.’
‘Then he’ll send someone.’

‘Let him. His clerk turned back at the weir, if he’s got any sense, and if he hasn’t he’s still sitting on the far bank waiting for the ice to grow. Nobody follows a team across Corran this year without a driver who knows the old track, and there’s only two of us that do, and the other one’s in his bed with gout.’
It made her smile, which she suspected was the purpose of it. She pushed the pot towards him so that he could finish it, and he did, scraping the bottom with great thoroughness.
‘Tomorrow, then,’ she said.

‘Tomorrow. We’re away before dawn, across the top of the lake while the ice is hard, and up the valley road to Hollin. It’s a climb, and the dogs won’t thank me for it, but if the weather holds we’ll see the mine smoke by midday.’ He looked at her sideways. ‘And then you’ll knock on Mr Leckie’s door and ask him what’s in the vault.’
‘And then I’ll knock on Mr Leckie’s door,’ Tamsin said, ‘and see if he opens it.’

She thought of Pim, who would have Orla’s reading of her note by nightfall, or by tomorrow at the latest, and who would be telling half of Gilt Street that his sister was safe before he had his boots off. For once she did not mind it. Let them all hear it. Let Slade hear it, sitting by his own fire with his bad knee up on a stool, three days to the south, where he could do nothing about anything.

The fire had burned down to a red bed. Most of the drivers had gone up to their rooms or out into the cold, and the noise of the place had dropped to a mutter at the far end, by the barrels. Tamsin felt the long day settle into her shoulders all at once, the lake and the yard and the pawnbroker’s counter, and the empty place against her ribs where the watch had been. She got up stiffly, and Kit got up after her, stretching until his knuckles brushed a beam.
That was when she saw the cup.

It stood on the broad top rail of the settle behind theirs, a pewter cup, half full, within a foot of where her own head had rested all evening. Below it, on the other side of the oak, was a shoulder in a bottle-green coat. As she looked, a hand came up and took the cup, and she saw the cuff of the sleeve, and the old ink stains on it, faded brown with washing.
Dace Wilmot had been sitting on the next settle the whole time, close enough to hear every word.

He did not hurry. He turned on the bench, unfolding his lean length from the corner of the stall, and looked up at her over the rail, and his face wore the same polite, attentive smile he had worn on the day he first introduced himself, as if they had met by appointment and he was pleased to find her punctual. He raised the cup to her, a small courteous inch, and drank.

scenes.title: The valley road

beats: They cross the last of Lake Dun before dawn and turn up the narrow valley where the river comes down from Hollin.
The road climbs between black pines, and the cold grows sharper.
Kit sings to the dogs to keep them going, and Tamsin thinks about what she will say to Leckie.

paragraphs: They crossed the last of Lake Dun before dawn, under a sky so thick with stars that the snow gave back a faint grey light of its own, and the dogs ran on it like shadows running on pewter.

Dunmere lay asleep behind them. Nobody had been about on the quay when they harnessed up but a boy with a lantern breaking the ice on the horse trough, and he had stared at them and said nothing. Tamsin had looked back once, at the dark shape of the Heron with its sign creaking on the bracket, and thought of a pewter cup lifted an inch in the firelight, and had not looked back again. Kit had said nothing about it either, not since the night before, when he had taken her by the elbow and walked her out of the Heron and up the stairs without a word, and then stood outside her door for a long time. She had heard the boards creak under him. She did not know when he had gone to bed, or whether he had gone at all.

Beyond the town the lake did not end at once. It narrowed into a long arm running north between two dark shoulders of hill, and the ice road ran up it, pole after pole, towards the place where the river came in. The air changed as they went. On the open lake it had been still and wide and almost mild for winter, but here in the narrows it came down to meet them off the hills with a smell of resin and stone in it, and it was colder, and getting colder, as if somebody up ahead had left a door open on the other side of the world.

The stars went out one by one. By the time the sky had turned the colour of ash, the last pole was behind them, and the head of the lake lay across their way like a white beach, and beyond it, cut deep into the hills, opened the valley.
‘There,’ Kit said. ‘That’s the Hollin road.’

The river came down the valley in a frozen staircase, falls and pools and falls again, locked into great swollen pillars of green ice that no runner could ever cross. Beside it, on the western side, a road went up. It was not much of a road. It had been cut into the hillside long ago by miners carrying ore down to the lake, and it climbed in one steep, narrow shelf between the river on one hand and the black pines on the other, and it was white with old snow and pocked with the marks of hooves and runners.

Kit stopped the team at the foot of it and walked forward along the line, checking each harness with his bare hands, talking to each dog in turn. To Hob he said something about honour. To Fen he said that she was a thief and he knew it. To Bracken he said nothing at all, only took his great black head between his hands and pressed his forehead to it for a moment, and Bracken stood and allowed this with his eyes closed. Then Kit came back to the sledge and looked at Tamsin.
‘You’ll walk,’ he said. ‘I’m sorry. Every pound they don’t pull is a mile they’ll give us at the top.’
‘I was going to walk anyway,’ she said, and climbed down.

The road climbed between black pines, and the cold grew sharper with every turn of it. She had thought she knew cold. She had grown up beside a frozen river and done her accounts in a clock-house where the ink thickened in the well, and she had been through the ice at Corran and come out of it alive. But this was another cold, high and thin and clean, that came through her coat and her shawl and the two shirts under them as if they were muslin, and set its teeth into her bones and stayed there. Her breath froze on the edge of her hood in a fringe of white. The splint, which she had stopped feeling days ago, began to ache again where the slats pressed, a dull, steady, nagging ache that kept time with her steps.
