She held on to the sledge rail with her left hand and walked in the runners’ track, where the snow was packed, and kept her eyes on Rusk’s grey hindquarters ahead of her, rising and falling.

The pines stood very close on the uphill side. Their trunks were black and straight and their branches heavy with snow, and every so often one of them let its load go all at once with a soft thump and a sigh, and a cloud of powder drifted out over the road and hung glittering in the air. On the other side, far below, the river talked to itself under its ice, a hollow, knocking sound like someone moving about in an empty house.

The dogs began to labour. She could see it in the way their heads went down, in the shortening of their stride, in Sloe’s ears going flat. On the third steep pitch Hob faltered and looked back over his shoulder, and Kit began to sing.

It was not a fine voice, but it was a big one, and it went out over the valley and came back off the far side as if there were two of him. The song had no tune worth the name and a great many verses, and every verse was about a dog. Hob was a gentleman who wore a silk cravat to church. Fen had stolen the parson’s supper and blamed it on the cat. Bracken was so handsome that a painter had begged to take his likeness. Sloe and Rusk were a pair of rogues who would come to a bad end on the gallows, singing all the way. Tamsin did not believe for a moment that it was a real song. She thought he had been making it up for years, a verse at a time, on a hundred roads like this one, and that the dogs knew every word of it. Their ears came up. Their heads came up. Hob leaned into his collar and the line tightened all the way down, and the sledge went on up the hill.
She walked behind it and let the song go over her, and thought about Edwin Leckie.

She had been thinking about him since Lantern Night, and she still did not know what she would say. She had tried a dozen beginnings in the dark at Ambry and at Corran and in the room at the Heron, and none of them would do. Some were too soft. Some were too sharp, and sounded, even in her own head, like her father’s daughter at her worst, frightened and cutting. You went away with half my father’s vault and never said a word to me. That was true, but it was no way to begin with a frightened old man who had given Pim sugared almonds out of his waistcoat pocket every Lantern Night since he was born. I need to know what happened to the four hundred and twelve crowns. That was true too, and he might shut the door on it.

She thought of him as she had last seen him, in the autumn, standing in the workshop on Gilt Street with his coat already on, turning his hat round and round by the brim. He had looked at her as if he wanted to tell her something. She had been busy with the quarter’s accounts and had not looked up for long enough. Two days later he was gone, and nobody on Gilt Street knew why.
Perhaps she would say only, Mr Leckie, I’ve come a long way, and let him decide what to do with it.

The sun came over the eastern ridge as they reached the top of the steepest pitch. It came all at once, in a flood, and turned the snow on the far side of the valley to gold and the shadows under the pines to blue, and the cold, without growing any less, grew bright, so bright that she had to narrow her eyes against it. Kit stopped singing and let the dogs stand. They stood with their sides heaving and their breath going up in clouds, and the whole valley lay open in front of them, climbing and climbing towards a wall of white hills.

Somewhere up there her mother had been a girl. She had carried water from a well at the top of a steep town and come down to the lake one summer and never gone home again. Tamsin had never been able to imagine it. Now, standing in the snow with the sun in her face, she found she could.
‘Look,’ Kit said, and pointed.

High up the valley, where it bent out of sight round a shoulder of grey rock, a thread of dark smoke stood up against the snow, and beside it another, and another, leaning all together in the same small wind like a row of pens in a jar.
‘Mine-heads,’ he said. ‘That’s Hollin.’
Tamsin took a fresh grip on the sledge rail. ‘Then sing them another verse,’ she said, and started up the road before he could.

scenes.title: The mountain town

beats: Hollin climbs the mountainside in steep streets of grey stone, with the mine-heads smoking above it.
Nobody will tell them where Edwin Leckie is; doors close.
They stable the dogs at the Copper Kettle, and Tamsin goes up through the town to the well at the top.

paragraphs: Hollin came on them all at once. One moment the valley road was nothing but black pines and the hiss of the runners, and the next the trees fell back and the town stood over them, climbing the mountainside in steep streets of grey stone, roof above roof, as though someone had begun a stair up the hill and lost heart halfway. Above the last houses the mine-heads stood against the snow, timber gantries and squat stone chimneys, and every chimney was smoking. The smoke went straight up into a white sky and hung there. It smelled of coal and wet iron, and of something sourer underneath that Tamsin could not name.
Kit called the dogs down to a walk. Hob put his ears back at the smell and went on only because Kit told him twice.
‘Four days north of Callowmere,’ Kit said, ‘and this is what’s at the top of it.’
‘You’ve been here before.’
‘Once. Summer, with a load of salt fish. It looked friendlier with the doors open.’

The doors were not open now. Tamsin saw that as they came in under the first houses. Every door in Hollin was shut, and most of the shutters too, and where a shutter stood back there was a face behind the glass that went away as soon as she looked at it. The street was hardly wider than the sledge. In places it had been cut into steps, shallow and worn hollow in the middle, and the snow on them was trodden to grey ice by boots that had all, by the look of it, gone indoors some time ago.

She had spent four days thinking of this town as an end. Leckie would be here, and Leckie would know, and whatever he knew would be better than the sewn page and the not knowing. She had not once thought of Hollin as a place with people in it, people who might have their own opinions about two strangers and a sledge coming up out of the valley at noon.

Somewhere above them a bell rang the hour, thin and flat, twelve strokes. Tamsin’s hand went to her coat pocket for her father’s watch before she remembered that it was lying in a pawnbroker’s drawer in Dunmere. She took the hand away again and put it back on the rail of the sledge, where it had been.
‘Noon,’ Kit said, unhelpfully.
‘I can count.’
‘I know you can. It’s your trade.’ He gave her a sideways look over his beard, grey eyes creased against the glare. ‘Ask, then. You’re the one with the name.’

The first door she tried belonged to a narrow house with a brass knocker in the shape of a fist. She knocked, and waited, and knocked again, and at last the door opened the width of a face. A woman of about her own age looked out: a round, pale face under a dark shawl, and a child’s fingers holding the shawl from behind.
‘I’m looking for Edwin Leckie,’ Tamsin said. ‘He came up from Callowmere this autumn. An old man, with a white beard. He has a sister here.’

The woman looked at her. Then she looked past her at Kit, and at the dogs steaming in their traces, and at the sledge with its load lashed down under the cover. Then she shut the door. She did not slam it. She closed it the way you close a door on a draught, and Tamsin heard the bar go down on the other side.
‘Well,’ said Kit.
‘Don’t.’
‘I said well. That’s all I said.’

They went on up. A man with a coal sack on his shoulder came down the steps towards them, saw them, and turned into an alley so narrow that he had to go sideways with the sack. Two boys stopped a snow fight to stare and were called in sharply from an upper window. At a baker’s, where the smell of bread came out warm under the door, Tamsin went in and stood at the counter, and the baker, a heavy man floured to the elbows, heard the name Edwin Leckie, turned his back, went through into the bakehouse and did not come out again. She stood a full minute among the loaves. Nobody came. In the end she put a copper on the counter, took a small brown roll, and went out.
‘Did he sell it to you?’ Kit asked.
‘I bought it. He wasn’t there to sell it.’ She tore the roll in half and gave him the bigger piece, because he was bigger, and because she wanted something to do that was not shouting at a shut door.

The thing that frightened her, she found, was not the shut doors themselves. It was how quiet they were. In Callowmere, if you knocked at the wrong door, you were told so at length, and sometimes had a bucket emptied after you for good measure. Here nobody told her anything. They looked at her as if she were weather, and then they went in out of it.
‘Someone’s warned them,’ she said. ‘Someone’s been here before us and told them not to answer.’
Kit chewed and thought about it. ‘Wilmot was behind us at the Heron last night. He wasn’t ahead of us this morning. Nobody passed us on that road.’
‘Then Leckie told them. Or his sister did.’

‘Could be. Could be they don’t like strangers.’ He swallowed the last of the bread. ‘The dogs want feeding and a roof, and so do you. There’s an inn. I remember it, if it hasn’t slid down the hill since.’

It had not. The Copper Kettle stood at a bend in the street a little above the bottom of the town, a long low building of the same grey stone, with a copper kettle the size of a barrel hung out over its door on an iron arm, gone green with weather. Behind it was a yard and a stable, and the stable was warm with horses and straw. The ostler, an old man with one eye clouded white, looked at the dogs and at Kit, named a price and took Kit’s coins without a word more. It was the most anyone in Hollin had done for them.

Kit unharnessed the dogs one by one, talking to each as he did it, the low steady talk he kept for them and never wasted on people. Hob first, then Fen and Bracken, then Sloe and Rusk. They shook themselves in the straw and lay down in a heap, all legs and tails, and Rusk put his chin on Bracken’s back and sighed. Tamsin watched Kit run his hands down each dog’s legs and feel the pads of their feet for ice cuts.
‘I’ll see to them,’ he said, not looking up. ‘You go in and get warm.’
‘I’m going up.’
‘Up where?’

She pointed with her chin. The street went on climbing past the inn, past a chapel with a squat square tower, past houses that grew smaller and meaner the higher they went, until at the very top, under the black shoulder of the nearest mine-head, there was an open space and a low stone wall round something, with a frame over it.
‘The well,’ she said. ‘Everybody in a town like this has to go to the well sooner or later. They can shut their doors, but they can’t carry water through the walls.’
Kit sat back on his heels. ‘And when they get there and see you, they’ll go home thirsty.’

‘Then I’ll have learnt something.’ She tightened the scarf at her throat. ‘Somebody in this town knows where he is. He didn’t walk up here in the autumn and vanish down a mine. Somebody took him bread, and somebody sold him coal, and somebody draws his water.’
‘And if somebody draws a knife instead?’
‘In front of the well, at noon?’ She managed something like a smile. ‘It’s a town, Kit. Not a robbers’ den.’
He looked at her a moment longer, and then he nodded, the way he nodded at a bad stretch of ice he had decided to cross after all. ‘Shout,’ he said. ‘I’ll hear you. Sound carries in these hills.’

She went out of the yard and up the street alone. The steps were steeper above the Kettle and the snow less trodden, and twice she had to stop with her back to a wall to get her breath in the thin, smoky air. The houses watched her go. She could feel them watching, every shuttered window a held breath. On the chapel step a woman with a broom stopped sweeping and stood quite still until Tamsin had passed, and when Tamsin glanced back the step was empty and the chapel door was shut.

Above the chapel the town gave out into a scatter of cottages and coal heaps, and then came the open space at the top, flat as a table and blown nearly clear of snow. The mine-head loomed over it, its great wheel still, smoke rolling from the chimney behind. The well stood in the middle with its low round wall and its winding frame and its bucket on a rope, and beside it, very small against all that grey, someone was standing with her back to the town, winding the handle round and round.

scenes.title: Isla Thorne

beats: At the well at the top of the town an old woman, Isla Thorne, is drawing water.
Tamsin asks her where Edwin Leckie can be found.
Isla tells her Leckie lies ill at his sister Bettany’s house below the chapel.

paragraphs: The old woman at the well was smaller than she had looked from below, and older than anyone Tamsin had passed on the climb. She was bent so far that the handle of the windlass came up to her shoulder, and she wore a man’s coat of brown frieze over a great many skirts, with a grey shawl crossed on her breast and knotted at the back. Her boots were bound in sacking against the ice. She wound the handle round and round without hurry and without stopping, and she did not turn, though Tamsin’s boots crunched loud on the frozen snow and there was nobody else on the whole flat top of the hill to make the sound.
The bucket came up dripping, the water in it black and smoking with cold. The old woman swung it on to the wall and began to tip it into the pail at her feet.
‘Good afternoon,’ Tamsin said.
The water poured.
‘I’m sorry to trouble you. I’m looking for a man called Edwin Leckie. He came up from Callowmere in the autumn, to his sister. I think he may be ill.’

The old woman set the bucket down on the wall and turned round at last. Her face was brown and folded like a walnut, and out of it looked two black eyes, very bright, like a blackbird’s. They went over Tamsin from her boots to her plait and back again, taking their time about it. Then she said something short and dry, in a voice like a gate on a cold morning, and turned back to her pail.

For a moment the words went past Tamsin altogether, because she had been listening for the wrong thing. Then they came back to her, the way a tune comes back, and she knew them. The old woman had said, in Hollish, that she had no words to spare for valley people, and that the valley was that way, down the hill.

Tamsin had not heard Hollish spoken aloud by anyone but herself since she was nine years old. She read it on bad nights out of her mother’s hymn book; she sang it under her breath over the ledgers when Pim was out. But that was her own voice, and she had long ago stopped hearing it. This was the real thing, rough and burred and full of the hill, and it went into her like cold water.

Behind her came a scrabble of claws and a man’s voice saying, ‘Steady, steady,’ and Kit came up over the lip of the hill with the dogs. He had them all on short leads, with Hob pulling ahead and his tongue hanging out.

‘Trough at the Kettle’s frozen to the bottom,’ he said, a little out of breath. ‘Thought I’d bring them up to drink. And I didn’t much like you up here on your own.’ He nodded to the old woman. ‘Afternoon, mother.’
The old woman looked at him, and at the dogs, and said nothing at all.
Tamsin drew a breath of the smoky air and went looking for the words. They were stiff from lying unused, like a coat taken out of a chest, but they were there.

‘Grandmother,’ she said in Hollish, ‘forgive me. I didn’t hear you rightly at first. I’ve come four days up the river to find Edwin Leckie, and nobody in this town will open a door to me long enough to tell me if he is alive.’
The old woman’s hands stopped on the bucket.

She turned again, slowly, and this time she looked at Tamsin as if she had not really looked before. Something moved in the walnut face, under all its folds, and for a moment Tamsin could not tell whether it was anger or something else.
‘Say that again,’ the old woman said.
Tamsin said it again.

‘Where did a valley girl get that voice?’ The words came quick now, sharp as pecks. ‘That is not chapel Hollish out of a book. That is a kitchen in Hollin. That is the top of the town, by the way you roll it, and a long time ago.’
‘From my mother,’ Tamsin said. ‘Ysolde. She was born here. She went down the river when she was young and married a clockmaker in Callowmere.’
For a long moment the old woman said nothing. Down in the town a dog barked and Fen answered it, and Kit hushed her.

‘Ysolde,’ the old woman said at last, and it was quite a different word in her mouth from the one Tamsin had always heard. ‘Ysolde, who sang flat in chapel and would fight you if you said so. Ysolde, who climbed that mine-head for a dare when she was eleven, and I set her ankle after.’ She came a step nearer and put up one cold, dry hand and touched Tamsin’s cheek just under the eye, the way you might touch a clock face to see whether the glass was dusty. ‘You have her chin. She stood like that too, as if the ground owed her money.’
Tamsin found that her eyes were stinging, and blamed the smoke.
‘Is she well?’ the old woman asked. ‘She never came back. They never do.’
‘She died when I was nine. The marsh fever. It comes up off the river in a wet autumn.’

‘The valley.’ The old woman said it like a curse, and then, more quietly, a word Tamsin had not heard since the night her mother was buried, the short hill word that means both rest and sleep. ‘I am Isla Thorne. I brought half this hill into the world, and I have seen most of the other half out of it. I knew your mother before she had all her teeth.’

Isla Thorne had no lowland speech at all. She had not been rude, Tamsin saw now, so much as plain. Now she was talking fast, in the old burred Hollish, and Tamsin had to listen with her whole body to keep up.

Kit stood by with the dogs and understood not one word of it. He looked from one woman to the other like a man watching a card game whose rules nobody had told him, and when Isla gave a single dry cackle he smiled politely, as if he had been in on the joke.

‘The man you want,’ Isla said, ‘is Edwin Leckie, who came up the road at leaf-fall with a cough on him and fear in his face. He lies at his sister Bettany’s house, below the chapel. Lung fever. I have been in to him morning and night since the first snow, and he is not dead yet, which is more than I promised Bettany.’
‘Below the chapel,’ Tamsin repeated. ‘Then why did the whole town shut its doors on me? Every one.’

‘Because he asked them to.’ Isla shrugged inside the big coat. ‘He came up frightened. He told Bettany that men from the city might come asking for him, and Bettany told the chapel, and in Hollin what the chapel knows by Sunday the whole hill knows by Monday. You come up from the valley with a big man and a sledge and his name in your mouth, what do you expect?’ She glanced at Kit. ‘He looks like a man from the city who comes asking.’
‘He’s from Dunmere. He drives dogs. He wouldn’t frighten a hen.’
Isla looked Kit up and down, from beard to boots, and said something dry about hens that Tamsin decided not to pass on.
‘What’s she saying?’ Kit asked.
‘That Master Leckie’s alive. He’s at his sister’s house, below the chapel. He’s very ill.’

Kit’s face cleared like a sky. ‘Alive. Well, then.’ He looked at the old woman with plain gratitude, and then he frowned, hunting for something, and came out with one of the only two words of Hollish he had ever owned up to. It was the word for thank you. He said it carefully, as if it might go off in his hands.
Isla stared at him. Then she laughed outright, the cackle again, and said something to Tamsin.
‘She says you have a voice like a bullock,’ Tamsin told him, ‘but better manners than most.’
‘I’ll take that.’

‘Bettany will not open to you,’ Isla said, turning back to her pail. ‘Not to strangers, and not by daylight with the whole street watching. Go at lamp-lighting, when I have been in to him with his draught and he is awake. Knock, and give her your name and your father’s name. That will do it, if anything will.’

She bent for the pail, and Kit, without being asked, stepped in and took it from her, dogs and all. Isla let him. Then she said in Hollish, without looking round, ‘And afterwards you will come to me, Ysolde’s girl, and tell me how she lived. All of it. I want to know.’
‘I will,’ Tamsin said. ‘I promise.’

The old woman nodded once, as if a bargain had been struck, and set off down the hill towards the chapel with her hands folded under her shawl. Kit followed with the pail in one fist and five leads in the other, and the dogs, smelling a house somewhere ahead, towed him after her at a stumbling trot.

scenes.title: Bettany’s house

beats: Bettany Leckie lets them in only when Tamsin gives her name.
Edwin Leckie lies by the stove, thin and feverish, afraid at first that Slade has sent them.
He weeps when he sees Aldous’s daughter, and says he has something that belongs to her.

paragraphs: The lamps of Hollin came on one by one as the dark came down, small yellow squares climbing the hill behind the shutters, until the mine-heads above the town were only black shapes against a sky the colour of slate. The cold came down with the dark. By the time Tamsin and Kit climbed back past the Copper Kettle, the snow on the steps had frozen to a crust that rang under their boots.

Bettany Leckie’s house stood a little below the chapel, where Isla had said: tall and narrow, with its gable end against the hill and a rowan by the door, bare of everything but a few shrivelled black berries. Light showed at the edges of the downstairs shutter, and smoke went up from the chimney. Tamsin knocked.
Nothing. She knocked again. The light at the edge of the shutter wavered, as if someone had carried the lamp away from the window.

‘Who’s there?’ It was a woman’s voice, close against the door, and it asked first in Hollish and then, before Tamsin could answer, in the river speech of the lowlands, flat and hard. ‘We’ve nothing for sale and no beds. Go down to the Kettle.’
‘I’m looking for Master Edwin Leckie.’
‘There’s no one here of that name.’
Kit shifted his weight behind her. Tamsin kept her voice low. The street was dark, but she did not think it was empty.
‘Mistress Leckie, Isla Thorne sent me. My name is Tamsin Orr. Aldous Orr was my father.’

There was a silence on the other side of the door. Then a bolt, and a second bolt, and the scrape of a bar lifted out of its brackets. The door opened a hand’s breadth, and then wider, and a tall woman stood in it with a lamp held high, so that the light fell full on Tamsin’s face and left her own in shadow.

‘Orr,’ she said. ‘Aldous Orr’s girl.’ She brought the lamp nearer, and her eyes went over Tamsin’s face as if she were checking it against something. ‘Edwin talks of you. Of your father too, when the fever has hold of him.’ She looked past Tamsin at Kit. ‘And who’s this?’
‘Kit Ansel. He drove me up from Callowmere.’
‘Then he can wipe his feet like anyone else. Come in, quick. You’re letting the heat out and the whole street in.’

Bettany Leckie was nearer sixty than fifty, tall and spare, with iron-grey hair scraped back under a linen cap and her sleeves rolled to the elbow over forearms reddened by washing. She had her brother’s long nose and none of his softness. Her lowland speech had the hill in it, every word clipped short, as though each one cost her something and she meant to get her money’s worth. She barred the door behind them before she did anything else.

The room was low and hot and very close. A black iron stove stood against the back wall with a kettle ticking on it, and bunches of something grey hung drying from the beams, and the air smelled of goose grease and mustard and of something bitter in a covered jug on the table. In the corner by the dresser stood a tall old clock painted with faded red flowers, silent, its hands stopped at a quarter past four; Tamsin’s father would not have let it stand idle a day. She noticed it the way she would have noticed a wrong figure in a column, and then she forgot it, because of the bed.

It was a settle bed, drawn up close to the stove and heaped with blankets and a sheepskin, and there was a man in it. He had woken at the sound of the bolts. He was struggling up on one elbow, the blankets sliding off him, his eyes huge and glittering in the lamplight.

‘Bet?’ His voice was a rasp. ‘Bet, who is it? Who’ve you let in?’ He peered past the lamp at the two shapes by the door, and Tamsin saw him take in Kit’s size and shrink from it. ‘Has he sent them? Has Slade sent them? Tell them I haven’t got it. Tell them I burned it. Tell them...’

The cough took him then, a long tearing cough that bent him double over the edge of the bed, and Bettany was there before it had finished, one arm round his shoulders and a cup of water in her other hand.
‘Hush, Edwin. Hush. Nobody’s sent anybody. Drink.’

His beard was white and cut square, and when he reached for the cup it was with his left hand; the forefinger of his right had lost its top joint to a lathe long ago. Tamsin had known that hand all her life. She had watched it on the lathe in the workshop on Gilt Street when she was smaller than the bench, working the chisel left-handed while he whistled through his teeth, and for years she had believed that left-handed was the proper way to turn brass and that her father did it wrongly.

But she had not known this face. He was terribly thin. The cheeks had fallen in under the beard, and the skin over the bones was thin and yellow as old paper, and the eyes had sunk so far back that the lamplight barely reached them. He was sixty-one, and looked eighty.
She came forward into the light and knelt by the bed, so that he would not have to look up at her.
‘Master Leckie,’ she said. ‘It’s Tamsin.’

He stared. For a long moment she thought the fever had him too far gone to know her. Then the cup shook, and Bettany took it from him, and his mouth worked under the beard without any sound coming out of it.
‘Tamsin,’ he said at last. ‘Tamsin Orr. Aldous’s girl.’

And he wept. He did not make a noise about it. His face simply crumpled, the way a child’s does, and the tears ran out of the sunken eyes and down into the white beard, and he put out his left hand and took hold of her coat sleeve and held it as though she might be taken away again.
‘You came,’ he said. ‘All that way. In winter, on the ice.’
‘Four days,’ she said. ‘It’s not so far.’

‘It’s far enough. It was far enough for him.’ He shut his eyes, and the tears went on running. ‘He came up that river every winter for brass, your father. Every winter. I used to tell him the ice would have him one day, and he used to laugh at me.’
Tamsin found she could not answer that. She put her hand over his where it gripped her sleeve. It was dry and burning hot, all knuckle.
‘And the boy?’ he asked presently. ‘Pim?’
‘Seventeen, and taller than the door. He’s minding the house.’
‘Minding the house.’ Something like a smile moved the beard. ‘He’ll have taken every clock in it to pieces by the time you’re home. Does he know? Have you told him?’
‘No,’ she said. ‘Not yet.’
He nodded, as if that were right, and his grip tightened. His eyes came open again, fever-bright, fixed on her face.

‘I have something of yours,’ he said. ‘Something that belongs to you, Tamsin. I should have given it you in Callowmere. I should have walked across Gilt Street and put it in your hand. I was afraid. I have been afraid since the leaves came down, and I am a coward, and your father would be ashamed of me.’
‘He would not,’ Tamsin said. ‘What is it? Master Leckie, what have you got?’

But the cough came again, worse than before, and this time it did not stop. Bettany pushed Tamsin aside without ceremony and held her brother up while he fought for breath, and Kit, who had stood all this while by the door with his cap in his hands, came and took the lamp from the table and held it where she could see.
When it was over Leckie lay back grey and slack against the sheepskin, his eyes half shut, his chest going up and down very fast under the blankets.

‘That’s enough,’ Bettany said. She did not raise her voice. She did not need to. ‘He’s been burning since noon. Isla said no talking, and here he is talking himself into the grave over his visitors. Whatever it is will keep till morning.’

Tamsin opened her mouth, and shut it again. Everything in her wanted to take the old man by the shoulders and have it out of him there and then; she had come four days for it, and very nearly drowned for it. But she looked at his face on the sheepskin and held her tongue.
‘Tomorrow,’ Leckie whispered. ‘When my head is clear. I’ll tell you all of it. I swear it on your father’s clock.’
‘Come in the morning,’ Bettany said, already moving them towards the door. ‘Not before it’s light, and not up the front street. Come round by the chapel yard, and knock twice.’

She lifted the bar. The cold came in round them like water. And as Tamsin stepped out into the dark she heard the old man behind her say, quite clearly, to nobody, ‘It belongs to her, Bet. Don’t let anyone else have it.’

scenes.title: The receipt

beats: In the morning Leckie tells Tamsin the truth: her father paid the debt in full, in gold, to Slade himself, the week before he drowned.
Slade signed a receipt and never entered the payment in the guild’s books; he kept the gold.
This autumn, when Slade began pressing him about the old debt, Leckie understood what the receipt meant and ran north with it.
Leckie has hidden the receipt and his key in the house and is too weak to fetch them; Tamsin must wait until he can.

paragraphs: The sky had cleared in the night, and the morning came up hard and blue over the mine-heads. They came round by the chapel yard as Bettany had told them and knocked twice. Bettany let them in, looked them over, and put on her shawl.
‘I’m going up to Isla for more of the draught,’ she said. ‘He’s cooler this morning. Don’t tire him.’ She said something more to her brother, about eating his porridge, and went out.

Leckie was propped against a bolster on the settle bed with the sheepskin round his shoulders. Someone had combed his beard. His face was still grey and his breath still came short, but the fever had gone out of his eyes in the night and left them clear and very tired. He looked at Tamsin, and then at Kit, who stood just inside the door turning his cap in his hands.
‘I’ll wait outside,’ Kit said. ‘There’s wood wants splitting.’
‘Stay,’ said Tamsin. ‘He knows about the debt, Master Leckie. All of it. He pulled me out of the river at Corran, and I told him afterwards.’
Leckie looked at Kit a while longer. ‘Then stay,’ he said. ‘If she trusts you, I must.’
Kit sat down on a stool by the stove, his big knees nearly up to his chin. Tamsin drew the other stool close to the bed.

‘I found the sewn page in Father’s last ledger,’ she said. ‘Four hundred and twelve crowns, borrowed from the guild against the house, and never repaid. At the Reckoning Slade will read it out, and the house will go to the guild.’
‘I know what the guild’s books say.’ He shut his eyes for a moment. When he opened them they were wet, but his voice was steady. ‘Tamsin. Listen to me.’
‘Your father paid it,’ Leckie said. ‘Every crown, in gold, into Slade’s own hands, the week before he drowned.’
Nobody spoke. In the corner the painted clock stood silent at its quarter past four, and Tamsin counted five, six, seven in her head before she found that she had stopped breathing and started again.
‘The guild’s books,’ she said.

‘The guild’s books say what Corvin Slade wrote in them. He was treasurer then, and the treasurer kept the books.’ Leckie’s hand moved on the blanket. ‘The bells cost more than the guild would pay. Your father wanted a proper ring for the great clock, and he would not let me share the cost. So he borrowed it, and never told me how. That winter the guild paid us for the clock at last, and he turned every penny of it into gold, walked across the Chain Bridge with it in a bag, and came back light.’
‘You saw him go?’

‘I saw him come back. That night in the workshop he took a folded paper out of his coat and put it in my hand. Put that by safe, Edwin, he said. The bells are paid for.’ The old man’s mouth twisted. ‘I thought he meant the bell-founder. I read it once and put it in my drawer with my bills, and the next morning he went north for the brass. And then the ice.’
Kit made a sound low in his throat. His hands were flat on his knees, pressing down hard, as if he were holding something in.
‘So that’s where it went,’ he said. ‘Four hundred and twelve crowns in gold, into Slade’s pocket. And her father in the river a week after, and nobody left alive who knew but Slade.’
‘And me,’ said Leckie. ‘Only I didn’t know I knew.’
‘Eleven years,’ Tamsin said. ‘Eleven years that paper sat in your box.’

‘I never thought of it. Then this autumn Slade sent for me to the Guildhall. He was very civil. He gave me wine. He said there was an old debt of Aldous’s against the house, four hundred and twelve crowns, never repaid, and it must come out at the Reckoning unless some arrangement could be made between friends. He wanted my name on a paper giving the house up quietly. When I said I must think about it, he said the river was very cold for old men who walked home late.’
‘He threatened you,’ said Kit.

‘Every week after that. Men in the lane at night. A dead rat on the step. But it was the number that stayed with me. I lay awake with it, and at three in the morning I got up and opened the drawer, and there it was. Paid in full, four hundred and twelve crowns in gold, received of Aldous Orr: C. Slade. Signed, sealed and dated. And then I understood what I had been keeping all those years, and what he would do to anyone who had it.’
‘So you ran,’ Tamsin said.

‘I ran. I took the paper, and I took my key, because he had asked after my key twice, and anything Corvin Slade asks for I have learned not to give him. I told myself they would come after me and leave you be. I meant to write. Then the cough took me on the road at Dunmere, and I have not held a pen since.’
‘Where is it now?’ It came out sharp, and she could not help it. ‘The receipt, and the key.’
‘Here, in this house. Hidden.’ He saw her eyes go round the room, and something like humour moved in the beard. ‘You won’t find it by looking, child. I made sure of that.’
‘Then tell me where.’

‘No.’ He said it gently, and his left hand closed over hers. ‘Not to you, and not to Bet, though she asks me every day. You say Slade’s clerk followed you up the river. If I tell you, you will fetch it, and then it is in your pocket in an inn with his man in the next room. If nobody knows where it is, nobody can be made to tell. When I can stand on my own two feet I will fetch it myself and put it into your hand. Not before.’
‘There are thirty-four days to Thaw Day,’ Tamsin said, ‘and four of them are the road home.’
‘Then I had better mend quickly. Isla says I shall. She is generally right, and very disagreeable about it.’
Kit cleared his throat. ‘He has the right of it, Tamsin,’ he said, not happily. ‘I don’t like it either. But he has.’

She found nothing to say that would not be shouting. Leckie’s eyes were already closing. His hand slackened on hers, and in a little while he was asleep, his mouth open in the white beard and the sheepskin rising and falling.
When Leckie had done talking, Tamsin sat a long time without moving. Kit got up once, quietly, and fed the stove, and sat down again.

She thought of her father on the ice below Corran Weir, eleven winters ago, with a sledge-load of brass behind him, hurrying to beat the thaw bell. She had always pictured him anxious on that last journey, a man with a debt at his back. He had not been. He had been a free man going home, with the bells paid for and the receipt put safe away. And all the while Slade had sat in the Guildhall with her father’s gold in his keeping and the debt still standing in his books, and had waited eleven years to call it in.

The anger came slowly, and then all at once, so hot that it frightened her. And under it, the way warmth comes back into numb fingers, painful and unmistakable, came hope. The house could be saved. It was true, and it could be proved, and the proof was somewhere within twenty feet of her.

She took her pocket book and pencil from her coat and sat down at Bettany’s table. A thing not written down had not happened: it was the first rule of the counting room, and her father had taught it her. She wrote with her left hand, slowly, the splint on her right wrist lying stiff and useless on the table edge, and the letters came out shaky as a child’s, wandering above and below the line. She did not care. She wrote the day, the thirteenth day, counting Lantern Night, and then everything Leckie had said, as near his own words as she could make it: the bells, the gold, the folded paper, the wine at the Guildhall and the river that was cold for old men. She read it through twice and put it away inside her coat.
Outside, the sound of the axe had started up some time ago, steady as a clock. She found Kit in the lean-to behind the house, splitting logs with his coat off, his breath going up in clouds.
‘Bettany’s woodpile is a disgrace,’ he said, without stopping. ‘I’m mending it.’
Tamsin bent and gathered an armful of kindling from the splinters at his feet, holding it against her chest in her good arm.
‘Where does it go?’
‘By the stove. Mind the step, it’s glass.’ He swung, and the log fell neatly in two, and he looked at her over it. ‘We’ll get it, Tamsin. Whatever he’s done with it, we’ll get it.’
‘I know,’ she said, and found that for the first time since Lantern Night she did, and went in with the kindling.

scenes.title: The Copper Kettle

beats: A blizzard shuts the valley; no sledge can leave Hollin for weeks.
Dace Wilmot arrives at the Copper Kettle half-frozen, on the last sledge up before the road closed.
Wilmot offers Tamsin money for Leckie’s papers, and she refuses.
Kit wants to throw him out into the snow; Tamsin stops him.

paragraphs: The snow came down the valley on the fourteenth day, not so much falling as arriving: a grey wall that swallowed the mine-heads first, then the chapel roof, then the houses across the street. By noon Tamsin could not see the well at the top of the town from the door of the Copper Kettle. By dusk the landlord had barred every shutter and hung a lantern in the passage, and the miners in the taproom were telling one another, in Hollish, that the road down to the lake was gone and would not come back until the wind allowed it.
‘How long?’ Kit asked, when she had put it into plain speech for him.
‘Weeks, they say. The man by the fire says until the thaw, but he has been saying that since he sat down, and he is on his fourth cup.’

Kit looked at the barred shutters as if he could see through them to the stable behind the inn, where Hob and Fen and Bracken and Sloe and Rusk lay curled nose to tail in the straw. He had been out to them twice that afternoon, swearing cheerfully at the cold. He did not swear now. He sat with his big hands round his cup and said nothing at all, which in Kit Ansel was worse than any oath.

Tamsin did her sums instead, because sums were what she had. It was the fourteenth day, counting Lantern Night as the first. The Reckoning sat on the forty-seventh. That left thirty-three days, and four of them would be wanted for the run home down the ice, if the ice held and the dogs held and nothing else went wrong. Under her sleeve the splint itched where the bandage had worked loose. She could not scratch it. She could not hurry the snow. She could only count, and keep counting, and not let the number frighten her.

Near midnight someone beat on the inn door with a fist. The landlord grumbled down the passage with his lantern, and when he drew the bar the wind came in ahead of him, a long scouring howl that set every candle in the taproom streaming sideways. Two men came in with it. One was a squat carter in sheepskins with ice in his eyebrows, swearing in Hollish that his was the last sledge up before the road closed and he the last fool to try it. The other he was holding up by the collar.

The second man was lean and grey in the face, and his lips had gone the colour of slate. His coat was stiff with frozen snow, but where the snow had cracked away the cloth showed bottle-green. When the landlord lowered him onto the settle by the fire he sat with his hands in his lap like things that did not belong to him, and Tamsin saw the ink on his cuffs.
Kit was on his feet before she was.
‘Leave it,’ she said, low.
‘That’s him. That’s the clerk.’
‘I know who it is.’

Dace Wilmot lifted his head. It took him a long time to find her across the room, but he managed it: the polite smile came up through the frost like something rising slowly through dark water. ‘Miss Orr,’ he said. His teeth were chattering so hard that the words came out in pieces. ‘What a fortunate meeting.’
The landlord’s wife fetched blankets and a pan of snow to rub his hands with, and Tamsin sat where she was and watched. She was ashamed of not helping. She did not help.

For six days the snow did not stop. It came sideways down the valley and filled the streets to the sills, and the town dug narrow trenches between its doors and went about bent double in them. Every morning Tamsin and Kit roped themselves together at the inn door and fought their way down past the chapel to Bettany Leckie’s house, where Bettany let them in without a word and barred the door behind them, and Edwin Leckie lay by the stove and coughed and tried to smile. He was no stronger. He would not say where he had put the things he had brought north, not to Tamsin, not even to his sister, and Tamsin had stopped asking, because asking made him weep. And every evening Dace Wilmot sat in the corner of the taproom by the fire, thawed and shaved and courteous, writing in a little pocketbook with a pencil, and every evening he rose and bowed to her when she came in.

He paid for his board in silver. He praised the landlord’s mutton in careful lowland speech that the landlord did not understand. He never followed them down the hill; Tamsin looked back for him every morning and never once saw the green coat in the trench behind them. That was almost worse. It meant he had no need to.
On the twentieth night he brought his cup to their table and sat down without asking.
‘You’ll find another chair,’ Kit said.

‘This one does very well, thank you.’ Wilmot turned the cup in his long fingers. The ink on his cuffs had been scrubbed at and had not come out. ‘Miss Orr, I will not waste your evening. I think it is time we spoke plainly. I have a good ear, and the walls of inns are thin. I know what you came north for.’
‘I came north to fetch my father’s partner home.’

‘Of course you did.’ The smile again, patient as a schoolmaster’s. ‘And Mr Leckie is a sick old man, and sick old men keep papers, and papers are a great deal of trouble to carry about the country in winter. I am empowered to take that trouble off your hands.’ He set the cup down, folded his stained hands beside it, and waited until she looked at him.
‘Fifty crowns,’ Wilmot said, ‘for the old man’s papers, and you can go home in the spring with money in your pocket.’

It was more than the house paid her in two years, and Wilmot knew it to the penny. For the space of a breath she let herself see it as he meant her to: a purse, a room somewhere for herself and Pim, an end to sums done in the dark. Then the bookkeeper in her found the catch, written small at the bottom, the way catches always were.
‘In the spring,’ she said. ‘After Thaw Day.’
‘The roads will be kinder then.’

‘And the house will be gone, and the guild will have it, and I shall have fifty crowns and a brother to feed and nowhere to put him.’ She heard her voice sharpen, the way it always did when she was frightened, and let it. ‘You keep books for a living, Mr Wilmot. So do I. Don’t insult me with a column that doesn’t add up.’
‘Then name your figure.’
‘There isn’t one. Mr Leckie’s papers are Mr Leckie’s. I am not selling what isn’t mine, and if it were mine I would not sell it to you.’
Wilmot sighed, as a tutor sighs over a slow pupil. ‘That is a pity. It is a long winter, Miss Orr, and a small town, and so very much snow. People do have accidents in snow.’

Kit moved. He was round the table before his bench had finished scraping, his fist was in the bottle-green collar, and Wilmot came up out of his chair like a sack on a hoist. The taproom went quiet. Kit dragged the clerk two long strides towards the door, and the lantern in the passage swung on its hook.
‘Kit.’
‘He can go and talk about accidents to the snow,’ Kit said. ‘See what it says back.’
Tamsin got up and caught his arm with her left hand, the only one she had. It was like catching hold of a tree in a gale. She did not let go.
‘If you put him out tonight he’ll be dead before he reaches the chapel.’
‘Yes,’ said Kit.

‘And then there is a dead guild clerk in a Hollin drift, and a Dunmere driver who put him there, and a whole taproom to swear to it. They would hang you, Kit. And they would say I set you on, and they would be glad to say it. He wants something to carry home. Don’t give it to him.’

For a long moment Kit stood breathing hard, the clerk’s toes just brushing the boards. Then he opened his hand. Wilmot dropped, staggered, caught the back of a chair, and stood. He straightened his collar and his cuffs, and when he looked up the smile was back in its place as if it had never left.
‘Thank you, Miss Orr. That was very nicely reasoned.’
‘I didn’t do it for you.’
‘No,’ Wilmot said. ‘But I shall remember it all the same.’

He picked up his cup, which had not spilled, and carried it back to his corner by the fire. Kit sat down heavily at the table, and Tamsin sat beside him and found that her knees were shaking under the table. Behind the shutters the wind went on and on, and in the corner the pencil began to move again across the little book.

scenes.title: Isla’s cure

beats: Weeks pass in snow; Tamsin sits with Leckie, who is slowly mending, and learns the hill songs again from Isla.
Isla cuts the splint away.
The wrist is thin and weak; Isla gives her a ball of beeswax to squeeze until it is strong.

paragraphs: The snow stayed. After the first great storm it came more softly, but it came every day, and the valley filled with it the way a cup fills under a slow tap. The road down to the lake lay somewhere under twelve feet of white, the men at the Copper Kettle said, and nobody went to look. The mine-heads still smoked above the town, because the mines went down where the weather could not follow, and every morning the shifts climbed the hill in a black line with their lamps, and every evening they came down again. Between those two lines of lamps the days ran together, until Tamsin had to count them on her fingers to be sure of them.

She spent them at Bettany’s house. Edwin Leckie was mending, but slowly, the way old men mend: a little gained in the day and half of it lost again in the night. In the second week of the snow he sat up. In the third he ate a whole bowl of Bettany’s barley broth and asked for more, and Bettany turned away to the pot so that nobody should see her face. By the fourth he could sit in the chair by the stove for an hour at a time with a blanket over his knees, and talk a little about clocks. He did not talk about the other thing. When Tamsin came in each morning he looked up at her with his wet, frightened, fond eyes and said, ‘Not yet, my dear. Soon,’ and she said, ‘I know,’ and sat down beside him and read aloud from one of Bettany’s three books, of which one was a herbal and one an almanac older than Pim.

Kit came down with her most mornings and went back to the inn in the afternoons, where he had made the stable into a workshop. He had taken every strap of harness off the Long Patience and was going over it inch by inch with an awl and waxed thread and a pot of tallow, mending what was frayed and replacing what was past mending. When she looked in on him at dusk he would hold up a trace or a collar for her to admire, and the five dogs would thump their tails in the straw as if they admired it too.
‘Something to do with my hands,’ he said, when she teased him. ‘Else I’d be down that valley with a shovel.’

Isla Thorne came most afternoons, stumping down from the top of the town with her bundle of simples under her shawl. She listened to Leckie’s chest with her ear pressed to his back, brewed him something black and bitter that made him shudder, and scolded him in Hollish, which he did not understand and bore meekly. Then, the work done, she would sit on the stool by the stove with her small bent hands folded in her lap, and sing.

Tamsin had known the songs once. Her mother had sung them over the washing and over the bread and over Tamsin’s cot, and after the marsh fever took her there had been nobody to sing them, and Tamsin had let them go a word at a time, the way a language goes when there is no one left to speak it to. Now they came back. Isla would sing a verse, and Tamsin would find the tune waiting for her like a coat on a peg, and halfway through the second verse find she had the words as well, or most of them. Where she stumbled, Isla stopped and gave her the word again, patiently, and laughed out loud when she got it wrong. There was a song about the lambs brought down from the high grazing before the first snow, and a song for counting stitches, and a long sad one about a hill girl who married a man from the plain and never came home again, which Isla sang with her bright black eyes on Tamsin as though there were a lesson in it.
‘Your mother sang that one badly,’ Isla said in Hollish, when it was done. ‘She always cried at the end and lost the tune.’
‘So do I,’ Tamsin said.
‘Then sing it badly. It is a bad song. It makes everybody cry, and then they ask for it again.’

Leckie, who had understood none of it, had his eyes shut and was smiling. ‘Ysolde used to sing that one,’ he said. ‘In the workshop on Gilt Street, with Aldous hammering away at the bench and pretending not to listen. I never knew what the words were.’

Tamsin did not tell him. She thought of Gilt Street instead, as she did every night now when she lay awake in her narrow room under the eaves of the Kettle: the shop with its thirty clocks all going at once, the smell of oil and brass and coal smoke, the bench under the window where Pim folded his long legs and hummed while he worked. She wondered whether Pim remembered to bank the stove. She wondered whether he was eating, and who was talking to him, and what he had been told, and by whom. The snow pressed against the inn shutters like a hand against a door, and somewhere far below it, four days south, the river ran under its ice to the sea and the city, and she could not reach either of them.

On the thirty-third day Isla came in the morning instead of the afternoon, and instead of going to Leckie she went to Tamsin, took hold of her arm above the splint, and turned it to the light from the window.
‘Thirty days since you fell,’ she said in Hollish. ‘Let us see what your lowland bonesetter did.’

She unwound the bandage, which had been white when Hesketh Fane put it on in his shop that smelled of camphor and was now the colour of old porridge. Under it the slats of the splint lay neat and true in their lashings. Isla grunted over them as one craftsman grunts over another’s joinery.
‘He knew his trade, your old man.’
‘He would like to hear you say so.’
‘Then you will tell him.’ Isla drew a little hooked knife from her belt and slipped it under the last of the cords. ‘Hold still.’

Isla cut the splint away on the thirtieth day after the fall, and Tamsin’s right wrist came out of it thin and white and weak as a fledgling. She had not seen it for a month. She had imagined it, under the bandage, as it had always been, and the thing that lay on the table in front of her now was not that. It was smaller than Pim’s had been when he was ten. The skin was wrinkled and flaking and smelled stale, and the blue veins showed through it like cracks under ice. When she told her fingers to move they moved, slowly, as if they had to be asked twice. When she tried to bend the wrist itself, a white pain went up her arm to the elbow, and she shut her eyes and did not cry out.
‘Yes,’ Isla said, quite gently. ‘It forgets. Bones remember, but the flesh forgets. We will remind it.’

She washed the arm in warm water with something green steeped in it, and rubbed it with a salve that smelled of pine, and bent the fingers one by one, and then the wrist, a little further than Tamsin wanted and not as far as she feared. Tamsin bit her lip and watched the window. Across the room Leckie had opened his eyes and was watching her with such distress that she made herself smile at him.
‘It’s nothing,’ she told him in his own speech. ‘She’s being kind to it.’

When it was over, Isla felt in the pocket of her apron and brought out a ball of beeswax, brown-gold and the size of a small apple. It was warm from her pocket and smelled of honey and summer, and of the candle-ends Tamsin’s mother used to save in a jar on the dresser to polish the table on feast days. Isla closed Tamsin’s thin fingers round it, one by one, and folded her own hands over them.

‘Squeeze,’ she said in Hollish. ‘A hundred times in the morning and a hundred at night, and whenever you are frightened, and whenever you are bored. When you can crush it flat as a coin, the hand is yours again. Not before.’

Tamsin squeezed. It was like trying to crush a stone. She managed a dent so shallow she had to tilt the ball to the window to see it, four faint ovals where her fingertips had been, and her arm trembled with the effort to the shoulder.
Isla laughed, delighted, and patted her cheek. ‘Good. Now you have something to do with your hands besides worry.’

Leckie leaned forward in his chair. ‘May I see?’ She held it out to him, and he took the wax in his good left hand and turned it to the light as though it were a movement he had been asked to mend. ‘It will wind a clock again,’ he said at last. ‘By Thaw Day it will wind the great one.’
He gave it back to her. Tamsin closed her fingers on it, and squeezed, and made a second dent beside the first.

scenes.title: The key and the snowbell

beats: Leckie, strong enough to stand, takes the receipt and his vault key from inside the case of Bettany’s old clock and gives them to Tamsin.
Tamsin sews the receipt into the lining of her coat.
Isla brings her something to carry home, and tells her something in Hollish that Kit cannot follow.

paragraphs: On the thirty-eighth day Edwin Leckie stood up.

He did it without warning, in the middle of the morning, while Bettany was out at the chapel and Kit was telling him about the dogs. He put both hands on the arms of his chair and pushed, and his face went grey and then pink, and he was standing, swaying a little, with the blanket slipping off his knees to the floor. Kit was beside him in one stride with an arm behind his back.
‘Steady, sir.’
‘I am quite steady, thank you, Mr Ansel. Be so good as to walk me to the clock.’

Bettany’s old clock stood in the corner of the kitchen beside the dresser, a tall Hollin case painted with faded red flowers, its hands stopped at a quarter past four. Tamsin had looked at it every day for nearly a month without thinking about it at all, except, once or twice, that it was a shame nobody wound it. Leckie crossed the room to it on Kit’s arm, five slow steps and a rest and four more, and leaned his forehead against its painted door for a moment, breathing. Then he opened the door with a little key from his waistcoat and reached down inside, behind the hanging weights, to a ledge in the back of the case that Tamsin would never have known was there.
‘A clockmaker hides things in clocks,’ he said, a little out of breath. ‘Your father would have laughed at me. He always said I had no imagination.’
He brought out a flat packet of oilskin tied with tarred twine and put it into her hands.

Tamsin did not remember untying the twine. Her fingers were clumsy, and the knots were Leckie’s, small and many, and at some point Kit took out his knife and cut them for her without a word. Inside the oilskin was a folded half-sheet of heavy paper, gone the colour of weak tea, and under it a key. It was small and old and made of brass worn smooth with handling, and it hung from a loop of plaited cord.

She unfolded the paper. At its head was the guild’s seal, the scales and the anchor, and below that a date eleven winters gone. Below the date, in a thin, careful hand she knew from every notice that had ever been nailed to the Guildhall door, were the words she had come four days up a frozen river to find. Paid in full, four hundred and twelve crowns in gold, received of Aldous Orr: C. Slade.

She read it three times. The third time the letters began to swim, and she put the back of her hand to her eyes and found it wet. She had not known she was going to cry. She had thought, when this came, if it came, that she would feel cold and clear and clever, the way she felt when a column of figures balanced at last after a long night. Instead she felt thirteen years old, and she was laughing as well as crying, and could not stop either.
‘Is that it?’ Kit said. ‘Tamsin. Is that it?’
‘That’s it.’

He let out a whoop that rattled the plates on Bettany’s dresser, and then, recollecting himself, looked anxiously at Leckie, who was crying too, quite openly, his white square beard wet with it. Kit lowered him back into the chair by the stove and tucked the blanket round his knees with enormous care, and then came back and put his big arms round Tamsin and lifted her clean off the floor, and set her down again, and said, ‘Sorry,’ and did not look sorry at all.

‘I kept it eleven years,’ Leckie said from the chair. ‘Eleven years in a drawer with my bills, and never once understood what it was. Not until he started asking after it. Forgive me, my dear. I was a coward and a fool.’
‘You were neither,’ Tamsin said. ‘You brought it here. That’s all anyone needs to know.’

She weighed the key in her palm. Beside it, on her belt, hung the Orrs’ key, which she had worn every day for eleven years; she lifted it on its chain and held the two together, and they lay side by side in her hand like a pair of gloves. She slipped Leckie’s key into her coat pocket and buttoned the flap over it, and put her hand on the flap, and kept it there.

The paper was another matter. A pocket could be picked; a pocket could be turned out. She took off her coat and laid it inside-out across the kitchen table, and fetched Bettany’s workbox from the dresser.
‘I could do that,’ Kit offered. ‘I’ve been sewing harness for a month.’
‘You sew like a sailmaker. This wants doing small.’

She unpicked six inches of the lining seam at the left breast, where the coat lay closest against her heart, and folded the receipt once more and slid it in flat against the wool. Her fingers were stiff still, and twice she had to stop and flex them and take up the needle again, and Kit watched her with his arms folded and said nothing, which she was grateful for. She sewed the receipt into the lining of her coat with small, tight stitches. When it was done she put the coat on and buttoned it to the throat, and could feel the paper there, faintly, when she breathed.

Isla came in the early afternoon, with snow on her shawl and something flat wrapped in a clean cloth. She looked at Leckie standing by the stove, for he had insisted on standing again to show her, and clicked her tongue and pushed him back into his chair, and then she looked at Tamsin, and at the coat buttoned to the throat, and nodded once as if a thing she had been waiting for had come.

‘For the old man in your city,’ she said in Hollish, and unwrapped the cloth. ‘The bonesetter whose wife came from the hills. You told me you had made him a promise. A promise to a widower should be kept.’

Isla gave her a snowbell pressed flat between two leaves of paper, and Tamsin put it inside her mother’s Hollish hymn book to keep. It was very small, a single bell, white with a breath of blue, on a thread of stem, gone faintly transparent with pressing, and it had been picked, Isla said, on the high grazing above the mines last spring, when the snow first went back. Tamsin closed the hymn book on it gently and wrapped the book in its oilcloth again, and thought of Hesketh Fane in his shop on Gilt Street with the camphor and the dusty jars, and how he would hold it to the window.

Then Isla took her by the elbow and drew her to the door, away from the stove, and stood close, so that Tamsin could smell the woodsmoke and the herbs in her shawl. Her bright black eyes had gone quite still.

In Hollish, low, Isla told her that Edwin Leckie’s heart was failing and he would not see the summer, and that no lowlander was to hear it, not even him. She said it plainly, the way she had said thirty days and hold still: a thing that was so, and could not be mended by being sorry. She said that she had listened at his chest every day since the snow came and heard it, under the cough, a beat that stumbled and caught itself and stumbled again, like a clock with a worn pallet. He might have a few months. He would have them easier if he did not know.

Tamsin looked past her at Leckie in his chair by the stove. He had a little colour in his face for the first time since she had come, and he was telling Kit something about the clock in the corner, drawing its works in the air with his maimed forefinger, and Kit was nodding as if he followed it.
‘I give you my word,’ Tamsin said in Hollish. Her voice did not come out quite right, and she said it again. ‘I give you my word.’

Isla touched her cheek with one dry fingertip and went out into the snow without another word to anyone. Kit, at the window, had not understood a word. He turned when the door shut and looked at Tamsin’s face, and his own changed.
‘What did she say to you?’
‘Hill business,’ Tamsin said. ‘About the snow.’

She could see he did not believe her, and he did not ask again. Leckie looked up from his chair, pink and pleased and tired. ‘Come and sit by me, my dear,’ he said, ‘and tell me again what you will say to Corvin Slade when you lay that paper in front of him,’ and she went and sat beside him, and began.

scenes.title: The night visitor

beats: Tamsin wakes in the night to someone at the shutters of Bettany’s house, where she and Kit are sleeping now the road is open again.
Kit catches Dace Wilmot in the kitchen with a knife, prising at the clock case, and throws him out into the snow.
Kit cuts a hiding place for the key.
Late at night, Tamsin decides Pim must be warned at once that the Warden’s man has found them.

paragraphs: Tamsin woke in the dark and did not know what had woken her.

She lay still on the pallet by the stove in Bettany’s front room and listened. The fire had burned down to a red seam. The house ticked and settled around her the way old houses do in a hard frost. Upstairs, in the chair beside her brother’s bed, Bettany was asleep; she had sat up with him for nearly six weeks and slept now, she said, like a felled tree, and Isla’s draught held the old man down until morning. Across the room Kit lay on the settle under his coat, one arm hanging to the floor, breathing slow and deep. They had moved down to Bettany’s house two days before, when the road opened again and the Copper Kettle filled up with carters and ore-men, and Bettany, who had decided by then that she trusted them, said that they would sleep under her roof until they left. The sledge stood loaded in her yard. The dogs were bedded in her woodshed.

Then she heard it again: a scrape, very soft, at the shutters behind her head. Something thin was being worked into the gap between the boards, patiently, and drawn out, and worked in again a little lower down.

She did not move. Her heart was going so hard she thought the sound of it would carry through the shutters. The scraping stopped. She heard the snow creak once outside, under a weight, and then nothing. She counted to fifty. She had got to forty-one when the creaking came again, further off, going round the side of the house towards the back.
She slid off the pallet and crossed the floor in her stockings and put her hand on Kit’s shoulder. He woke the way the dogs did, all at once, his eyes open and his body still.
‘Someone’s at the house,’ she breathed. ‘They’ve gone round to the kitchen.’

He was off the settle without a sound, which in a man his size she would not have believed if she had not seen it. He did not light a candle. He took his knife from his belt and went down the passage in the dark with one hand on the wall, and she went after him, though he turned once and pushed the air at her with his palm to tell her to stay.

The kitchen was full of cold. The shutter over the sink stood open and the snow was blowing in through it, a thin white drift already lying across the flags, and by the light of it Tamsin saw a man on his knees in the corner by the dresser. He had the door of Bettany’s painted clock open and a long knife in his hand, and he was working the blade along the back of the case, feeling for the ledge, prising at the joints, his breath coming fast and white. He had got two boards loose already. The weights swung and knocked against each other in the dark like something trying to get out.
‘Get up,’ said Kit.

The man came up and round in one movement, and the knife came with him. It was Dace Wilmot. Tamsin knew the coat before she knew the face: the bottle-green had gone dull and stained with weeks of wear, and the face above it was thin and unshaven and not smiling at all. Word in the town was that the landlord of the Kettle had turned him out of his room a week ago, when the silver ran out, and that he slept in the back of the smithy for the warmth of the forge.
‘Stand away from me,’ Wilmot said. ‘I have no quarrel with you, Ansel. Stand away.’

Kit did not stand away. He walked straight at the knife, and when it came at him he took it on the thick leather of his forearm, and caught the hand that held it, and turned it until the blade dropped ringing on the flags. Wilmot cried out. Kit got him by the collar and the seat of his breeches, as a man lifts a sack of meal, and carried him across the kitchen and kicked the back door open with his heel.
‘You said accidents,’ Kit said. His voice was quite quiet, which was the worst of it. ‘At the Kettle. You said people have accidents in the snow. I’ve thought about it every day since.’

He threw Wilmot out into the yard. The clerk went headlong into the drift by the woodshed, and the dogs woke all at once and set up a roar of barking, Hob’s deep bay over all the rest. Wilmot floundered up, white to the waist, and stood swaying in the snowlight.
‘It’s a mild night,’ Kit said from the doorway. ‘Mild enough. You’ll live to the smithy. Come near this house again and you won’t.’

For a moment Wilmot only stood there. Then he turned and went, wading, up the slope towards the chapel and the dark streets beyond it, and did not look back. Kit shut the door and dropped the bar across it and leaned on it, and Tamsin saw that his sleeve was cut through and the leather under it scored white.
‘You’re hurt.’
‘He spoiled my coat. That’s all.’ He picked up Wilmot’s knife from the floor, looked at it, and threw it into the woodbox. ‘Is it there?’

She was already at the clock. The door hung open, the loosened boards stuck out like broken teeth, and the ledge behind the weights was bare. She knew it would be bare. She had stood in this kitchen two days ago and watched Leckie take everything out of it. Still she put her hand in and felt along the ledge to the end, and found only dust, and the cold, smooth wood.
‘Empty,’ she said. ‘He found it empty.’ Her hand went to her coat pocket of its own accord, and closed over the small hard shape through the cloth. ‘He’ll know now that somebody has it.’

‘He’ll know it’s you.’ Kit came and stood beside her and looked at the gutted clock. ‘And next time it won’t be a clock he goes through. It’ll be your pockets. A pocket’s the first place anyone looks, Tamsin. Every thief in the world knows that.’
‘Then where?’
He looked at her for a long moment in the snowlight from the window. Then he looked down at her boots, standing by the stove where she had left them to dry, and went and fetched the left one.

Kit cut a hollow in the heel of her left boot with his knife, and the key went into it, and he pegged the heel shut again. He did it at the kitchen table by a single candle, with the shutter nailed back across the window and the snow melting off it in a dark stain down the wall. First he prised off the heel, a lift at a time, with the point of the blade; then he cut out a little bed in the layered leather, a fraction bigger than the key, and tried the key in it, and cut a fraction more. She slipped the cord off and gave him the key bare. He laid it in its place and set the heel back over it, and whittled four pegs from a stick of kindling and drove them home with the handle of his knife. When he gave her the boot she could not tell, turning it over in the candlelight, which heel it was.
‘Walk in it,’ he said.
She pulled it on and walked up and down Bettany’s kitchen. She felt nothing at all except the boot.
‘It’ll do,’ Kit said, and blew out the candle.

He went back to his settle, but she did not think he slept, and she knew she would not. She sat by the stove with both boots on and her coat buttoned to the throat and the receipt lying flat against her heart, and listened to the house. Wilmot was in the town. Wilmot had no money and no lodging and nothing to go home with, and now he knew there was something to find, and who had it. The road down the valley was open. Every day carters went down it to the lake, and any one of them might carry a letter in his coat for the price of a drink, and a letter could go on from Dunmere faster than five tired dogs could follow it. She thought of the house on Gilt Street. She thought of Pim at the bench under the window, alone, who opened the door to anyone with a kind word and told everyone everything, and who did not know there was anything to be afraid of.

Pim must be warned. Not when she was home, not tomorrow on the road, but now, before any carter got down the valley with Wilmot’s letter and before the Warden’s man could think what to do with what he knew. But the last bird would not fly in the dark, and there was nothing to do but wait for first light.
She sat by the stove with her boots on and watched the shutters for the first grey.

scenes.title: The last pigeon

beats: At first light Tamsin sends word home to Pim from the Hollin road.
She says goodbye to Leckie, who presses her hands and tells her to give Slade nothing.
Isla blesses her at the edge of the town, and the sledge starts down the valley with five dogs.

paragraphs: Hollin was still dark when Tamsin went up through it with the basket on her arm. The night’s frost had glazed the steps between the houses, and the mine-heads breathed their smoke into a sky the colour of slate, with one thin seam of pallor along the eastern ridge. A dog barked once behind a door and thought better of it. She kept to the cinders in the middle of the lane and went carefully, because she was carrying the one thing in Hollin she could not afford to drop.

Kit had come with her, though she had told him there was no need. He walked half a pace behind with his hands in his armpits, and every so often he looked back towards the shuttered front of the Copper Kettle, the way a man looks at a dog he does not trust. Nobody had seen Dace Wilmot since Kit had put him out into the snow in the night. That did not mean he had gone.

The road out of Hollin left the town below the chapel and went down the valley in long white loops towards the head of the lake. At the first bend there was a mounting stone, and Tamsin set the basket on it and lifted the lid. The bird inside regarded her with one round orange eye, unimpressed, its feathers puffed against the cold. It was the smallest of the three Orla Finch had given her, a slate-blue hen with a white bar on one wing, and for a month it had lived on barley and grievance in the corner of an inn room.

She had written the note the night before by Bettany’s candle, on a strip of paper no wider than her finger, in letters that were her own again, small and upright. It was for Pim, but Pim would only turn it about and frown while the words slid off it like rain off a slate, so she had begun by asking Orla to read it to him, and then put down only what mattered. They were coming home. The Warden’s man was about and knew their business. Pim was to bar the shop at dark, open to nobody he did not know, and keep his own counsel. She had drawn a line under the last of these, knowing it was the one thing in the note her brother could not do.

Now she rolled the strip tight and slid it into the little tube on the hen’s leg, and the bird bore it with the air of a duchess being fitted for shoes. Then there was nothing to do but wait for the light. By daylight only, Orla had said, never after dark, and only ever home.
‘Will she find it, from here?’ Kit said.
‘She’ll find it from anywhere. It’s the whole of what she knows.’

The seam above the eastern hills widened and went the colour of weak tea, and then of brass, and the snow on the valley floor turned from grey to white. It was light enough. She lifted the hen out in both hands, felt the quick, hot heart going under the feathers, and opened her fingers. The bird went up in a clatter of wings, circled once above the chapel roof as if to take its bearings from the smoke, and then set off south down the valley, low over the snow, a small dark stitch against the white, smaller and smaller until she could not tell it from the specks that drifted in her own tired eyes. At first light she sent the last pigeon home from the Hollin road, and after that the basket was empty.
Kit picked it up and turned it over, as if there might be another one hiding in the straw.
‘Do we keep this?’
‘Orla will want it back,’ Tamsin said. ‘She counts them.’

They went down through the waking town to Bettany’s house below the chapel, where the sledge stood loaded in the lane and the dogs lay curled in the snow in their harness. Bettany had said her piece at the door before it was light, pressed a cloth of oatcakes into Kit’s arms, and gone off up to the well with her buckets, as if a farewell were a waste of good daylight.

Edwin Leckie was dressed and sitting by the stove. His white beard had been combed and trimmed square, and the effort of dressing had put a faint colour in his cheeks that might almost have been health. He had been better these last days. He coughed less. Tamsin looked at the colour in his face and knew what Isla had told her in the hill tongue, and she held her face quite still, and kept her word.
‘You’ll not sit,’ Leckie said. ‘I can see you won’t. You’ve the look of a woman with a road in front of her.’
‘I’ll stand a minute.’
‘You have them both? The paper and the other thing?’
‘The paper is in my coat,’ she said. ‘The other thing is under my heel.’

He nodded, and then he pushed himself up out of the chair, his left hand hard on the arm of it, and Kit made a movement towards him and stopped when Leckie glared. When he was upright he reached out and took both her hands in his. His were dry and light and colder than hers, and she felt the blunt tip of the forefinger that had lost its top joint to a lathe before she was born.
‘Listen to me,’ he said. ‘He will be courteous. He will be so courteous you will want to thank him for it. Give him nothing, Tamsin. Not a word more than you must. Not a penny. Give Slade nothing.’
‘I have nothing to give him,’ she said. ‘You’ve seen my purse.’

He laughed, and the laugh turned into a cough, and he held on to her hands through it rather than let go. When it had passed he said, ‘When the river opens I’ll come down. I want to see it going again. I want to stand in the square and hear it strike.’
‘We’ll keep you a place by the stove,’ Tamsin said, and her voice did not shake, and she was more proud of that than of anything she had done in Hollin.
He let her go. Kit shook his hand very gently, as though it were made of eggshell.
‘Look after her,’ Leckie said.
‘She does that herself,’ Kit said. ‘I only carry the luggage.’

The old man smiled into his beard. At the door Tamsin looked back once. He had turned his chair to the window and was sitting very upright in it, with the grey light on his face, and he raised his left hand to her, and she raised hers.

Isla Thorne was waiting where the last houses gave out and the road began its long drop to the lake. She stood in the middle of the track in her black shawl, small and bent and perfectly still, and the dogs, who were afraid of nothing, swung wide of her.

Tamsin went to her. Isla reached up and took her face between her two hands, the thumbs resting on her cheekbones, and looked at her for a long moment with those bright black eyes that missed nothing. Then she spoke the blessing in Hollish, the old one, the one Tamsin’s mother had said over her at bedtime when she was small enough to be lifted: hard ground under your feet, the wind at your back, and your own fire burning at the end of the road. She said it slowly, so that every word went in.
‘You have your mother’s mouth,’ Isla said, still in Hollish. ‘She never knew when to keep it shut either. Keep it shut now, until it is time to open it.’
‘I will,’ Tamsin said in the same tongue. ‘I have a great deal to keep it shut on.’
Isla’s eyes went past her, back up the lane to Bettany’s house, and came again to her face, and asked their question without a word. Tamsin gave her the smallest nod. Isla let go of her.
Then the old woman turned to Kit, looked him up and down, and said something short and decided.
‘What was that?’ Kit said.
‘She says your dogs are too fat and you are too thin, and she does not know which of you is feeding the other.’

Kit considered this. Then he pulled off his cap and said, in a Hollish so mangled that it was barely the language at all, the one of his two scraps of it that fitted, which was thank you. Isla stared at him, and then she cackled, a high delighted sound like a hinge, and flapped her hand at him to be gone.

Tamsin climbed onto the sledge and pulled the robe over her knees. Kit stepped onto the runners behind her, called up the dogs, and Hob rose out of the snow and leaned into his collar, and Fen and Bracken behind him, and Sloe and Rusk at the back. The traces came taut. The sledge jerked, slid, gathered itself. Five dogs took them down the valley road in the new light, with the smoke of Hollin hanging over the mine-heads behind them and the whole white country falling away in front, south, towards the lake and everything beyond it.

scenes.title: The pawnbroker

beats: At Dunmere Tamsin goes to the pawnbroker on the quay to buy back her father’s watch with the last of her money.
The pawnbroker sold it a fortnight ago; it is gone for good.
Kit says nothing, but buys her a hot pie and makes her eat it.
