At the lake’s edge the sledge sticks in a drift, and Tamsin hauls it free.

paragraphs: They had come down into Dunmere after dark, the last miles of the valley road done by the light of the snow, and slept at the Heron like the dead. In the morning the lake lay under a sky so pale it was hardly a colour at all, and the quay was busy with men knocking ice off ropes and shouting about the weather. Tamsin dressed by the window. Then she sat on the edge of the bed and counted the money in her purse for the third time since waking, as if it might have bred in the night.

It had not. It was the last of what she had, and it was enough, just, to buy back her father’s watch with the interest owing on it. She had worked the sum out on the road down and then worked it out again, because it mattered more than any she had ever totted up in the clock-house. There would be nothing left over for the road home. She found she did not care. She put the ticket in her glove, against the palm, where she could feel it.

Kit walked her along the quay without being asked. He did not say why, and she did not ask him. The pawnbroker’s shop was where she had left it a month before: a narrow front between a chandler and a fish-shed, with three brass balls over the door so tarnished they were nearly green, and a window full of other people’s bad winters. A fiddle with no strings. A christening cup. A pair of skates hung by their straps. A sword nobody in Dunmere could have had any use for.
‘I’ll wait,’ Kit said, and leaned on the wall beside the door, and folded his arms.

The bell over the door was cracked and gave a sort of cough as she went in. Inside it was dim and close and smelled of lamp oil and damp wool and old metal. The pawnbroker was the same small man in the same fingerless mittens, with his spectacles pushed up on his forehead where they could do him no good. He looked at her as she came to the counter, and she saw him place her, and she saw something close in his face like a shutter.
She laid the ticket on the counter and smoothed it flat, and put her purse beside it.
‘I’ve come to redeem this,’ she said. ‘A silver pocket watch. I can pay the interest. I’ve counted it.’
He did not pick up the ticket. He did not need to. He looked at it lying there, and then he looked at her, and pulled the spectacles down onto his nose as if they might help.
‘It says a fortnight, miss,’ he said. ‘On the ticket. A fortnight’s grace.’

‘I know what it says. I wrote my name under it.’ She heard her own voice go sharp and thin, the way it did when she was frightened, and could not stop it. ‘I was in Hollin. The snow shut the valley. Nobody came down that road for a month, not a sledge, not a man on foot. You know that. Everyone on this quay knows that.’

‘Nobody came up it either,’ he said, not unkindly. ‘I held it past the day. I held it three days more, because you had an honest face and I thought you’d come. Then I had a man in who wanted a watch and had the silver for it and didn’t argue.’

He reached under the counter and brought up a long book bound in green cloth, and opened it where a strip of leather marked the place, and turned it round so she could see. The entry was in a small, cramped, careful hand, not unlike her own. A date, a fortnight gone. A description. A price, which was rather more than he had given her for it. A line, ruled through. The pawnbroker had sold her father’s watch to a drover going down to the coast, and it was gone for good.

She read the entry twice. She was aware of the clock on the wall behind him, a cheap thing with a painted face, ticking loudly and badly; she could have told him it was losing four minutes in the hour, and that the crutch wanted bending.
‘What was his name?’ she said. ‘The drover.’

‘Didn’t give one. Didn’t ask. Big man, red muffler. Said he was taking beasts down to the coast and would sell them there and go on to the islands, maybe. He liked the lid, I remember. The way it shut.’ He took off his spectacles again. ‘I’m sorry for it, miss. I am. It was a good piece. It went to somebody who wanted it.’

That was meant as a comfort, and she took it as one, because the other thing to do was to say something cutting to a man who had held her goods three days past the day, and she was not quite so far gone as that. He had been within his rights. He had been, by the lights of the quay, generous. It made no difference at all.

‘Thank you,’ she said, and her voice came out small and polite and quite steady, like the voice of someone else. She picked up her purse and the ticket. Then she put the ticket down again, because it was no use to her now and she did not want to carry it, and went out with the coughing bell behind her.
Kit straightened off the wall. He looked at her face, and then at her empty hands, and then at her face again.

He said nothing. He did not ask, and he did not say he was sorry, and he did not tell her it was only a thing, or that things could be got again, or any of the other words that people use to fill a hole. He put one hand under her elbow and turned her along the quay, away from the shop, and walked her past the fish-sheds and the rope-walk to the end where a woman kept a brazier going under a bit of sailcloth and sold pies out of a box lined with straw.

He bought one. He paid for it out of his own pocket, and Tamsin, who could have told him to the farthing what it cost and what it ought to cost and what the woman cleared on each, found that she had nothing to say about it. He broke the crust with his thumb so the steam came up, and he put it into her hands, and stood there.
‘I’m not hungry,’ she said.

He looked at her. He looked at the pie. He folded his arms, the way he had outside the shop, and settled his weight like a man prepared to stand on that spot until the thaw came and the lake rose round his boots.

She ate it. It was mutton and onion, too much pepper, scalding, and the gravy ran down her glove. It was the best thing she had eaten in a month. The heat went down into the cold place under her ribs and sat there, and after a while it was easier to breathe round it. When she had finished he took the paper from her and screwed it up and dropped it in the brazier, and only then did he say anything at all.
‘Dogs,’ he said. ‘Light’s wasting.’

They harnessed up in the Heron’s yard, and Kit checked every buckle twice and every paw once, and Tamsin stowed the bags and the empty basket and lashed the load down tight, because her hands wanted something to do and the knots were a thing she could get right. Her purse sat heavy in her pocket. She thought, quite coldly, that it would pay for three nights’ lodging on the road south and fish for the dogs besides, and that she would spend it carefully, and that she would not think about the lid and the way it shut. Then they were out through the gate and down the slipway to the shore, Hob pulling for the open ice, the others yelping, the whole sledge rocking with their eagerness.

At the edge of the lake the runners sank into a drift. The wind had piled the snow there overnight in a long soft ridge between the shingle and the ice, and the sledge went into it nose first and stopped as if it had struck a wall. The dogs floundered to their bellies. Kit swore and heaved at the handlebar, and the load only settled deeper. Tamsin was off the sledge before she had thought about it. She waded round to the front, took hold of the harness beside Hob with both hands, set her boots and threw her whole weight forward and down, the way she had seen Kit do it a hundred times on the road north. Her right wrist flared, a hot hard ache up into the bone, and she set her teeth and did not let go. It held. She felt it hold. Something gave under the runners, the drift broke and slid, and the sledge came lurching up out of the snow and onto the lake ice with Kit running behind it, shouting, and Tamsin stumbling ahead with the traces in her fists and the dogs hauling past her, and the whole grey width of Lake Dun opening out in front of them to the south.

scenes.title: The thaw bell

beats: They come down to Corran Weir in a warm wind, with water lying on the ice.
Tamsin goes down to the edge of the ice below the weir and remembers the worst night of her girlhood.
The thaw bell begins to ring above the weir, and Brannock comes out to tell them the ice road is closed.
They will have to take the bank road the rest of the way.
card.goal: Get past Corran before the thaw.

paragraphs: The wind changed in the night, and by morning it was coming up the river from the south-west, soft and damp and smelling of earth, which was a smell Tamsin had not breathed since autumn. It was the wrong wind for the season and everyone on the ice knew it. By the time they had been an hour on the road, there was water lying on the surface in long grey sheets, an inch deep, then two, and the runners went through it with a sound like tearing silk. The snow on the banks had gone the colour of old sugar. Here and there a black stone stood out of it, steaming faintly. Rooks went over in ragged lines, calling.

Kit drove hard and talked to the dogs all the way, low and steady, as he did when he did not want her to hear what he was thinking. Hob ran with his ears flat. Every so often the whole team checked and splayed and went on again, and Tamsin felt through the sledge the faint, soft give of ice that had stopped being a road and was beginning to remember it was a river. She sat with her hands fisted in the robe and said nothing, because there was nothing useful to say and Kit had enough to manage.

They came down to Corran Weir a little before noon. She heard it before she saw it: not the roar it would make in spring, but a deep, muffled grumbling under the ice, as if something enormous had woken below them and was turning over in its sleep. Then the river bent and there was the weir itself, the long grey wall of stone across the valley, and the bell tower standing up on the west bank, and the weir-keeper’s house beside it with no smoke from the chimney. The sledge track left the ice and went up the bank there, past the house and round, to come down again below the weir where the road went on south. Kit took the dogs up it at a scramble and stopped them in the lee of the house, and stood for a moment with his hand on Hob’s back, breathing.
‘We’ll rest them a quarter of an hour,’ he said. ‘No more. I don’t like the look of the day.’

Tamsin knocked at the house. Nobody came. The tower door was shut, and when she tried it, it was barred from inside. She stood on the step and looked down the bank to where the river came out below the weir.

She had not meant to go down. She found that she was going, all the same, down the path the weir-keeper had trodden in the snow, past the woodstack, past an upturned skiff with its seams stuffed with tow, to the place where the bank ran out and the ice began. Below the weir the ice was always thin; everyone said so, Brannock had said so on the way north, standing exactly here with his pipe. Today it was not ice at all so much as a grey crust over moving water. She could see the water moving. Out in the middle there was a patch the size of a table where it had broken through altogether, and the river showed in it, black and quick and very cold, turning over and over on itself without a sound.

That was the place. Not that patch, perhaps, not to the yard; nobody could say to the yard. But that stretch of river, below that wall, under that sky. Somewhere there, eleven winters ago, the ice had given way under a sledge loaded with brass for the clock-house, and a man in a hurry had gone down through it, and the river had kept him until the spring.

She remembered the soup. That was the stupid thing. She had made soup every night that week, barley and leeks, because he was coming home and he liked it, and she had kept it hot on the back of the stove for three hours, stirring it so the bottom would not catch, getting cross. Pim was six. He had been put to bed twice and come down twice in his nightshirt to ask whether Father was home yet, and the second time she had let him stay, wrapped in a blanket on the settle, and he had fallen asleep there with his mouth open. She was thirteen and thought herself very nearly grown. And on the third night, a knock, late, too late for any honest caller. A man she did not know, a guild runner, with snow on his shoulders and his cap in his hands, who asked for her mother, and would not come in and would not look at her and said it all on the doorstep in about a dozen words, and the last of them was Corran. She had shut the door very quietly afterwards, so as not to wake Pim. She remembered that too. She had taken the pot off the stove and set it on the cold hearth, and it had sat there till morning.
‘Tamsin.’
Kit had come down the path behind her. He stood a little way off, not too near, the way he stood with a dog that had been hurt and did not yet know whether it wanted handling.

‘This is where,’ she said. She did not turn round. ‘Below the weir. He was coming down from Hollin with a load of brass for the house. He was late. He wanted to be home before the thaw. He wanted to be home before the bell.’
Kit said nothing for a while. Then he said, ‘How old were you?’

‘Thirteen. Pim was six. He doesn’t remember it. He remembers the funeral, in the spring, because it rained and somebody gave him a sugared plum. That’s all.’ She heard her voice, dry and level, a bookkeeper reading out a column. ‘I kept the soup hot. Three hours. Isn’t that a foolish thing to remember?’
‘No,’ Kit said. ‘I remember Davey’s boots by the door. Five years. I still see them when I come in.’

She turned then, and looked at him, and he looked back at her steadily, his grey eyes unhappy in his weather-burnt face, and he did not try to make anything better, and she was grateful to him for that beyond anything she could have put into words.
The thaw bell began to ring above Corran Weir, and from that hour the ice road was closed.

It was a great flat bronze voice that seemed to come out of the stone itself and out of the sky at once. It rolled down the valley and across the river and back off the far hills, and the dogs up by the house set up a howl, all of them together, and somewhere down the bank a flock of rooks went up out of the alders in a black burst, cawing. Tamsin felt it in her teeth and in the soles of her boots. She had heard of it all her life and never heard it. It went on and on, a stroke, a long humming pause, a stroke, and with every one of them she felt the river close like a door.

They went back up the bank together, quickly, not speaking. The ringing slowed and grew uneven and stopped, and the last of it hung in the air for a long time, fading, until there was only the grumbling of the water under the ice again. Then the tower door was unbarred from inside and swung open, and Old Brannock came out, stooping under the lintel, rubbing his palms on his breeches where the rope had burned them.
He saw her and stopped dead. His weathered old face did something complicated.

‘Well,’ he said. ‘Well, now. They told me you’d gone through above the weir. They told me Kit Ansel hauled you out like a bag of wet meal. I didn’t look to see you again this side of the summer, if I’m honest. I didn’t look to see you at all.’
‘He did haul me out,’ Tamsin said. ‘And here I am.’

‘Here you are.’ He came and took her by both arms and looked at her, and his eyes were wet, which might have been the wind. ‘I’m glad of it, girl. I’m right glad. I’ve had enough of your family going into my river.’
Then he let her go and turned to Kit, and was the weir-keeper again, the Wardens’ man on the river, with the law in his voice.

‘You heard it. That’s the bell, and it’s rung, and the road’s shut, by the Wardens’ order and the old law both. Nobody takes a runner on that ice again till next winter. Not you, not me, not the Warden himself. Where are you bound?’
‘Callowmere,’ Kit said.

‘Then it’s the bank road for you, the whole way, and God help you, for it’ll be a bog from here to the city gate in this wind.’ He jerked his chin at the slope behind the house, where an old track went up through the trees to the west. ‘Up there. Keep the river on your left hand and don’t come down to it for anything.’
Kit looked at the river for a long moment, and then at the slope, and then at Tamsin.
‘Bank road,’ he said, and went to turn the dogs.

scenes.title: The flooded road

beats: They take the sledge up the bank onto the old road along the west bank, the dogs floundering in wet snow.
Where the road dips past Ambry Fen, meltwater has flooded it from side to side, black and running fast.
There is no way round; they must get across.

paragraphs: The bank was steeper than it looked from below, and the snow on it had gone to porridge. Kit put the dogs at it from the bottom with a run and a shout, and they went up the first third in a rush, scrabbling, and then the sledge bogged and the whole team sank to their chests and stopped. After that it was inches. Kit hauled at the front with Hob, his boots skidding, and Tamsin pushed from behind with her shoulder against the load and her heels dug into slush that gave under every shove. Fen went down on her side and came up again plastered grey. Rusk sat in the snow and howled about it. It took them most of an hour to reach the top, and when they got there they stood with their hands on their knees and steamed like horses, and the dogs lay down where they stopped.

The old road along the west bank was hardly a road at all now. It was a long trough between hedges and stone walls, where the snow had drifted all winter and was now settling and sweating in the warm wind, rotten and wet and knee-deep in the hollows. Nobody had broken it since the autumn. In places the hedges met overhead and they went through tunnels of black thorn dripping with meltwater, and in places the walls had fallen and the road opened out across a hillside and the wind came at them sideways. The river lay on their left, far below, grey and sullen and closed to them. Tamsin did not look at it more than she had to.

They went on south. There was no other way to go. The dogs floundered and recovered and floundered again, and Kit stopped every half mile to clear the balls of ice from between their toes, kneeling in the slush and talking to each one in turn, and every time he did it Tamsin stood and shivered and counted, without meaning to, the hours of light that were left. The sky had come down low and yellowish. A fine rain began, so fine it hardly fell, only hung in the air and soaked everything it touched. Her coat grew heavy on her shoulders. She thought of the paper sewn into the lining and put her hand flat against the place, feeling for the small stiff square of it through the wet wool, and it was there.
‘How far,’ she said once, ‘to anywhere?’
‘Far enough.’ Kit wiped the rain out of his beard. ‘We’ll find a roof before dark if we’re lucky. If we’re not, we’ll find a wall.’
‘That’s a great comfort.’
‘I thought it might be.’

In the afternoon the road began to come down off the higher ground, in long shallow bends, towards the flat country where Ambry Fen lay between the hills and the river. In summer it would be reed and sedge and sky as far as one could see. Now it was a vast grey sheet of standing water, steaming, with the tops of the reeds poking through it in brown tufts and here and there a pollard willow standing up to its knees, and the noise of water everywhere, running and gurgling and dripping, in the ditches, in the drains, under the snow, as if the whole valley were emptying itself at once. Kit stopped the dogs on the last of the high ground and stood looking down for a long time without saying anything.
The low road ran straight into the water.

There was no mistaking where it went. The walls on either side marched down the slope and simply disappeared, side by side, into a broad black stream that came pouring off the fen from the right and across the road and away to the left, down towards the river, fast and smooth and humped in the middle where it ran deepest. Thirty yards across, perhaps. Perhaps a little more. On the far side the walls came up out of it again and the road went on, white and dry and climbing, as if nothing had happened. To the right there was only the fen, water and reeds to the horizon. To the left the bank dropped away to the river ice, and the river ice was closed by law, and in any case had begun to groan.
‘There’s no way round,’ Tamsin said.
‘No.’
‘Then we go back.’

‘To where?’ Kit said, not roughly. ‘To the weir, and wait? Wait for what? It’ll be worse tomorrow. It’ll be worse in an hour.’ He was uncoiling the long rope from the side of the sledge. ‘Over. Here, now, while there’s light.’

He took off his coat and gave it to her. He tied one end of the rope round the trunk of an old willow at the water’s edge, with a knot he tested twice with his whole weight, and paid out the rest behind him as he waded in. Tamsin stood on the bank and held the coil for him and could not breathe. The water came to his knees, then his thighs, then his waist, and in the middle it pushed at him so that he leaned upstream against it like a man leaning on a door, and went on, one slow step and then another, and came up out of it on the far side, streaming. He made the rope fast round the stump of a gatepost there and hauled it taut, so that it ran across the flood a foot above the water from the willow to the post.

Then he came back for the dogs. He took them over on the rope with the sledge behind, his hand in Hob’s collar, the water to his chest at the deepest. The dogs had to swim, paddling with their heads up and their eyes white, and the sledge lurched and turned and half floated, and once Sloe went under and came up again sneezing, and Tamsin made a sound she did not know she could make. Then they were out, all of them, shaking themselves on the far bank in great silver sprays, and Kit came back along the rope for her.

She could not swim a stroke, and Kit knew it; he made her loop the rope twice round her waist before she went in. It was the free end, the tail he had left at the willow knot, so that if her hands failed her she would hang from the tree and not go down the stream to the river. She tied it herself. Her fingers would hardly do it. He checked the knot and said nothing about how long she took.
‘Hands on the line,’ he said. ‘One and then the other. Don’t look at the water. Look at me. I’m on the downstream side. Nothing gets past me.’

She went in. The cold took her at the knees like teeth and she gasped, and then it was at her thighs, and then at her waist, and every inch it climbed was an inch she had sworn since she was seven years old that it would never climb again. She heard herself breathing in quick little sobs and could not stop. She held the rope. Left hand, right hand. The current leaned on her, steady and enormous and utterly indifferent, and her feet slid on stones she could not see, and the water came up over her ribs to her chest and pressed there so that she could not fill her lungs. Her right wrist burned on the rope. She did not let it go.

‘Look at me,’ Kit said. He was beside her, a solid shape between her and the long black run of the water, one hand on the rope just behind hers, not holding her, only there. ‘Look at me, Tamsin. Halfway. You’re halfway.’

She looked at him. She thought of being found in the spring. She took her left hand off the rope and put it further along, and then her right, and then her left again, and the bottom began, very slowly, to rise under her feet.

On the far side the dogs were barking at her. The water went down to her waist, to her thighs, to her knees, and then she was crawling up the bank on her hands with the rope still round her middle, and Kit was cutting it free with his knife, and she was shaking so hard her teeth knocked together and she could not have said one word if her life had hung on it.
He put his coat round her, over her own, and hauled her up onto her feet.
‘South,’ he said. ‘Keep moving, or you’ll stiffen. Walk with me.’
She walked with him. The road climbed out of the fen, white and dry, and the dogs went ahead of them, steaming, towards Callowmere.

scenes.title: Camp at Ambry Fen

beats: They camp in a ruined shepherd’s fold above the fen and dry out by a fire of dead willow.
Kit sees to each of his dogs in turn, feet and harness.
They talk late by the fire about what comes after Thaw Day.

paragraphs: They had come through the floodwater the afternoon before, and the whole of this day had gone in getting round the fen. Where the bank road had not drowned it had turned to a grey slurry of old snow and meltwater, and three times Kit had cut a way through the alder scrub with the hatchet while Tamsin held the dogs. By the time the light began to thin they had made perhaps nine miles, and the only shelter in sight was a shepherd’s fold on the rise above the fen, roofless, its walls tumbled to the height of a man’s waist along one side.
‘That’ll do us,’ Kit said, looking at it the way he looked at most things, as if it had agreed beforehand to be useful.

It did. The fold had been built into the slope, so that its back wall was the hillside itself, and in the corner where the stones still stood shoulder-high there was a dry patch the size of a kitchen table, floored with sheep droppings gone to dust. Tamsin kicked it clear while Kit unhitched. Along the edge of the fen the willows grew low and thick, and half of them were dead, left standing grey and brittle as kindling in a box. She went down with the hatchet in her left hand and came back three times with her arms full. The third time she found she had carried the bundle against her right wrist without thinking, and that it ached but did not give. She stood a moment in the dusk, closing and opening her fingers, before she went in.

Dead willow burned fast and hot and smelt faintly of the river. Kit built the fire against the back wall so that the stones would throw the heat out at them, and when it was going he drove two forked sticks into the earth on either side and slung a line between them, and over the line they hung everything that had been in the water. Her skirts. His leggings. The rope itself, the long one, which Kit had coiled with a care that made her look away. Steam rose off all of it into the dark.

She kept her coat on. It had dried on her through the day, more or less, and she turned herself before the flames like a joint on a spit until the lining was warm right through and she could feel, under her left arm, the stiff square of paper sewn between the cloths, flat and whole. She had felt for it a dozen times since the water. She felt for it again now, and Kit, coming back with the last of the willow, pretended not to see.
‘Still there?’ he said.
‘Still there.’
‘Good.’ He dropped the wood. ‘You were in to your chest yesterday. I thought you’d come out with nothing but your shift and a temper.’
‘I came out with the temper.’
‘You did.’ He was grinning at the fire. ‘I heard it from the far side. I’d say the whole of Ambry heard it.’

She had not known she was shouting. She remembered only the rope, and the cold closing round her ribs like a fist, and Kit’s hand on the rope beside hers the whole way across, never pushing, only there.

Kit saw to the dogs before he saw to himself. He had done it every night since Callowmere, in snow and in the yard behind the Copper Kettle and out on the open ice of the lake, and he did it now with his own leggings still dripping on the line and his beard silvered with damp. He brought the dogs one at a time into the firelight, and one at a time he took their feet in his hands.

Hob first, because Hob was the lead and would sulk otherwise. Kit sat on a stone with the big dog’s forepaw in his palm and parted the toes one by one, working out the little hard balls of ice that packed between the pads, and talking all the while in the low, foolish voice he kept for the dogs and for nobody else. ‘There’s my lad. There’s the best dog on the Varrow. Who brought us round the fen? Who never put a foot wrong all day?’ Hob bore it with the patience of a bishop at a christening, and when Kit let him go he came and lay down at Tamsin’s side with a groan.

Then Fen, who had cut a pad on something under the slush and had to have it washed with warm water from the pot and smeared with goose grease out of a tin. Then Bracken, whose harness had rubbed him raw behind the shoulder where the wet leather had shrunk; Kit cut a square from the end of his own scarf to pad it. Then Sloe, the dark one, who would not keep still and had to be held between his knees. Then Rusk, who was young and silly and tried to eat the goose grease.

Tamsin sat with her chin on her arms and kept her eyes on his hands. Kit went over the harness strap by strap, trace by trace, and when he came to the end of the line he stopped, and for a moment his hands were still on the last buckle, the small one, where there was no dog to fasten.
‘She’ll be eating Hanne Roe out of house and home,’ Tamsin said.

He looked up. ‘Tansy? She will. Mina’ll have her sleeping on the bed by now, and fat as a pudding.’ He set the little buckle down on the coiled trace. ‘It’s daft. Five dogs is a good team. Five dogs brought us down the valley and round the lake and through all this. I keep counting six.’
‘So do I,’ she said, which was true, and surprised her.
Rusk came and leaned his whole silly weight against Kit’s shoulder until Kit put an arm round him.

The sledge stood on its side against the wall of the fold where Kit had tipped it to keep the bed dry, and the firelight moved over the name burned into its backboard. She had seen that name every day for five weeks. She had slept against it, and she had never once asked.
‘Why the Long Patience?’ she said.
He was quiet so long that she thought she had trespassed. Then he reached out past Rusk and laid his palm flat on the backboard, the way a man lays a hand on a horse’s neck.
‘My mother used to say the lake has a long patience,’ Kit said. ‘So that’s what I called her.’
‘After Davey.’

‘After Davey.’ He took his hand away. ‘She meant you can cross Lake Dun a thousand times, and it doesn’t mind. It doesn’t want you. It only waits. It only needs you to be in a hurry the once.’ He scratched Rusk behind the ear. ‘She stood on the quay every morning that spring, till the ice went out and there was nothing left to wait for, and she’d say it to anyone who came and stood with her. I hated it then. I thought it was the sort of thing you say instead of crying.’
‘And now?’
‘Now it’s burned into my sledge, so I see it every morning when I hitch up.’ He shrugged his big shoulders. ‘So I’m never the one in a hurry.’
She thought of a sledge piled with brass coming down to Corran in the dark, and a man driving it who would not wait for morning. She did not say so. She thought Kit knew.
Later, when the dogs were curled nose to tail in a heap against the wall and the willow had burned down to a red bed, he said, ‘And after?’
‘After what?’
‘Thaw Day. Say it all goes the way it ought. What does Tamsin Orr do with herself when it’s done?’
She had not let herself think so far. For five weeks there had been only the next mile and the next night and the thing sewn into her coat.

‘Sleep,’ she said. ‘For a week. In my own bed, with the shutters closed. Then I’ll pay the coal merchant and the chandler and write it all down in a clean hand, and sit in the counting room with the window open the first day the river runs.’ She heard her own voice going soft and could not stop it. ‘And Pim will have the great clock going. He will, Kit. He’s been itching at it since Lantern Night. And the whole town will hear it strike, and they’ll know.’
‘They’ll know,’ he agreed.
‘And you?’

He considered the question as if it were a doubtful bit of ice. ‘The river’s shut now till the boats run. So I’ll wait in Callowmere till it opens, and then go home up the water and see how my girl’s getting on at Hanne Roe’s.’ He was smiling. ‘I’ve never seen inside a clock-house.’
‘It’s mostly dust and Pim.’
‘I’ll take my chances.’
Callowmere was a day south of them, downriver. She lay down at last with her back to the warm stones and her coat buttoned to her throat, and Hob shifted against her legs and sighed.
‘Go to sleep,’ Kit said. ‘It’s a long day yet to the gate, and the dogs won’t wait for you.’

scenes.title: The city gate

beats: The last day’s run south down the bank road, with Callowmere’s smoke ahead.
Kit eyes the smooth river ice beside the road, and Tamsin will not have it.
They reach the north gate as the light goes, and the Warden’s men search her.

paragraphs: They were away from the fold before it was light, the dogs stiff and grumbling in their traces until the first mile warmed them. In the night the wind had gone round into the north and the slush of the fen had set hard, so that the bank road rang under the runners like a pavement, and for the first time in two days they went at the dogs’ own pace and not the mud’s. Kit ran beside the sledge on the rises and rode the runners on the flat, and Tamsin sat in the bed with her satchel on her lap and the rug up to her chin and let the country go by.

It was farm country now. The last of the hills fell away behind them into long white fields walled with stone, and there were people on the road again, the first they had seen in days: a carter with a load of turnips who pulled his horse into the ditch to let the dogs pass and stared at them as if they had come down from the moon; two boys with a hand-cart of firewood, who ran alongside shouting until Kit growled at them; a woman at a farm gate who came out with a jug of buttermilk when Kit hailed her, and would take nothing for it.
‘You’ve come a long road,’ she said, looking at the dogs and not at them.
‘From Hollin,’ Kit said.

The woman whistled through her teeth. ‘In this? You’re madder than you look, and you look mad enough.’ She took back the empty jug and wiped its lip on her apron. ‘Callowmere by dark, if your beasts hold. Mind the hill by the gibbet. It’s gone to glass.’

The beasts held. Kit talked to them all the morning, in the same low run of nonsense he had used all the way from the north, and they leaned into their collars and went. The milestones began a little after noon, old guild stones half buried in the drifts, the miles cut deep into their faces, and Tamsin counted them down under her breath. Nine. Eight. At seven the road climbed the long shoulder of the gibbet hill, and she got out and ran beside the sledge to spare the dogs, slithering and gasping, her breath smoking, the cold catching at the back of her throat like a hand. At the top she stopped, bent over, and Kit stopped beside her.
‘There,’ he said. ‘Look.’

She had taken it for weather. Low in the south, where the white sky met the white land, there lay a long brown smudge that did not move as clouds move, and under it, when she screwed up her eyes, a darker line that was roofs. Callowmere’s smoke. The breweries and the dye-works and the forges of the wharf, and the ten thousand kitchen chimneys of the town, and somewhere among them the one chimney she cared about. She stood and looked at it until her eyes watered with the wind.
‘Is it the same?’ Kit said. ‘As when you left?’
‘It’s dirtier.’
‘That’ll be the thaw coming. Brings the smoke down.’ He clapped her on the shoulder, gently, on the left side, the way he had learned to. ‘Get in. You’re no use to me with your lungs out.’

She got in. The dogs went down the far side of the hill with their tails up, as though they knew, and perhaps they did; Hob had his nose high and kept turning his head to the south, and when the wind gusted towards them she caught it too, faint and sour under the clean cold smell of the snow: coal and tar and tanning pits, horses, the sea. Home, in other words. She had not known she could miss a smell.

The road widened. There were more carts, and a drover with a string of bullocks who swore at the dogs and was sworn at by Kit, and a coach-and-four that came up behind them with its horn blowing and threw slush over them all as it passed. Six. Five. The farms gave way to market gardens under snow, and the market gardens to the first mean cottages of the outskirts, with washing frozen stiff on their lines and children who stopped in their play to stare. Four. The smoke was no longer a smudge but a ceiling, and the sun had come down under it, and the afternoon had gone the colour of weak tea.

The light was going. Somewhere ahead of them in all that smoke Pim would be lighting the lamps in the workshop, or forgetting to, and she would have given a great deal to tell him she was nearly home, an hour or two now, no more; to have him hear it from her and not from the street. She had no bird left to send and no watch to tell the hour by; she judged it by the sun, low and red over the far hills.

Below the road on their left the river lay wide and still between its banks, grey-white and smooth as a table, with the old stakes of the ice road still standing in it in a crooked line, running straight down towards the city. Out there the thaw had not yet shown itself at all. There was no water lying, no crack she could see, nothing but a broad level road with nobody on it, going exactly where they were going.
Kit had seen it too. She knew he had, because he had stopped talking to the dogs.

‘It’d save us the best part of an hour,’ he said, not quite looking at her. ‘Straight down to the stand, and no carts, and no hills. The weir’s a long way back. It’s solid here. It’s solid as a floor; look at it.’
‘The ice is shut,’ Tamsin said. ‘The bell rang. We keep to the road.’
‘There’s not a Warden on the river to see us.’
‘I’d see us.’

He looked at her then. She did not know what her face was doing, but she saw him take it in, and she thought he was remembering a quay at Dunmere and a woman standing on it, and the name burned on his own backboard, and she saw him let it go.
‘The road, then,’ he said, and clicked his tongue to Hob, and they went on in the dusk with the river beside them all the way, smooth and grey and patient, and neither of them looked at it again.

They came to the north gate as the last of the red went out of the sky. The gate stood open, as it always did until the curfew bell, but there were lanterns lit under the arch, and a brazier, and more men about it than the two old gatekeepers she remembered: four of them, in the guild’s dark coats with the badge of the wharf on the shoulder. One of them stepped out into the road and held up his hand, and Kit stopped the dogs.
‘Miss Orr,’ the man said. He was young and heavy and he did not trouble to smile. ‘We were told you’d be along. The Warden asks that we look over your things.’
‘The Warden has no right to,’ Kit said.
‘The Warden has the gate, friend, and the gate has the right.’ The man did not take his eyes off Tamsin. ‘The satchel, if you please, miss.’

She gave it to him. It was the quickest way, and she was too tired to be clever. She stood in the lantern light with her hands at her sides and her face as still as she could make it, and felt the stiff paper lie flat against her ribs under her coat, and did not let herself so much as glance at the other place, the one Kit had made for her in Hollin by candlelight.
The Warden’s men turned out her satchel and her pockets at the north gate and found nothing.

They found a hairbrush, and a clean shift, and a stub of pencil, and her purse with four pennies in it, which the young man weighed in his hand and gave back with something like pity. They found her mother’s Hollish hymn book, and one of them held it up by its spine and shook it, and her heart stood still, but nothing fell out of it except a little dust, and the folded paper between its leaves held. They found a handkerchief and a twist of string and the crust of one of Bettany’s oatcakes, gone hard as wood, which she had kept for no reason she could have given. They laid it all out on the gatekeeper’s bench in a row and looked at it, and looked at her, and the young man’s mouth went thin.
‘That’s all?’
‘That’s all I own in the world,’ Tamsin said. ‘You may tell the Warden so. You may tell him I’m home.’

scenes.title: Home

beats: Tamsin comes home to Gilt Street after dark, and Pim throws the door open before she can knock.
Pim tells her what went wrong at the house while she was away, and about the letter from the Guildhall.
They sit up late by the kitchen fire.

paragraphs: Gilt Street was dark when they turned into it, every shutter closed, every shop asleep. The snow along the gutters had gone to grey slush and the cobbles shone wet in the light of the one lamp at the corner, and the dogs’ claws clicked and skidded on the stones so that Kit got down and walked at Hob’s head. They passed Hesketh Fane’s shop, with a candle burning in the room above and the old smell of camphor seeping out under the door into the cold, and Tamsin thought, tomorrow, and could not hold the thought. They passed the Marrables’ and the empty shop that had been empty since she was a girl. Then there was the clock-house, tall and narrow and black against the sky, with a line of yellow light under the kitchen shutter at the back.

She got down. Her legs had forgotten how to be legs. She went up the two steps to the door, holding the rail, and raised her left hand to knock, and before her knuckles touched the wood the door flew inward and the light came out and Pim came out with it.

‘I heard the dogs,’ he said. ‘I heard them from the end of the street, I knew it was you, nobody else would bring dogs down Gilt Street in a thaw,’ and then he had hold of her, the whole long gangling height of him, and her feet were off the step.
‘My wrist, Pim—’
‘Your arm!’ He put her down at once and stared at it. ‘Where’s the splint? What’s happened to the splint?’
‘Off. Weeks ago. It’s mended.’ It was nearly true. ‘Let me in, you great heron. Let me in and shut the door.’

He let her in. He let Kit in too, and shook Kit’s hand as if he had known him all his life, which was how Pim shook everybody’s hand, and asked him the dogs’ names, and forgot them, and asked again. Kit took the dogs round to the yard and bedded them down in the old coal shed with straw from the loft above the workshop, and when he came in Pim had the kettle on the fire and three cups on the table, and was talking.

He talked as he always talked, everything at once and all of it at the same speed. The workshop stove had smoked for a week and he had taken the whole flue down and found a jackdaw’s nest in it. Master Garrow had come for his tower clock, the half-finished one, and taken it away on a cart to the Penhallows’ house, very civil, until things were settled, he said. The coal merchant would not give credit any more and wanted coin. Somebody had put a stone through the shop window on the second night after she left, and Mr Fane had come round in his nightgown with a poker. And men had come from the guild, three of them, with a clerk and a lantern, and gone through the whole house from cellar to garret and written down every lathe and every file and every clock on the wall, and chalked numbers on things, and been very polite about it.
‘They chalked a number on Father’s bench,’ Pim said. His cheerful face had gone tight. ‘I washed it off. They came back and chalked it again.’
‘When?’
‘After the letter.’

He got up and went to the dresser and took it down from behind the clock on the shelf, where it had been propped all this while with its broken seal facing outwards: thick guild paper, folded in three, gone soft at the creases from handling. Orla Finch had read him the letter; he had carried it up to the loft, the way he carried up anything with writing on it. He held it out to her now and did not let go of it at once.

She did not need to unfold it. She knew what it said before she had broken the creases. The house of Orr & Leckie was summoned to the Reckoning on Thaw Day to answer for a debt owing to the guild and unpaid; failing which, the house and all within it would be forfeit, according to the custom. There was no sum. There did not need to be.

‘I told Orla it was a mistake,’ Pim said. ‘I told Mr Fane it was a mistake. I told the coal merchant, and the men with the chalk, and everybody at the Lantern, and they all looked at me the way Mr Fane looked at me.’ He sat down across the table from her. ‘It’s not a mistake. Is it?’
Kit got up quietly and said he would see to the dogs, though the dogs were seen to, and went out to the workshop, and she heard him moving about among the lathes, and then nothing.

She told Pim everything: the ledger, the debt, Leckie, the receipt. She told it the way she would have laid out a set of accounts, from the beginning, in order, leaving nothing out: the sewn page she had found on Lantern Night with the clock stopped over the city; the sum, which made him close his eyes; their father borrowing it that autumn for the great clock’s bells; Mr Leckie gone north with the second key; the road, the ice, the weir. She told him how their father had paid every coin back, in gold, a week before he died, and who he had paid it to, and what that man had done with it. She told him what Mr Leckie had kept for eleven years without knowing what it was. She did not tell him about Mr Leckie’s heart. That was not hers to give.
When she had finished Pim sat very still, which was not a thing she had often seen him do.
‘You knew,’ he said. ‘On Lantern Night. Before you went. You knew all of it.’
‘Not all of it. Not the gold.’

‘You knew there was a debt, and you told me you were going north to fetch Mr Leckie because of the clock.’ His voice cracked across the middle like a boy’s. ‘I said goodbye to you on the ice thinking it was about the clock.’
‘Pim.’
‘You told Mr Fane. You must have told him; he knew, I could see it in his face every time I said mistake. You told him and you told Kit. You told a man you’d known a week.’

‘Because you can’t keep a secret,’ she said, and hated how it sounded. ‘You know you can’t. You’d have had it up and down Gilt Street by breakfast, and the Warden would have known I knew before I was out of the gate.’
He did not answer that, because it was true, and they both knew it. He looked down at his hands on the table, long clever hands, black at the nails with brass and oil.
‘I’d have kept that one,’ he said at last. ‘For you. I would.’
She reached across and put her good hand over his, and he let her.

Then his head came up, and she saw their father in him so plainly that it was like a blow: the same jaw, the same fair brows drawn down. ‘He took Father’s gold,’ Pim said. ‘He took it and he let them say Father never paid. He let them look at us on Lantern Night. He sent men to chalk on Father’s bench.’ He was on his feet. ‘I’ll go over there now. I’ll stand outside his house and shout it till the whole town—’
‘Sit down.’
‘Tamsin—’

‘Sit down, Pim. Two days. We have the paper and we have the key and we have two days, and on Thaw Day we lay it in front of the whole guild in the daylight where he can’t make it go away. Not before. Not shouted in the street.’ She unbuttoned her coat and turned back the front of it and took his hand and laid it flat against the lining under her arm, where the stitches were. ‘There. Feel it.’
He felt it. His face changed.
‘That’s it?’
‘That’s it.’

They sat up long after that, by the kitchen fire, with the kettle singing and going quiet and singing again. Pim made toast and burned it and made more. He asked about the dogs, and Hollin, and whether it was true the old women up there spoke nothing but Hollish, and she told him, and some of it made him laugh. Through the wall she could hear Kit snoring in the workshop, on the bench by the stove where she had made him up a bed with every blanket in the house.
Somewhere past midnight Pim said, without looking up from the fire, ‘I want to go up the tower. Tomorrow. I want to see her.’

scenes.title: The loft

beats: Tamsin climbs to the loft to thank Orla.
Orla tells her the town says the Warden means to take the house on Thaw Day.
Pim goes up the Guildhall tower that afternoon and comes back sure he can make the great clock go.

paragraphs: The guild loft stood on the roofs above the wharf, a long shed of tarred boards on top of the old sail warehouse, and the way up to it was an outside stair that zigzagged up the brick in four flights, then a walk along the roof leads with a rope for a rail, then Orla’s ladder, all of it built, Tamsin had always thought, by a man who disliked visitors. The thaw had got into it overnight. Every tread ran with water, and the rail was slick with it, and the wind off the river came round the corner of the warehouse with nothing to stop it between there and the sea.
Pim went up ahead of her, two steps at a time, and waited at each landing, and pretended he was not waiting.
‘You needn’t,’ she said at the third landing. ‘I’ve climbed worse.’

‘I know. I’m resting.’ He was not even out of breath. ‘You should have seen me at the tower door when the clock stopped. After that first look I tried to get up those stairs six times the first week. The porter got so he’d shut the door when he saw me coming.’

At the top landing she stopped, whatever Pim might think of it, and held the rail and looked. The whole town lay under her in the grey morning, roofs and chimneys and smoke, and the wharf below with its cranes standing idle and its boats still locked in the ice, and the river beyond, gone a dirty yellow-white now, scored with dark seams where the thaw was working at it from underneath. Across the water the Guildhall stood up out of the roofs with its tower and its great dial, and the gilt hands on the dial stood where they had stood since Lantern Night, at seven minutes to midnight. From up here she could see a crack of light between the long hand and the short. It looked like something waiting to be said.

The loft door stood half open, and the noise came out of it before they reached it: that low, endless, comfortable sound of a great many birds talking to themselves in the dark. Orla Finch was inside with a scoop and a sack of grain, in her leather apron and her man’s hat, and she did not stop scattering when she saw them. She looked Tamsin up and down once, all over, the way she might have looked over a bird that had come in late from a hard flight.
‘So,’ she said. ‘You’re back.’
‘I came to thank you.’
‘Thank them.’ Orla jerked her chin at the perches. ‘They did the work.’

All three birds had come home to the loft safe. Orla took her along the perches and showed her each one, as though they were people Tamsin ought to be introduced to properly. The first had come in from Corran at dusk on the ninth day, with frost in her feathers and the light all but gone, and Orla had stood at the trap for an hour before her, cursing. The second had come from Dunmere in the afternoon two days after, straight as a thrown stone. The third had come only five days since, from the Hollin road, the longest flight of them all, and had dropped onto the landing board so tired she let Orla pick her up without a peck.

‘That one,’ Orla said. She put her finger out, and the little grey hen on the end perch looked at it with one orange eye and decided against it. ‘I’d not have given you odds on her. She’s small. But she knows where home is, I’ll say that.’
‘They all do,’ Pim said. ‘That’s what pigeons are. You told me.’
‘I told you they only fly home. I never said they all get there.’ Orla turned back to Tamsin. ‘Every one of yours did. I took each note down to him myself. He’ll have told you.’

‘He told me,’ Tamsin said, though Pim had not, in all that talk by the fire, thought to mention it, and she saw him go red. She put out her own hand to the small grey hen, and the bird considered it, and stepped onto her finger, light as a dry leaf, warm.

Orla watched this without comment. Then she put down the scoop and wiped her hands on her apron, and drew Tamsin a little way down the shed, away from the door and from Pim, who had found a broken latch on one of the coops and was crouched over it with his tongue between his teeth.
‘You’ll want to know what’s being said,’ she said.
‘I can guess.’
‘Guess, then.’
‘That the house is finished.’

‘That the Warden means to take it.’ Orla’s voice was low and flat. ‘On Thaw Day, in front of the whole guild, and make a show of it. That’s what they say on the wharf, and in the Lantern, and at the fish stalls, and up and down every stair in the town. They say he has a man ready to put in. They say he’s had his clerks over your house with chalk. They say the old clock will stand dumb until it’s his man who winds it, and that it serves Callowmere right for trusting an Orr.’ She looked at Tamsin from under the brim of the hat. ‘I don’t say I believe it. I say it’s what is said.’
‘And his man in the green coat?’
‘Not back. Nobody’s seen him since he went north after you.’ Orla’s mouth twitched. ‘There’s some on the wharf have noticed that, too.’

Tamsin stood with the bird on her finger and let it all settle in her. She had known. It was another thing to hear it in Orla’s plain voice, in this plain shed with the river wind coming through the boards.
‘Thank you,’ she said again, and meant something different by it.
‘Go home,’ Orla said, and took the bird back. ‘And come and tell me how it goes. Not before. I’ve no patience for hope.’

Pim went over the river to the Guildhall after their dinner, with a bag of tools on his shoulder and a pocketful of caraway biscuits for the tower porter, who had a sweet tooth and had known their father. Tamsin did not go with him. Kit had taken the dogs down to the wharf to beg scraps from the butchers’ stalls, and the house was quiet, and she spent the afternoon in the counting room behind the shop with the house’s books open in front of her, going over every column she had ever written, every figure, as if the guild might ask her for any one of them tomorrow and she must have it ready to hand.

It was a strange, slow afternoon. Every clock in the house was going, the long-case in the hall and the bracket clocks on the shop shelves and the little brass carriage clock on her own desk, and their ticking came up through the floors and walls to her like the sound of a house breathing in its sleep. Across the river, the great clock said nothing at all. She caught herself, again and again, lifting her head from the figures, and twice she went out into the yard to look across the river at the tower, as though she might see a small fair head come out at the top of it and wave.

The light had gone when Pim came back. She heard him on the stair, taking it at a run, and then he was in the doorway, oil to the elbows and a smear of black across one cheek, his hair standing straight up where he had pushed his hands through it, and his eyes so bright that she put down her pen.
‘What is it? What’s happened?’

‘A pin,’ Pim said. ‘In the escapement. The pin in the pallet arbor, sheared clean across. That’s all. That’s all it is. I had the lantern right in on it, and the broken end was lying in the dust at the bottom of the case. Somebody’s been up and looked and never seen it.’ He held up his thumb and forefinger, a hair’s breadth apart. ‘That big. That’s what stopped her. The hands are still standing at seven minutes to midnight, and every gear in her is sound, I went over every one, and all she wants is a pin.’
‘Can you make one?’
He looked at her as if she had asked whether he could breathe.

‘I can make one tonight. Give me the lathe and a bit of good steel, and an hour up there in the morning, and she’ll go.’ He was already turning away towards the stair, towards the workshop, pulling his sleeves higher. ‘She’ll go, Tamsin. I’d swear it on Father’s bench.’

scenes.title: Thaw Day

beats: On the morning of Thaw Day Tamsin and Pim set out from the clock-house for the Guildhall.
The streets are full; the whole town has come to see the house of Orr & Leckie fall.
At the Guildhall doors the guild’s porters let them through.

paragraphs: Tamsin locked the door of the clock-house behind them and stood a moment on the step, as if the house might have something to say before she left it. It said nothing. The shutters were up, the brass plate that read ORR & LECKIE shone where Pim had polished it at some unholy hour of the night, and through the workshop window she could see the long bench where Kit had slept these two nights under a horse blanket, the blanket folded square now at one end. Kit had gone out before light to see to the dogs at the livery and to keep a place near the front of the hall. He had said he would be there when they came in. She believed him. She had never yet known him say he would be somewhere and not be there.

Pim had put on their father’s good grey coat, which he had grown into at the shoulders and out of at the cuffs, so that a hand’s breadth of shirt showed whenever he moved his arms, which was always. He had wetted his fair hair and flattened it, and it was already rising again at the back like a hayrick in a wind.
‘You look like an alderman,’ she said.

‘I look like a heron somebody has buttoned into a sack.’ He tugged at the cuffs, which did no good at all. ‘Is it time? It feels like time. I can’t tell, with the clock stopped. I keep looking across the river at it out of habit, and it keeps telling me it’s seven minutes to midnight.’
‘It has told everyone that for forty-six days.’
‘Well, it’s wrong,’ said Pim, with the deep offence of a clockmaker, ‘and by tonight it won’t be.’

She did not answer that. She had no watch to tell the hour by, and had not had one since Dunmere; she judged it by the light, which lay thin and yellow along the gutters and had not yet climbed the fronts of the houses opposite. Mid-morning, or near it. The Reckoning sat at noon. They had time enough to walk the length of the town twice over, and she would have liked to, if only to put off arriving.

She felt the key with every step. Kit had cut the hollow in the heel of her left boot with his knife, by candlelight in Hollin, and pegged the heel shut again, and for a week she had walked on it without thinking. Now she could think of nothing else. It was a small hard knot under her left heel, there and gone, there and gone, like a second pulse. The Warden’s men at the north gate had turned out her satchel and her pockets and never once thought to look at her feet. The receipt was quieter. It lay sewn into the lining of her coat, over her ribs on the left side, and only when she drew a deep breath did she hear it, a faint dry whisper of paper against wool. The Orrs’ key hung from her belt where it always hung, where anyone might see it. Let them look. One key opened nothing.

The thaw had come in the night. Every eave on Gilt Street dripped, the snow in the gutters had gone grey and sullen and full of holes, and a brown thread of meltwater ran down the middle of the cobbles, carrying straw and orange peel towards the river. Hesketh Fane’s shutters were still closed, with no lamp behind them.

By the time they reached the foot of the street they were no longer walking alone. People came out of doorways and alleys and fell in behind them, or beside them, or ahead, all going the same way, down towards the west wharf and the bridge. Fishwives with their arms folded over their shawls. Apprentices let off their benches for the feast. A knot of guildsmen in fur collars who talked heartily about the weather and did not look at her at all. Children on their fathers’ shoulders, sucking barley sugar. It was a feast day, and Callowmere loved a feast. It loved a fall better. The whole town had come out to see the house of Orr & Leckie go down, and brought their dinners.
‘That’s her,’ someone said behind them, not quietly. ‘That’s the Orr girl. The bookkeeper.’
‘Poor lamb.’
‘Poor lamb nothing. Her father ran up the debt, didn’t he? Somebody has to stand for it.’

Tamsin kept her eyes on the street ahead and her chin where her mother had taught her to keep it. Beside her she felt Pim swell like a cockerel and draw breath, and she took his arm hard above the elbow.
‘Don’t,’ she said.
‘But they’re—’
‘I know what they are. Let them talk. They’ll talk differently by supper, or they won’t, and nothing you say this morning will make a farthing’s difference either way.’

He let his breath go, mutinous. A moment later he had forgotten to be angry and was waving to the cooper’s boy across the way, and calling good morning to the woman who sold hot chestnuts on the wharf, and asking a carter whether his near horse had thrown that shoe yet. Pim talked to everyone; he always had. It was the thing she loved best in him and the thing that had kept her awake half the night, staring at the dark.
‘Pim,’ she said, low. ‘Not a word. Not about anything.’

‘I know.’ He bent his head to hers, and his eyes were bright with the effort of virtue. ‘I haven’t told anybody. I’ve been not telling people all morning. I didn’t tell the baker. I didn’t tell the baker’s cat. I want you to know it has been very hard on me.’
In spite of everything she laughed, and a woman nearby turned to stare at her as though laughter on such a day were a kind of indecency.

The wharf was black with people. Above it, on the roofs, the guild’s pigeons were out on the morning air, wheeling and settling and wheeling again over the loft, and she watched them for a moment and found that her throat had gone tight. Then the crowd took them both and carried them on towards the bridge.

They crossed the Chain Bridge with the crowd, past the step where she had fallen. The bridge-wardens had scattered ash on the stone steps at the west end, but the ice still lay in the worn hollows like glass in a frame, and the press of feet had polished it. She went up with her right hand on the iron chain that served for a rail, gripping it hard, because she could. The bone had knit clean in Hollin. It ached now and then of an evening, a dull remembering ache, but it held. On the fourth step she felt her boot slide an inch on the old ice and her heart go over, and then Pim’s hand was under her elbow, and they were up and on the planking and walking out over the river.

The river was going. All winter it had been a road, white and hard and ringing under the runners, and now it was something else: a grey, sodden, sulking floor, cracked into great plates with black water showing in the seams between them. The ice-road stand below the bridge was deserted, its flags taken down since the bell had rung at Corran, and the snow round it was trodden to slush and empty. Upriver, north, the way she had come, the ice ran away grey between the banks until the haze hid it. She looked at it once and then did not look again.

‘I made the pin last night,’ Pim said. He patted his coat pocket. ‘While you were asleep. Good steel, and I turned it twice, because the first one was a hair too fat. The old one sheared clean through, you know. Right in the escapement. Somebody ought to have looked at it years ago.’
‘Somebody is looking at it now.’
‘Somebody,’ said Pim, ‘is going to make it go.’

The Guildhall square on the east bank was packed from wall to wall, and the noise of it came up off the stones like heat. Over all of it stood the tower, and in the tower the great dial, its hands still fixed at seven minutes to midnight. Pim looked up at it the way a man looks at a sick friend through a window. At the top of the Guildhall steps the guild’s porters stood in their russet livery with their staves crossed, holding back the crush, and a sour murmur rose as the Orrs pushed through to them.
‘Name and house,’ said the nearest porter, a big slow man with a broken nose.
‘Tamsin Orr. Orr & Leckie, clockmakers, of Gilt Street. We are summoned.’

The porter looked at her a moment, not unkindly, and then lifted his staff. The other porters drew back their staves to let them through, and closed them again behind, and the doors of the Guildhall stood open on a dimness that smelled of beeswax and wet wool. She set her left heel down on the flagstones of the threshold, felt the key bite, and walked in.

scenes.title: The Reckoning

beats: The guild sits in the long room under the stopped clock, and the Warden opens the Reckoning.
Slade reads out the house’s debt and calls on Tamsin to pay or forfeit.
Tamsin asks for the vault to be opened, turns both keys, and lays her father’s receipt before the guild.
Dace Wilmot stands up and says he will swear against the Warden.

paragraphs: The long room of the Guildhall ran the whole depth of the building beneath the tower, and the great clock was overhead, somewhere above the painted ceiling, its wheels standing where they had stood since Lantern Night. Pim said that when it went you could hear it in here, a slow iron step coming down through the plaster like a man pacing an upper floor; today there was nothing to hear at all, and the quiet sat on the room like snow on a roof. The light came in grey and greenish through the tall windows down one side, and fell across the long table under the clock, where the books of every house in the guild lay stacked in their bindings, waiting.

Her father’s ledger was among them. She had given it up at the door to an under-clerk who wrote her name in a list and would not meet her eye, and she could see it from where she sat, its spine cracked where she had cracked it on Lantern Night.

The benches filled. The guild sat by houses, as it had always sat, black gowns and fur collars and the flat bright faces of men who have come to see something happen to someone else. The summoned bench stood apart at the front, a little below the rest, and she and Pim sat on it alone. Behind them a wooden rail crossed the room from wall to wall, and behind it the townsfolk stood packed to the back doors, coughing and craning.

Kit was where he had said he would be. He stood at the rail directly behind her, a head taller than the men around him, his beard combed for the occasion. When she turned he gave her one nod, slow and steady, and his grey eyes said what they had said on the ice above Corran Weir and on the flooded road: I have the rope. She turned back to the front with her heart a little quieter.

Pim could not keep still. He jiggled one long leg until she put her hand on it, then whispered that the plaster was cracked right under the going train and wanted seeing to, and then was quiet for nearly a minute.

With the great clock stopped, the guild had sent across to the harbour chapel for the hour. When its thin bell came over the water striking noon, the beadle struck the floor three times with his staff, and the room hushed. From the high chair under the clock the Warden declared the Reckoning open, in the old words, and the beadle struck the floor again.

Then the houses were called, one by one, in guild order, and their books laid open. Tamsin, who had kept books for eleven years, could not help following it with a kind of professional interest even now. Merrow’s, chandlers: clear. Pellow and Daughter, ropewalk: clear, once a small sum was paid there and then out of a purse, to laughter. Old Master Haverill, eldest of the guild, a chronometer-maker with a voice like a heavy door, read out each balance and each verdict, and the room grew bored and then, as the list wore down, less bored.
‘Orr & Leckie,’ said Haverill. ‘Clockmakers, of Gilt Street.’
Tamsin stood up. Her legs held. The room went so quiet that she heard the drip of the thaw from the high windows.

Slade rose and went to the lectern. He did not hurry; he never did. He was tall and thin in his black gown, and he leaned on his silver-headed cane at every second step, favouring the stiff right knee that the wharf steps had given him long ago, so that his slow progress up the room had the stateliness of a procession. At the lectern he propped the cane against the wood, opened the guild’s great book at a place already marked with a ribbon, and looked down the hall. His eyes were pale, a washed and wintry blue, and they rested on Tamsin for exactly as long as courtesy required.

‘The house of Orr & Leckie,’ he read. His voice was low and dry, and it carried to the back doors without his seeming to raise it. ‘In the autumn eleven years past, Aldous Orr, master of that house, borrowed of the guild four hundred and twelve crowns against the house and its goods, to pay for the bells of this tower. No repayment stands entered against that sum. The debt has lain unpaid eleven years, and the guild has been patient.’ He lifted his eyes. ‘Mistress Orr. Can the house pay four hundred and twelve crowns this day, before this guild? Or does it stand forfeit?’
‘The house has paid,’ Tamsin said. It came out higher than she meant, and she stopped and began again, lower, the way she would read out a column to a customer who did not believe it.
‘It paid eleven years ago, in full and in gold, the week before my father drowned. It paid into the treasurer’s hand. I ask the guild to open the vault.’
The murmur went round the room like wind in barley. Slade waited for it to pass, as patient as the guild.

‘The vault opens only to two keys turned together, Mistress Orr, as every child in Callowmere knows. You wear one. The other went north this autumn with Master Leckie, who has not seen fit to come home and answer for it.’ The smallest smile. ‘Unless you mean to tell us he is here.’
‘He is in Hollin,’ said Tamsin. ‘His key is not.’
Haverill looked at her a long moment over his spectacles, and then said that any house might ask the vault opened at the Reckoning, it was the old right, and he would go down himself.

They went down by the narrow stair behind the dais: Haverill with a lantern, two senior guildsmen, Slade on his cane, one step at a time, his stiff knee taking each stair like a hurdle, then Tamsin, and Pim behind her breathing hard. The vault door stood at the bottom in a cold that smelled of iron and old stone, with two keyholes a hand’s breadth apart. Tamsin unhooked the Orrs’ key from her belt and set it in the left-hand lock. Then she sat down on the bottom stair, pulled off her left boot, and prised the pegged heel open with Pim’s penknife while four grown men watched her in silence. She drew Leckie’s key out of the heel of her boot, and the two keys turned together. She turned them herself, one in each hand, and her right hand did not shake.

Inside, on iron shelves, stood the guild’s chests and, above them, the old treasurers’ books in their row. Haverill took down the one for that year and opened it under the lantern. There was the loan, four hundred and twelve crowns to Aldous Orr, entered in a fine sloping hand. There was no repayment. And at the foot of every page, in the same hand, under the guild’s seal: C. Slade, Treasurer.
Back in the long room she unpicked the lining of her coat with Pim’s knife, stitch by stitch, while the whole guild leaned forward, and laid the receipt on the long table beside the open book.

‘Paid in full, four hundred and twelve crowns in gold, received of Aldous Orr,’ Haverill read aloud, slowly. ‘Signed, C. Slade. Sealed, and dated eleven winters ago.’ He laid it against the foot of the page, and looked at the one and then at the other, and said nothing at all, which was worse than anything he might have said.

‘A paper eleven years in a frightened old man’s drawer,’ said Slade into the silence. ‘Hands may be copied. Seals may be stolen. The guild will not overturn its books on the word of a ruined house and a runaway.’
Dace Wilmot stood up at the back of the hall and said that he had heard the Warden boast of Aldous Orr’s gold, and would swear to it.

Every head turned. He came forward to the rail, lean as a rake, in the same bottle-green coat, though it hung on him now, and his cuffs were still stained with ink. The polite smile was gone. Tamsin had never seen his face without it, and it looked raw.

‘I served the Warden nine years,’ he said. ‘He sent me north after Mistress Orr, and when the snow came down on Hollin he left me there without a penny, to freeze or to beg. I begged. I have had leisure to think.’ He looked at Slade, and Slade looked back, and neither of them blinked. ‘Three winters ago, at the wharf-dues supper, he told me in his cups that the clockmaker had brought him four hundred and twelve crowns in a leather bag, and that the river had saved him the trouble of entering it.’

The room broke like ice. Pim had both her hands and was crushing them; behind her Kit gave a great bark of a laugh; and at the lectern the silver-headed cane slid sideways and fell to the boards with a crack like a pistol shot, and nobody stooped to pick it up.

scenes.title: The great clock

beats: The guild strikes the debt from its books and orders the Warden’s own accounts opened.
Slade leaves the hall on his cane, and nobody looks at him.
Pim climbs the tower, and at the stroke of four the great clock starts again.

paragraphs: It took Haverill a long while to get silence, and he got it in the end by the simple method of standing up and waiting, a small old man in a black gown with his hands folded on his stomach, until the guild grew ashamed of itself. When the room was still he did not make a speech. He said only that the guild had heard the book, and the receipt, and the clerk, and he would put the question.
‘Is it the guild’s will that the debt of the house of Orr & Leckie be struck from its books, as paid?’

The ayes came down from the benches like a wave coming in over shingle. Tamsin heard them and did not quite believe them, and then the under-clerk who had taken her father’s ledger at the door was dipping his pen, and drawing the guild’s great book towards him, and ruling a line through the entry, steadily, from margin to margin. She had ruled lines through debts a thousand times, in her own neat hand, by candlelight, in the back room on Gilt Street. She had never seen one so beautiful. The ink lay wet and black across four hundred and twelve crowns, and then the clerk blotted it, and it was dry, and it was done.

‘And is it the guild’s will,’ said Haverill, in exactly the same voice, ‘that every book the Warden keeps, the guild’s accounts and the wharf dues together, be opened and laid before this guild within the week, and that the Warden keep none of them meanwhile?’
The ayes came again, louder.

Slade stood at the lectern through both. He did not argue. Tamsin had thought he might, and had braced herself for it, the low dry voice and the reasonable words, and it did not come. He looked down at his cane where it lay on the boards. No one moved to give it to him. After a moment he bent for it himself, slowly, the stiff right knee locked straight and the other taking all his weight, and she saw his hand grope once along the floor before it found the silver head. Then he straightened.
‘As the guild pleases,’ he said, with perfect courtesy, to no one.

He came down from the dais and walked the length of the long room. It was a long way. The cane struck the boards and the stiff leg swung after it, tap and drag, tap and drag, and the sound was very loud, because nobody spoke. Nobody looked at him either. The guildsmen looked at their hands, at the ceiling, at the books on the long table, at the windows; the townsfolk at the rail found that they had something to say to their neighbours, low, or something in their pockets to look for. Tamsin had thought that she would want to watch him go. She found she did not. She looked at the line in the book and listened to the cane, tap and drag, all the way down the room and through the rail and out at the back doors, where the noise of the square swallowed it. She thought of her father hurrying south on the ice to beat the bell, with the receipt safe in Leckie’s drawer and the gold already gone into another man’s pocket. Then she put the thought away, carefully, the way she would close a ledger, and turned round.
Pim was already on his feet.
‘Master Haverill,’ he said, and his voice cracked in the middle, so that he had to say it twice. ‘Master Haverill. May I go up?’
The old man looked at him over his spectacles, and something moved under the white eyebrows that might have been a smile.
‘The guild,’ he said, ‘has been waiting forty-six days for somebody to ask.’

Pim went down the room like a hound let off the leash. He had his tools in a roll inside the grey coat, and the new pin in his pocket, and he had them all out on the bench by the tower door before Haverill had finished drawing his watch from his waistcoat. It was a fine old chronometer, the case worn smooth with thumbs.
‘Twenty minutes to four,’ said Haverill. ‘Can you do it by the hour?’
‘I can do it by the hour,’ said Pim. ‘Somebody stand at the bottom and shout the minutes.’
Kit said he would stand at the bottom, and did, his great shoulders filling the tower doorway. Tamsin went up after Pim.

The tower stair was a stone screw, worn hollow in the middle of each tread by three hundred years of boots, with a greasy rope looped through iron rings for a rail. She climbed with her right hand on the rope and her left on the wall, and the cold came down the stair to meet her. Halfway up there was a narrow landing with a slit window over the square, and an open doorway into the clock chamber, and there she stopped. She could see from there. And she would not have gone farther; it was Pim’s place, not hers. She had been up here once before, at twelve years old, the week the clock was finished, with her father’s hand on her collar to keep her back from the wheels. He had lifted her to look at the escapement and told her it was the heart of the thing, that everything else only did as it was told. She had thought him very grand. She had not known then that he had borrowed for the bells, or that he would be dead within the year.

The works of the great clock filled the chamber like the bones of some enormous animal: the iron frame, the going train and the striking train side by side, wheels upon wheels, each tooth as big as her thumb, and the long pendulum hanging dead still down its shaft into the dark below. Her father and Edwin Leckie had built it twelve years ago, and had borrowed for its bells, and the bells hung above in the dimness, silent and green. Pim was in among the wheels with a lamp, talking to the clock. She could hear him. He was telling it that it had been very brave and that this would not hurt.
‘Ten minutes!’ came Kit’s voice up the stair, booming round and round the stone.

Pim drew out the old pin, sheared clean in two, and dropped the halves into his pocket. He fitted the new one, tapped it home with a small brass hammer, three light taps, and sat back on his heels to look at it. Then he wound. She watched him lean his whole weight on the winding handle, the gangly length of him folding and straightening, and heard the ratchet clack, and the weights go creaking up out of the dark. Then he set the hands, working the motion through until the great dial outside should stand at four exactly; and then he put a wooden wedge into the escapement to hold it, and set his hand on the pendulum rod, and waited.
‘Two minutes!’ called Kit. Then, ‘One!’ Then, ‘Haverill says now!’
Pim lifted the detent on the striking train.

The first stroke went through the tower like a blow to the chest, and dust came sifting down from every beam. Out in the square the roar of the crowd stopped as if a hand had closed on it.
