The second stroke. The third. Tamsin had her hands pressed flat to the cold stone of the doorway and did not know it. On the fourth Pim pulled the wedge and gave the pendulum its push, and the long rod swung out into the dark and back. At the fourth stroke the great clock of Callowmere began to go again.

Below the slit window the square went up in one great shout, and then another, and caps flew, and somewhere a child was screaming with delight and would not stop. Over all of it, under all of it, came a sound she had not heard since Lantern Night and had not known she was listening for: slow, deep, unhurried, the beat of the escapement, as steady as a heart.
Pim turned round in the lamplight with soot on his nose and his face shining.
‘Listen,’ he said. ‘Tam. Listen to it.’

scenes.title: Snowbells

beats: Kit says he will stay in Callowmere until the river is open, and then go home to Dunmere, if she will come and see the lake in summer.
Tamsin calls on Hesketh Fane at his shop on Gilt Street.
Walking home, she hears the great clock strike noon across the river.

paragraphs: On the morning after Thaw Day the river began to move. Tamsin heard it before she saw it: a long low groaning in the dark before dawn, like a great beast turning over in its sleep, and then a crack that rattled the panes on Gilt Street. By the time she and Kit came down to the river stairs below the west wharf the whole grey floor of the Varrow was on the go, breaking into plates and rafts and slabs as big as barn doors, grinding past one another on their slow way south to the sea. Gulls rode on them. Black water opened between them and closed again. Where the ice-road stand had been there was nothing at all.

They sat on the third stair from the top, because the lower ones were awash. Kit had brought a paper of hot chestnuts from the woman on the wharf, and he peeled them with his thick fingers and passed her the best ones without comment, as he had passed her the best of everything all these weeks.

‘I’ll stay till the river’s open,’ he said presently. ‘Properly open. Boats running, and the bank road dried out, so the dogs needn’t swim for it. Your Pim says I can keep the bench in the workshop if I mind his lathes. And I’ve told the livery I’ll pay them in firewood, which they think is very funny.’ He split a chestnut and blew on it. ‘Then I’ll go home to Dunmere. Hanne Roe will have spoiled Tansy past mending, and the others are pining for her, though Hob would die before he said so.’
‘That will be a while yet,’ said Tamsin. ‘The road.’

‘Three weeks. Four.’ He looked out at the moving ice and not at her. ‘The lake’s a different creature in summer, you know. You’d not know it. Blue as a jay, and the hills standing upside down in it, and the boats out after perch, and the light going on till near midnight. I thought, if you’d come up and see it. In the summer. When the books are done, or whenever bookkeepers get let out.’

She was quiet. She thought of the lake as she had last seen it, white and endless, with Davey somewhere under it these five years, and of the millrace at Ambry, and of her own cold terror of any water higher than her knees. He knew all of that. He had pulled her out of the river by a dog-line and brought her across a flooded road on a rope, and he was asking anyway, with his eyes on the ice.
‘I shan’t go in it,’ she said at last. ‘Not above the knee. Not for you, nor for all the perch in Dunmere.’
‘No one asked you to go in it. You can sit on the jetty.’
‘And do what?’
‘Keep the accounts,’ said Kit, ‘and tell me I’m charging too little.’ He turned then, and grinned at her through his beard. ‘You’ll come, then.’
‘I’ll come,’ said Tamsin. ‘In the summer.’ And then, because her face had gone hot in the cold wind and she would not have him see it, ‘Give me the last chestnut. You’ve had more than your share.’

Fane’s shop smelled of camphor and cold ashes, as it always had. The little bell over the door gave its cracked jangle as she came in, with Kit stooping under the lintel behind her, and a voice came from somewhere among the shelves of jars and bundles and stoppered bottles.

‘Shut it, shut it, the cold gets into the liquorice,’ Hesketh Fane said, before he saw who it was. Then he came out from behind his counter, thin and stooped and blinking, his white whiskers standing out on either side of his face like the tufts of an owl, and took both her hands in his.

‘I heard it,’ he said. ‘The clock, yesterday. I was sitting just there, grinding orris root, and it struck four, and I am not ashamed to tell you I wept into the mortar. It will taste of salt for a month.’ He peered past her. ‘And this is the sledge driver. Come in, come in, you are letting out the warm. There is no warm, but you are letting it out.’
Kit came in and stood among the jars with his elbows tucked in, like a bear in a china shop, sniffing the camphor with deep suspicion.

Fane did not let go of her right hand. He turned it over, palm up, and then took her wrist between his thumbs and fingers and pressed along the bones, slowly, the way he had pressed them two days after Lantern Night, when she had come in white and sick with the arm held against her chest. She held still for him. He bent the hand back, and forward, and from side to side, and watched her face while he did it.
‘Does that hurt?’
‘No.’
‘That?’
‘A little. Of an evening.’

‘Of an evening it will, for a year or so, and then it won’t.’ He let her go, and looked pleased in the way he only ever looked over a bone well set, his whole thin face lifting. ‘That is a clean knit. Clean as a whistle. Who cut the splint?’
‘Isla Thorne. In Hollin. She cut it with a knife she uses for everything, and then she made me squeeze a ball of beeswax every night for a fortnight.’
‘Did she now.’ He nodded slowly. ‘The hill healers. Elsbet used to say they could set a bone by singing at it. I always said that was nonsense. I begin to wonder.’

Tamsin opened her satchel and took out her mother’s Hollish hymn book. It was small and black and soft at the corners, and it fell open of its own accord at the place where it had been pressed shut for ten days, since Hollin. She gave Hesketh Fane the snowbell from Hollin, pressed flat and still faintly blue, and he held it a long while without speaking.

It lay across his palm, a single nodding stem with its one drooping bell, thin as paper now and nearly transparent, the blue of it only a breath, like the colour left in a winter sky after the sun has gone. It had come to her between two leaves of paper, from Isla’s own hands. Kit, by the door, had gone very still.
‘You said you would bring me one,’ Fane said at last. His voice was not quite steady. ‘I thought, when you went, that you would have a great deal else to think about.’
‘I did. I brought it anyway.’

‘So you did.’ He looked down at it. ‘She used to tell me about these. Every winter, near the end, when she was tired of the town. How they came up through the last of the snow on the hillsides above Hollin, whole slopes of them, so that you could not tell where the snow stopped and the flowers began. I meant to take her to see them one spring. We kept putting it off. There was always the shop.’ He was quiet a moment. ‘Three winters now. Thank you, Tamsin.’

He laid it in a shallow box lined with a scrap of white linen and set the box on the shelf behind the counter, between the jar of camphor and the brass scales, where he could see it from his stool. Then he blew his nose, at length, and turned on Kit as though nothing had happened.
‘And you, sledge driver. Are you going back to your lake?’
‘When the river’s open,’ said Kit. ‘Not before.’

‘Not before,’ Fane repeated, and looked from Kit to Tamsin and back again over his spectacles, and said nothing more, in a manner that said a great deal. Tamsin bought a twist of liquorice root she did not want, to give her hands something to do, and he would not take her money.

They walked home up Gilt Street in the thin noon sunshine, Kit beside her with his hands in his pockets, the gutters running and the shopfronts dripping and somebody singing in an upper room. The clock-house was only a few doors along. She had her hand on the latch when it came to her across the river from the Guildhall tower, clear and deep and unhurried over the roofs and the moving ice: the great clock striking noon. She stood on the step with her hand on the door and counted every stroke.
